paragraphs.text: This concerns the holy, great and ecumenical synod of bishops that was assembled at Nicaea from practically every province of the Roman world, and from Persia as well. It met by the grace of God and by decree of our God-beloved and pious emperor Constantine, in defense of the apostolic and orthodox faith against the wicked and impious doctrines of Arius, the enemy of God. Long, long ago, while I was still living in my father's house, I read everything that was said, done and formulated at that virtuous and holy synod. I found it all written in a very ancient book on parchment that contained everything without omission. These parchments had belonged to the divine and celebrated Dalmatius, who had been archbishop of the holy catholic church of the splendid metropolis of Cyzicus. They had then passed to the man who was once master of our household, my father according to the flesh, who had been honored with the rank of presbyter in that same most holy church. I came upon this sacred book and spent a great deal of leisure on it. I could not keep everything in memory, for no human being could carry that boundless ocean of material by heart. But I noted down a great many things. I noted the doctrines of our holy fathers and bishops, their teaching of sound doctrine, and their counter-arguments against the Ariomaniacs. I noted the written refutations of the blasphemy that the abominable Ariomaniacs uttered against the Son of God, and indeed against the Holy Spirit too. I noted the objections that the philosophers hired by Arius raised against the bishops, and the clear answers our side gave them from the teachings of Scripture against those same sophistries. These concerned the one pre-eternal Godhead of the Son and the Holy Spirit, which has no beginning and ever coexists with God the Father. They also concerned the ineffable incarnation of the Son of God himself, God the Word, from the Virgin Mary, the Theotokos, in the last times for the sake of our salvation. I noted, too, the apostolic ordinances of the church. In short, I learned from that sacred book the whole of the business transacted there, and above all the divine and truly apostolic thoughts of the most faithful emperor Constantine, who also sat with the synod. I took such delight in what that sacred book contained that I said to the Lord: "How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth!" That is how greatly I rejoiced in what was recorded there about the spotless, blameless, orthodox and apostolic faith.

Some time later I came here, I mean to the province of Bithynia. By God's good pleasure, a very great deal of agitation and dispute arose here during the revolt of the unholy Basiliscus against the apostolic and catholic church of God and the apostolic faith practiced in it. The faction of those who shared the views of the heretic Eutyches was especially inflaming and stirring up the palace. They put it to us deceitfully that we should hold to the faith set out by the fathers at Nicaea, as they put it. But we showed that they were its enemies, for they did not know what they were saying or what they were making assertions about. When I brought forward what the Lord had uttered in the Holy Spirit through that holy choir of God's orthodox priests, the wretches recoiled from us. With their tongues they uttered things worse than Arius's blasphemies against what had been defined there, and they hurled anathemas at those who held these views. Our holy and orthodox faith has been practiced in the church of God, our mother, from the beginning, handed down from the holy apostles and from our holy fathers gathered at Nicaea, whom I have already mentioned. Because of these attacks on it, and many others, I searched as thoroughly as I could, everywhere and by every means, leaving no stone unturned, as the saying goes. I wanted to find out what had been done at that sacred synod to define that same holy and apostolic faith. The church of God received this faith not from human beings, nor through a human being, but from our Savior and the God of us all, Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God himself. He carried out the dispensation of his coming in the flesh, which is truly the great mystery of godliness, as it is written: he was "manifested in the flesh" and "seen by angels." For the Only-begotten could not be seen even by angels in the essence of his Godhead, had he not become flesh. He fulfilled everything that belonged to the dispensation, and he yielded his holy and sinless flesh to the voluntary passion on our behalf, to burial and to resurrection, and through that flesh he made our race immortal. Then, as he ascended into heaven, he himself established the divine and venerable definition of this holy and blameless faith, and he thundered mightily, as it is written: "The Lord went up into heaven and thundered"; and elsewhere: "The Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High uttered his voice." What did he thunder, and what voice did the Most High utter? Speaking to the apostles, he says: "Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." It is as if he said: "Out of love for humanity I have taken on your flesh, endowed with soul and mind, from the all-venerable and holy Virgin Mary. Yet taking on flesh has added nothing to the Trinity of the Father, myself and the Holy Spirit; the Trinity remains a Trinity. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit."

The holy apostles received this holy and venerable definition of the right and blameless faith from the Lord and proclaimed it to the whole church of God under heaven. So the prophetic word was fulfilled in it, which says: "Their voice has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world." This is the definition and venerable gift that the Son of God gave to us through the divine apostles. A very long time afterward, when the persecution against the church of God had ceased, the enemy of our salvation armed himself again through Arius against that same holy and blameless faith. He brought in strange and blasphemous words against the Savior, and with them he threw the Lord's church throughout the world into turmoil.

For this reason the most faithful emperor Constantine assembled that great synod at the city of Nicaea. As I said above, I already knew all of its proceedings. Even so, when I searched, I could barely find clear records of what was discussed and written there among various scholarly men. One was a certain John, a presbyter and an old man, very learned in the Scriptures, who had them in very old quires, though not complete. Others were various writers, such as Eusebius Pamphili, bishop of Caesarea, and Rufinus, a presbyter of Rome, who also took part in that holy synod, and a great many others. But I did not find in them the orderly sequence of the whole account that was in the sacred book I had read earlier, as I said above. Only the admirable Eusebius Pamphili traveled unswervingly along the highway of truth, from the coming of the Lord to the times of the great Constantine. Even so, I could not find everything. Still, I have found some things that I knew already and that are true to the book I had read before, and I have gathered others from other sources. I thought it necessary to write all this down in this book, for the common benefit and support of those who will read it.

My account will now begin, with God the ever-living Word leading the way and guiding my steps. It starts from the time of the reign of the most pious and Christ-bearing emperor Constantine, who ordered the synod of bishops to assemble in the city of Nicaea. In another work, God willing, I will set down the story of his birth and the course of the reign of his father, the most God-beloved emperor Constantius.

The tyrants Diocletian and Maximian laid aside the imperial purple and returned to private life. As Eusebius says, not much time had passed after this when the emperor Constantius died by the common law of nature. All his life he had shown himself most gentle and most kindly to his subjects and most friendly to the divine Word. He left his legitimate son Constantine as emperor and Augustus in his place. After his death he was granted every honor that could be owed to an emperor, for he had been a most excellent and most gentle ruler. He alone in our time spent the whole period of his rule in a manner worthy of the office. In every other respect he showed himself most capable and most generous to all. He met a glorious and thrice-blessed end. He alone died during his reign graciously and gloriously, leaving as his successor a legitimate son who was in every way temperate and most pious. His son Constantine, from the very start of his reign, was proclaimed most perfect emperor and Augustus by the armies, and long before that by God himself, the King of all. He made himself an imitator of his father's piety toward our faith. And later Eusebius says: Constantine, as we have said, was an emperor born of an emperor, pious and the son of a most pious father, temperate in all things, and he was honored for wisdom and piety. God, the King of all and the Savior, raised him up against the most impious tyrants. He drew up his forces for a lawful war, and God fought on his side in a most extraordinary way. Maxentius fell at Rome at Constantine's hands. The tyrant in the East did not survive him long. He too ended his life by a most shameful death at the hands of Licinius, who had not yet gone mad at that time and whom the most God-beloved emperor Constantine had sent against him. Constantine, first in honor and in imperial rank, was the first to take pity on the people tyrannized at Rome. In his prayers he called on the God of heaven and on his Word, Jesus Christ himself, the Savior of all, as his ally. Then he advanced with his whole army, seeking to win back for the Romans the freedom of their ancestors.

So much for Eusebius. Rufinus did not set down in his history the orderly sequence and harmony of the truth that the excellent Eusebius Pamphili did. Even so, as I said above, I will gather from Rufinus himself and the other writers whatever I find that agrees with Eusebius's work, and I will put it into this little book. Rufinus too says this:

After the abdication of Diocletian and Maximian and the death of Constantius, these were the emperors who were left ruling the Roman empire at the same time. Constantine received his father's share. This began with what is called Europe and stretched to the Danube. It included both Scythias, all the Celts, the Illyrians and the Sarmatians, the barbarian land that reaches to the river Rhine, Macedonia and the sea beside it, Thessaly and Achaea, and all the lands toward the setting sun that the Ionian Sea bounds. Maximin, the son of Diocletian, governed all the nations of the East, as Eusebius says. Maxentius governed Rome and the lands that stretch from Italy to the Ocean itself.

Constantine gave his father the burial the law required and paid him the customary honors. After that, given the misfortune of the Romans, he considered it a loss to stay idle. He heard that the city of Rome was suffering under the evils of Maxentius, whose rule had turned into the cruelty of a tyranny. Maxentius put many officials to death without trial. He imposed fines, exiles, redistributions of land and penalties without any inquiry. He also lusted after other men's wives, and he either seduced them with flattery or forced them by his commands. As a result it was no longer safe to have a beautiful wife, and there was a great deal of bloodshed in the city because people tried to protect their wives' chastity. The most God-beloved Constantine heard of these things and of many others that do not belong in the present work, and he was provoked. For injustice done to others is felt as a personal grief by men who love God.

So he decided to take up arms and come to the aid of the Romans who were suffering such things. To rescue them from their evils was as good as saving all mankind. First he resolved to win back the cities that were breaking away from Roman rule, some by words, some by arms, and some by acts of kindness. He made their taxes lighter, provided fair dealing in the markets, and wisely put an end to revolts and acts of madness, using silence rather than fear. He knew that the nations of the Saurians [?], the Franks and the Germans loved novelty, were easily stirred up to rise against emperors, and often made their own opinion their law. He also brought under his rule the Spaniards, the Britons, the islands there and the remaining peoples. He subdued all those who witness the setting of the sun. These are said to know whether the sun truly sinks into the Ocean, or whether, after reaching the water, it returns to us by another route. He also conquered by force of arms the barbarian tribes in those parts, treating the fighting as a sideline to his main task. Some he subjected, some he paid, and others he turned from enemies into friends and from old foes into close companions. In this way he made them all his allies, without harming anyone or besieging anyone, as he hurried on to save others. For where God fights on one's side, everything goes well, beyond all human reckoning. With such God-loving intent, the most faithful Constantine crossed the Rhine on his right. With a small army he crossed many mountains and many nameless rivers, subdued many barbarian nations and won over ten nations of the Gauls, Franks and Spaniards. Then he led his army on to the mountains of Italy.

When Maxentius heard of this, he was thrown into unexpected alarm. He had never expected anyone to cross so great a territory, fenced in as it was by mountains, rivers and all kinds of barbarians, and by the natural hardships of the wilderness. For the desolation of a region often turns out to be the greatest bulwark of a kingdom. So he decided to march his army out of Rome with great speed to meet Constantine and to check him first somewhere in Italy. But when the armies were drawn up against each other and saw each other's standards, the prospects of battle were unequal. The troops from Rome rushed out ahead and poured forth in their phalanxes. They had enjoyed a long truce and rest, so they seemed ready for battle and showed a spirit worthy of their city and a match for it. Those drawn up with Constantine had conquered a great deal of land and taken much plunder and many spoils of war, but they were worn out with toil. They had spent their time in the race for victory rather than in enjoying what they had won. By now they were giving in to exhaustion and yielding under their constant labors.

The battle was not yet decided and the armies were evenly matched when God armed Constantine from heaven. He showed him the saving sign of the cross, shining with light in the sky. Letters declared the meaning of the vision. They said: "By this conquer."

Unbelievers think this story is a myth, a fiction made up to please the followers of our doctrines. But to those who are used to believing the truth, the evidence for the event is plain. For God, the painter of this sign, afterward showed by deeds how true the grace of the inscription was. Perhaps we are not yet persuading anyone of what we write, since we are copying from the histories of earlier writers, because we are gathering useful things from his life from a little further back. But one must not disbelieve what follows. In our own generation, those who fought alongside Constantius, the son of Constantine, saw such things with their own eyes and cured the old unbelief with new sightings. Suppose the people who dispute these things are Hebrews. Their books contain much less believable things, and they believe them: a sea crossed on foot, water standing like a wall, a path through the deep, God speaking in a bush, a flame giving the law, a trumpet with no instrument sounding through the desert, angels fighting in the ranks, commanders of the Lord's host defending the battle line, hailstones and fiery arrows hurled instead of the usual spears. Yet all right-thinking people accept these without question, for when God wills it, nothing is impossible. Or suppose those who reject the miracle are Greeks. We could say a great deal, though we prefer not to. We could tell how many divine signs the oracle-mongers announced to Alexander when he was about to cross over for the battle at the Granicus and for the battle against Darius, though their fictions have no visible proof. We could tell how a spirit used to warn the philosopher Socrates with a voice about the outcome of things he should not do, and we could tell what his disciples wrote about Pythagoras of Samos. I pass over the fictions of the poets, and how some of the famous men among them [?] had some of those they regarded as gods fighting on their side. I do not want anyone to think that I am comparing myths with truths, or things that never happened with things that did. For the mighty grace of Christ, from the time it blossomed among human beings, has been, is and will be a healing remedy in heaven and on earth, in the sea, in plants and in wood, in garments, in sickness and in health, in food and in drink. Those who have experienced it know this, and as our history goes on we will set it out at the proper time.

So Constantine turned the vision of the miracle into the form of a trophy. He had it put together with stones set in gold and made in the shape of a very tall spear, and gave it to the horsemen riding in front to carry, looking now to see the promise of the letters fulfilled in deeds. Nor was he disappointed in his hope: he had been quick to believe what he had seen, and he received the victory even more quickly than he had believed.

Constantine, then, cut short the long toil of the war by his faith. Not fearing the army from Rome, he nobly drew up his forces against it. Maxentius, however, dreaded Constantine's prowess and was also wary of the Romans' hatred, since most of them had turned against him because of his debauchery. So he decided to carry out his plot by guile. The guile was a bridge, built by men of his kind as a kind of contrivance. Above, what could be seen was a crossing ready to receive Constantine. Hidden beneath was a deceitful trap laid for his steps. He would only have to cross a little way, and the contrivance would come apart. The enemy would be caught, and the place would become his unexpected tomb. But while Maxentius was preparing these snares at the crossing, divine grace entangled the craftsman of evil in his own devices. Before Constantine could be caught, the tyrant himself fell first into his own trap. There he became his own tyrant-slayer, and the plot he had devised turned out well, though against himself. Before Rome, at the bridge called the Milvian, the aforementioned Maxentius himself sank into the river and perished by drowning. So the whole Roman people cried out, saying, as Eusebius son of Pamphilus records: "Let us sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea. He has become my helper and protector for salvation," and, "Who is like you among the gods, O Lord? Who is like you, glorified among the holy ones, marvelous in glory, working wonders?" To this the same author adds: "With these words, and others akin and similar to them, Constantine hymned by his very deeds God, the Ruler of all and the author of the victory, and his only-begotten Son Jesus Christ, and rode into Rome with songs of victory. All of them together, even small children and women, the members of the senate and the other most distinguished men, with the whole Roman people, received him with shining eyes and with their whole souls as redeemer, savior and benefactor, with acclamations and boundless joy. But he had an inborn piety toward God. He was not in the least shaken by the shouting or elated by the praises, for he was well aware that the help had come from God. At once he ordered that the trophy of the saving Passion be placed in the hand of his own statue. They set up the statue, holding the sign of the cross in its right hand, in the most public place in Rome, and he commanded that this very inscription be engraved on it, word for word, in the language of the Romans: 'By this saving sign, the true proof of courage, I have saved your city and freed it from the yoke of the tyrant; and I have also freed the senate and the Roman people and restored them to their ancient distinction and splendor.'"

So much from Eusebius. Rufinus, that is, Gelasius, tells it this way: "After this the Roman senate asked that Licinius, who was the brother-in-law of the God-beloved Constantine through his sister Constantia, should reign together with Constantine. Constantine then sent him to the East against the tyrant there, out of concern for the safety of the Christians in those parts. Having enjoyed such great benefits from God, the pious Constantine was eager to offer thank-offerings to his Benefactor. These were to release the Christians from persecution, to recall those in exile, to set free those in prison, to restore their property to those whose estates had been confiscated, and to rebuild the churches. He did all this with great eagerness, for his mind was set on the things of Christ. Being a Christian in all things, he did everything as a Christian. He raised up the churches of God and honored them with costly offerings, and he also ordered the temples of the pagans to be torn down and destroyed by fire."

The tyrant in the East, however, was ravaging the churches of God. And this is the cause that brought about his downfall. He could not bear the greatness of the rule entrusted to him beyond his deserts. Lacking sober and royal judgment, he handled affairs crudely, and above all his soul was senselessly puffed up with arrogant boasting. So Maximinus had already ventured to act insolently even against his partners in the empire. He did so even against Constantine, who surpassed him in every respect, in birth, upbringing and education, in rank and understanding, and, the crowning point of all, shone forth in self-control and in piety toward the true God. Maximinus set out to rank himself first in honors. Pushing his madness to the point of folly, he broke the treaties he had made with Licinius and launched a war without truce. Then in a short time he threw everything into confusion and stirred up every city. He gathered every army, countless thousands strong, and went out to battle against Licinius, and so against both Licinius and Constantine who had sent him. But when he came to close quarters, he found himself bereft of God's oversight, for the one God of all awarded the victory to Constantine, who was then in power. First the wretch lost the mass of heavy infantry on which he had relied. Stripped of his bodyguards, with everyone deserting him and going over to the victor, the miserable man slipped out of the royal attire that did not suit him as fast as he could. He stripped it off in a cowardly, ignoble and unmanly way, slipped into the crowd and then ran off. Hiding in the fields and villages, he barely escaped the soldiers' hands, thinking only of saving himself. By these very events one can show how faithful and true the divine oracles are, where it is said: "A king is not saved by great power, and a giant will not be saved by the greatness of his strength. A horse is a false hope for safety, and by the greatness of its power it will not save. Behold, the eyes of the Lord are on those who fear him, on those who hope in his mercy, to rescue their souls from death." The impious man was suddenly struck by the scourge of God in the second clash of the war, and so ended his life. His end was not like that of generals and war leaders who often show their courage in war for the sake of virtue and their friends and boldly meet a glorious death. Since he was impious and an enemy of God through and through, he stayed at home in hiding while the battle line was still drawn up before the field. There he suffered the punishment he deserved. Suddenly struck by the scourge of God, he was driven by terrible pains and agonies until he fell prostrate. He wasted away from hunger, and all his flesh was melted by an invisible fire sent by God. As it dissolved, every trace of his former appearance vanished, and he was reduced to dry bones alone, left like a phantom long [?] withered into a skeleton. Those present could think only that his body had become a tomb for his soul, buried in a form that was dead and had wholly wasted away. As the fever burned him still more fiercely from the depths of his marrow, his eyes bulged out and fell from their sockets, leaving him blind. Still breathing in this state, he confessed to the Lord and begged for death. At the very last he admitted that he had justly suffered these things because of his outrages against Christ, and gave up his soul.

So Maximinus was removed. He alone had remained, and he had proved the worst of all the enemies of godliness. By the grace of God the Almighty, the churches were renewed and raised up from their very foundations, and the word of Christ, shining forth to the glory of the God of the universe, gained greater freedom than before. These things were set down in the ninth book of the Ecclesiastical History by Eusebius son of Pamphilus, a man excellent in every way. As I said above, I am making a selection from his labors and from those of others, and so I am writing this little book in brief. I am hastening my account as quickly as I can toward the lofty, radiant, holy and divine mountain: the apostolic and virtuous synod of the priests of God at Nicaea. Above all, I see the prophet taking me by the hand and urging me on: "Come," he says, "let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will declare his way to us, and we will walk in it. For out of Zion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem." For truly, that divine assembly of the orthodox priests of God is Zion and Jerusalem, the most lofty mountain of the Lord and the house of the God of Jacob. By the Holy Spirit they examined and established, from the prophetic, evangelical and apostolic scriptures, the truth about the Word of life, that is, the Son of God. They showed most clearly that in the nature of his divinity he is truly uncreated and not a creature, as the God-fighting and most impious Arius blasphemed against him. They showed that he is of the same essence and the same substance as the Father who begot him before all ages, and likewise that the Holy Spirit is of the same divinity and essence as the Father and the Son. And truly this venerable and holy definition of the spotless faith is a lofty mountain of God from above, as the word foretold. It was given to us by the Lord himself through the apostles, and now made clear by his priests at Nicaea with testimonies from Scripture. My account will show more clearly what it is as it proceeds, with the help of God's grace. But let us return to the subject of ecclesiastical history before us. Let us take up again how God the King came to the aid of his people and overthrew the tyrants through his servant, the God-beloved emperor Constantine. Through him the only great Lord bestowed peace on his churches throughout the world. He alone does great and unsearchable wonders without number. He changes seasons and times, removes kings and sets them up, raises the poor from the earth and lifts the needy from the dunghill. He has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted the lowly; he has filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty. He has crushed the arms of the proud. He is the wonder-worker, the doer of mighty deeds, the Master of all, the Creator of the whole world, the Almighty, the all-good, the one and only God. To him we send up the new song, answering him who alone does great wonders, "for his mercy endures forever"; to him who struck great kings and slew mighty kings, "for his mercy endures forever"; "for in our humiliation the Lord remembered us." For all these things let us never cease to hymn the God of the universe and his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ our Lord. Together with the Father he is the cause of all our blessings. He brought us to the knowledge of God. He is the teacher of piety toward him, the destroyer of the impious, the slayer of tyrants, the reformer of life, the savior of those in despair. Let us all glorify Jesus with one mouth and one heart. He alone, by the will of the all-good Father, through the love for mankind of the Father, of himself and of the Holy Spirit, took thought for the salvation of us who lay below in corruption. He willingly put on our nature, and like the best of physicians he took up our infirmities and bore our diseases, and so worked salvation and life for the human race, both then and always. He is King of kings and ever takes thought for his own people. He armed Constantine, his friend and his own servant, with the weapons of piety and faith toward him, and raised him up against the impious tyrants, Maxentius in Rome and Maximinus in the East. Having destroyed them through him, he has restored a bright and deep peace to his own people.

"But the sight of these things," says Eusebius son of Pamphilus, "was not, it seems, bearable to envy, which hates the good, or to the demon, which loves evil. Nor was what had happened to the tyrants mentioned earlier enough to bring Licinius, now changed for the worse, to sober reasoning. His rule was prospering. He held the second rank of honor after the great emperor Constantine and had been granted marriage-alliance and kinship with him. Yet he fell short of imitating what was good and instead emulated the depravity and wickedness of the impious tyrants. He had seen their end with his own eyes, yet he chose to follow their way of thinking rather than the friendship and goodwill of his superior. So, consumed with envy toward his great benefactor, he waged an accursed and most terrible war against him. He did not spare the laws of nature, nor did he give a thought to oaths, to blood ties or to treaties. For Constantine, like the all-good emperor he was, had given him tokens of true goodwill. He had not grudged him kinship with himself, nor refused him a share in the splendid marriage of his sister." And after other things: "But Licinius did the opposite. Every day the God-hater devised every kind of contrivance against his superior and thought up every manner of plot, so as to repay his benefactor with evil." To this he adds: "But God was the friend, guardian and protector of the other man, of Constantine, I mean. God brought to light and exposed the plans the tyrant contrived in secret and in darkness. Such is the power of virtue, the great weapon of godliness, both to ward off enemies and to safeguard one's own safety. Fortified by it, our most God-beloved emperor Constantine escaped, with help from God, the tangled plots of that man of evil name. The tyrant saw that his secret scheme was by no means going as he had planned, since God was exposing every deceit and villainy to the God-beloved man. No longer able to keep his intentions hidden, he launched open war. Having resolved to fight Constantine hand to hand, he set out also to array himself against the God of the universe as Constantine's guardian, whom he knew Constantine worshipped. Then he began to persecute the God-fearing people under his rule." And after other things: "The manner in which he murdered them was strange, such as had never been heard of before. In the evils he ordered to be inflicted on Amaseia and the other cities of Pontus, he went beyond every extreme of cruelty. There some of the churches of God were again torn down from top to bottom, and others he ordered to be shut, so that none of the faithful could gather or render to God the prayers and worship due to him. He did not believe these were offered on his behalf (how could the God-hater have imagined it?), reckoning so from his own bad conscience. He was convinced that we did all this for Constantine, the God-beloved emperor, and were seeking God's favor for him. Provoked by this, he unleashed his wrath against us." And shortly after: "Many of the bishops were led away and punished, without any pretext, like murderers, though they had done no wrong. They suffered a new kind of death: their bodies were hacked into many pieces with the sword, and after this cruel and most horrifying spectacle they were thrown into the depths of the sea as food for the fish. Then once again all the God-fearing fled, men and women together, with their small children, and once again fields and deserts, glens and mountains received the servants of Christ, for the impious man had stirred up war against all." And shortly after: "—had not God, the exceedingly good guardian of souls, quickly forestalled what was about to happen. As in deep darkness and the gloomiest night, he suddenly made a great light and savior shine out for all: his servant Constantine, whom he led with a high arm and a most mighty hand. From heaven above he granted Constantine trophies of victory over the impious as a worthy fruit of his piety. And the God of Constantine and of us all cast the wretch down, with all his counselors and friends, prostrate beneath Constantine's feet. When Licinius drove his affairs to the extremes of madness, the emperor Constantine, the friend of God, judged it intolerable. Summoning his inborn sober and pious judgment and tempering the firm way of justice with love for mankind, he decided to come to the aid of those suffering under the tyrant. He set out to save the greater part of the human race by removing a few destroyers. For until then the most humane emperor Constantine had shown the impious man nothing but kindness and had pitied one who did not deserve compassion. But this did Licinius no good, since he did not give up his wickedness but rather increased his fury against the nations subject to him. And those he afflicted had no hope of rescue, crushed as they were by a terrible beast. So the giver of good things, mixing hatred of evil with his love for mankind, advanced with his son Crispus, a most humane emperor, from the West, from mighty Rome, to the East against the tyrant, stretching out a saving right hand to all who were perishing. With God, the King of all, and his Son Christ the Savior as their guide and ally, the father, the emperor Constantine, together with his son, the emperor Crispus, surrounded and broke up the battle line of the God-hated men on every side. They carried off an easy victory, for everything in the battle was made easy for them in accordance with the will of God, the King of all." So says Eusebius, the greatest lover of truth, son of the all-praiseworthy Pamphilus.

Rufinus says (and although he recorded no part of the events under Licinius, I will nevertheless read out the very words of the writer just mentioned and set them into my work), he says: "Now Licinius, who shared the rule with him" (that is, with Constantine, beloved of God), "held pagan opinions and hated the Christians. For fear of the emperor Constantine he held back from stirring up an open persecution against them, but he secretly plotted against many. Going further, however, he openly stirred up the persecution against everyone in the regions of the East, so that many martyrs of Christ were brought forth in various places. Because of this he roused the emperor Constantine to the greatest hatred against him, and they were enemies of one another." So much for Rufinus. Philip, the advocate of the truthfulness of Eusebius son of Pamphilus, says: "Dividing the army, the two of them, the father, the emperor Constantine, and the son, the emperor Crispus, set out against the impious tyrant. The son Crispus made his march with the army under him toward the regions of Asia, while the father Constantine made his way through Europe with his guards. But the God-hater, full of every impiety and bloodshed, came out of the East with a very great army, drawn up against them and boasting loudly. When he reached Nicomedia, knowing and understanding that the soul of Constantine, beloved of God, revered the priests of God and held them in every honour, he bribed Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, who had long been his partisan, to act against the pious emperor Constantine. He thought that through him and those around him he could destroy Constantine, who was fortified with the invincible arms of God. So the admirable Eusebius came to terms with him, won over by promises from Licinius, his partner in impiety." And that this is how things stand can be fully confirmed from the very letter of the Christ-loving emperor which he sent to the Nicomedians, where near the end of the letter he speaks roughly as follows: "Who is it who taught these things to so innocent a multitude? Clearly Eusebius, the accomplice of the tyrant's cruelty. That he had in every way become the tyrant's partisan can be seen from many sides. The slaughter of the bishops bears witness to it (of the true bishops, that is), and the most cruel persecution of the Christians proclaims it aloud. I will say nothing now of what he did against me, by which, at the very time when the forces of the opposing side were being mustered against us, he even sent spies to keep watch on me and all but supplied the tyrant with armed help as a service to him. And let no one think that I am unprepared to prove these things. There is exact proof, for it is established that the presbyters and deacons in Eusebius's company were openly arrested by me. But I have brought these things forward now not out of indignation but to shame those men. This alone I fear, this I ponder: that I see you being drawn into a share in the guilt. For through Eusebius's conduct and perversity you have taken on a conscience cut off from the truth. But the cure is not slow in coming, if at least now you receive a faithful and pure bishop and look to God. This is in your power at present, and it ought long ago to have depended on your judgment, had not the aforementioned Eusebius come here through the dreadful scheming of those who then helped him and shamelessly overturned the right order of things. But since it is fitting to say a few things to your charity about this same Eusebius, listen patiently. Your forbearance remembers that a synod of bishops took place in the city of Nicaea, at which I myself was present, as befitted the service of my conscience, wishing nothing else than to bring about concord for all, and above all to expose and cast off this affair, which had its beginning in the madness of Arius the Alexandrian but was at once strengthened by the absurd and destructive zeal of Eusebius. But this very Eusebius, most beloved and most honoured brothers, with what eagerness do you suppose, overcome as he was by his own conscience, and with what shamelessness did he stand by his falsehood, though it had been refuted on every side! He secretly sent me various people to plead on his behalf, and begged some support from me, so that, convicted of so great an offence, he might not lose the honour he held. God himself is my witness to these things (may he graciously remain with me and with you), that this same Eusebius even led me astray and unbecomingly carried me off; but divine providence brought me back to its truest path. This you too have recognized and will recognize. For at that time everything was done by him, by the unholy Eusebius, I mean, just as he wished, while he hid every kind of evil in his mind. But just recently, to pass over the rest of his perversity, listen, I beg you, to what in particular he has done together with Theognis, whom he has as partner in his unholy purpose. I had ordered certain Alexandrians who had withdrawn from our faith to be sent here, since through their agency the torch of discord was being kindled. But these fine and noble bishops, whom the truth of the synod had once spared so that they might repent, not only received those men and kept them safe in their own company, but even shared with them in the malice of their ways. Therefore I decided to deal with these ungrateful men as follows: I ordered them to be seized and banished as far away as possible. Now it is your part to look to God with that faith which it is fitting that you have always had and still have, and to act in such a way that we may rejoice in having bishops who are pure, orthodox and kind. But if anyone should thoughtlessly dare to be inflamed to remembrance or praise of those destroyers, he will immediately be checked in his audacity by the action of the servant of God, that is, by me. God will keep you safe, beloved brothers." These and similar things the letter of Constantine, the emperor beloved of God, showed most clearly about the impious Eusebius of Nicomedia, who became not only the partisan of the God-hated Licinius but also the accomplice and servant of his tyranny and impiety. From here I will proceed to the subject set before me, the history of the Church.

So Licinius set out from Nicomedia with the army that was with him for Byzantium, to move against Constantine, the emperor beloved of God, who was then there. When both military phalanxes had the Christ-bearing emperor in their midst, the wretch saw it and found himself deserted even by his own troops, who had fled for refuge to the shield of the stronger side. At first he tried to hide in Chrysopolis in Bithynia (this is the port of Chalcedon), but when he could not, and saw himself already lying prostrate at the feet of the emperor Constantine, he surrendered. The most gentle and most pious emperor, having taken him alive, treated him with clemency and did not kill him at all, but ordered him to live quietly in Thessalonica. For a short time he seemed to keep quiet, but afterward he summoned certain barbarians, took counsel with them and tried to reverse his defeat. When the most faithful emperor learned of this, he ordered the God-hater to be put to death, and so the tyrant who had opposed Christ and his servant was put to death.

Constantine, then, having become master of everything through the help given him by God and having been proclaimed sole emperor, was eager to advance the cause of the Christians still more and more. He did this in various ways, having an ardent faith and an inborn, most faithful piety toward the God of all, and the whole Church under heaven was in deep peace.

Let us hear, then, what is said at this point also by the finest ploughman of the Church's husbandry, the most truth-loving Eusebius son of the all-renowned Pamphilus. "Licinius, then," he says, "having followed the same path of impiety as the godless tyrants, was justly brought to the same precipice. But while he lay struck down in this way, the most mighty victor, Constantine Augustus, distinguished by every virtue of godliness, together with his son Crispus, an emperor most dear to God and in all things most like his father, recovered the East that was their own and made the Roman Empire one united whole as of old, bringing under their peace the whole circuit of the world from the rising sun on both sides, north and south alike, to the farthest limits of the declining day. All fear of those who had oppressed them was taken away from humankind, and people celebrated splendid and festive holidays. Everything was full of light, and those who had once been downcast looked at one another with smiling faces and shining eyes. They had hymns in the cities and in the countryside alike: first of all they honoured God the King of all and his true Son Christ, as they had been taught, and then they acclaimed the pious emperor together with his sons, beloved of God. Old evils were forgotten and all impiety consigned to oblivion; there was enjoyment of present blessings and, besides, the expectation of those to come. Ordinances full of the victorious emperor's kindness were published everywhere, along with laws bearing the marks of munificence and true piety. Thus, when all tyranny had been purged away, the empire that rightly belonged to them was kept secure and beyond envy for Constantine and his sons alone." So much, then, from Eusebius son of Pamphilus, the most trustworthy of the ancient writers on the Church. He undertook a great many labours and researches, and, gathering his material from straightforward sources, he has left us an accurate account of the history of the Church in ten full volumes, beginning from the coming of the Lord and completing it down to these times. He did not do it without toil (for how could anyone who had taken on so great a task keep the coherence of such a compilation?), but, as I said just now, he brought much zeal and an untold wealth of labour to it. But let no one suppose from the rumours spread about him that the man ever held any part of the blasphemous wickedness of Arius. Rather, let him be convinced that, even if he said or wrote something small that hinted at Arius's views, it was not in that man's impious sense but out of guileless simplicity, as he himself fully assured us, testifying to this in his apologetic discourse, which he sent to the assembly of orthodox bishops. And anyone of sound mind would take the man to be telling the truth, since from this too one can be persuaded that Arius's teachings had not yet been heard anywhere at that time. The struggles he waged at the synod of Nicaea against the impiety of Arius, on behalf of the apostolic and orthodox faith, will show this. But let us return to the course of the history of the Church. The Church of Christ our Saviour throughout the world now had deep peace, granted to it by God the King of all through his servant Constantine and his sons. After the martyrdom of the divine Peter, bishop of the church of Alexandria, who was perfected in that martyrdom and bound on the imperishable crown of the contest, the church there remained widowed for one year. After that year Achillas was ordained to the throne of this same holy martyr Peter, a sturdy and highly gifted man of holy mind, distinguished for piety together with very great wisdom, as the ancient and reliable writings tell us. After much entreaty he received Arius into the diaconate. He lived on for only five months, and then Alexander took up the office of high priest of the church of the Alexandrians there, a man honoured in all things by the whole clergy and people of the church: small in stature, generous, eloquent, gentle, God-loving, kind, a lover of the poor, good and courteous to all if ever anyone was. He too appointed Arius a presbyter, placing him closest to himself. In his time the peace of the churches was growing brighter and brighter day by day; they were united in one concord and honoured everywhere on earth by the prizes of the holy martyrs. But the devil, unable to bear such growth of the most faithful people of the Church in the heavenly worship of God within it, once again brought about a disturbance out of a certain contentiousness among its members.

For that presbyter whom we said Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, had judged worthy of such honour, Arius by name, a man pious more in outward show but otherwise an ardent lover of glory and novelty, began to put forward certain strange ideas about faith in Christ, which no one in earlier times had ever raised or introduced. He attempted to separate our only-begotten Lord Jesus Christ from the ineffable and eternal Godhead of the Father, and so became the cause of great disturbance in the Church. But Alexander, from the mildness of his nature, wanted to change Arius for the better by fitting admonitions and did not yet decide to pass sentence for the time being. Because of this the pestilent plague of the heresy spread to many, and then, as from a small spark, a great fire was kindled. The evil began in the church of the Alexandrians and ran through other cities and provinces as well. Finally, when he saw the evil going from bad to worse, Alexander convened a synod of the bishops under him, deposed Arius, and communicated the matter to his fellow ministers. Setting out the case of Arius at some length and urging them to zeal for the destruction of the heresy, he exhorted them to make ready in preparation for judging it, writing to them as follows:
"To the beloved and most honoured fellow ministers of the catholic Church everywhere, Alexander sends greeting in the Lord.

Since the catholic Church is one body, and the divine Scriptures command us to keep the bond of unity and peace, it follows that we should write to one another and report what happens among each of us, so that if one member suffers or rejoices, we may suffer or rejoice together. In our own diocese, then, lawless men, enemies of Christ, have now gone out teaching an apostasy that one might reasonably suspect, and even call, a forerunner of the Antichrist. I would have preferred to pass over the matter in silence, so that the evil might be used up among the apostates alone and not spread to other places and defile the ears of the innocent. But Eusebius, who is now in Nicomedia, thinks that the affairs of the Church depend on him, because he left Berytus and set his eye on the church of the Nicomedians without being punished for it. He has now made himself the champion of these apostates as well, and has set about writing everywhere to commend them, in order to draw some who do not know better into this latest heresy, which makes war on Christ. So, knowing what is written in the law, I have been compelled to keep silent no longer but to make it known to all of you. Then you will know who the apostates are and what the wretched phrases of their heresy are, and if Eusebius writes, you will pay no attention to him. For he wants to use these men to revive his old malice, which had been silenced by time. He pretends to be writing on their behalf, but in fact he shows that he is doing it to further his own interests.

Those who have become apostates, then, are Arius, Achilleus, Thales, Carpones, another Arius, Sarmates, Euzoius, Lucius, Julius, Menas, Helladius and Gaius, and with them Secundus and Theonas, who were once called bishops. And these are the things they have invented and teach, contrary to the Scriptures: “God was not always Father; there was a time when God was not Father. The Word of God did not always exist, but came into being from things that were not. For God, who is, made him who was not out of what was not. Therefore there was once a time when he was not. For the Son is a creature and a thing made. He is neither like the Father in essence, nor is he the Father’s true Word by nature, nor his true Wisdom. He is one of the things made and brought into being, and is called Word and Wisdom only by a misuse of the terms, since he himself came into being by God’s own Word and by the Wisdom that is in God, in which God made both all things and him. Therefore he is also changeable and alterable in nature, like all rational beings. The Word is foreign, alien and cut off from the essence of God. And the Father cannot be expressed to the Son, for the Word neither knows the Father perfectly and exactly nor can see him perfectly. Indeed, the Son does not even know his own essence as it is. For he was made for our sake, so that God might create us through him as through an instrument, and he would not have come into existence if God had not wished to make us.”

Someone, at any rate, asked them whether the Word of God could change as the devil changed, and they were not afraid to say, “Yes, he can, for he is of a changeable nature, since he is begotten and created.” Since Arius and his followers say these things and are shameless about them, we, together with the bishops of Egypt and the Libyas, nearly a hundred in number, met and anathematized both them and those who have followed them. Eusebius and his party, however, received them, eager to mix falsehood with truth and impiety with piety. But they will not prevail, for the truth conquers, and there is no fellowship between light and darkness, nor any agreement between Christ and Beliar. Who ever heard such things? Or who, hearing them now, is not astonished and does not stop his ears so that the filth of these words may not touch his hearing? Who, hearing John say, “In the beginning was the Word,” does not condemn these men when they say, “There was once a time when he was not”? Or who, hearing in the Gospel “only-begotten Son” and “all things came into being through him,” will not loathe them for declaring that he is one of the things made? For how can he be one of the things that came into being through him? Or how can he be only-begotten if, as they say, he is counted along with all the rest? And how could he come from things that were not, when the Father says, “My heart has poured forth a good word,” and, “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you”? Or how can he be unlike the Father in essence, when he is the perfect image and radiance of the Father and says, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father”? And if the Son is the Word and Wisdom of God, how was there once a time when he was not? That is the same as saying that God was once without Word and without wisdom. And how can he be changeable and alterable, when he says in his own person, “I am in the Father and the Father in me,” and, “I and the Father are one,” and through the prophet, “See me, that I am, and I have not changed”? For even if someone can refer this saying to the Father himself, it would be more fitting to understand it here of the Word, because even when he became man he was not altered; rather, as the apostle said, “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” And what persuaded them to say that he came into being for our sake, when Paul says, “for whom are all things and through whom are all things”? As for their blasphemy that the Son does not know the Father perfectly, there is no need to wonder at it. For once they have set themselves to make war on Christ, they also brush aside his own words when he says, “As the Father knows me, so I know the Father.” If, then, the Father knows the Son only in part, clearly the Son also does not know the Father perfectly. But if it is not lawful to say this, and the Father does know the Son perfectly, then clearly, just as the Father knows his own Word, so the Word knows his own Father, whose Word he is. By saying these things and opening up the divine Scriptures we have often put them to shame, but like chameleons they changed again, striving to draw on themselves what is written: “When the ungodly man reaches the depth of evils, he becomes contemptuous.” Many heresies have arisen before them, which dared more than was proper and fell into folly. But these men, by attempting in all their phrases to do away with the divinity of the Word, have made those others look righteous by comparison, since they themselves have come nearer to the Antichrist. That is why they have been publicly expelled and anathematized by the Church. We grieve, then, at their destruction, especially because they themselves were once taught the Church’s doctrine and have now leapt away from it. Yet we are not surprised, for Hymenaeus and Philetus suffered the same, and before them Judas, who followed the Savior, later became a traitor and an apostate. Nor have we been left without instruction about these very men. The Lord said beforehand, “Take care that no one leads you astray. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he,’ and, ‘The time is near,’ and they will lead many astray. Do not go after them.” And Paul, who learned these things from the Savior, wrote that “in later times some will depart from the sound faith, giving heed to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons that turn away from the truth.” Since, then, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ has given us warning about such people both in his own person and through the apostle, we, having heard their impiety with our own ears, have accordingly anathematized such men, as we said before, and have declared them strangers to the catholic Church and faith. We have made this known to your godliness as well, beloved and most honored fellow ministers, so that if any of them should be so bold as to come to you, you will not receive them, and so that you will not be persuaded by Eusebius or anyone else who writes about them. For it is fitting that we, as Christians, should turn away from all who speak and think against Christ, as enemies of God and corrupters of souls, and should not even greet such people, lest we become sharers in their sins, as the blessed John commanded. Greet the brothers who are with you. Those who are with me greet you.

While Alexander was writing such letters to people in every city, the trouble only grew worse. When the emperor Constantine learned of it, he was deeply grieved and regarded the affair as a misfortune of his own. Eager to put out at once the evil that had been kindled, he sent letters to Alexander and Arius by a trustworthy man, the bishop of Cordoba, one of the cities of Spain, whom the emperor loved and held in honor.

“Victor Constantine Maximus Augustus to Alexander and Arius. I learn that the present controversy began like this. You yourself, father Alexander, were asking your presbyters what each of them thought about a certain passage of what is written in the law, or rather you were inquiring about one part of a pointless question. And you, Arius, rashly raised an objection, something you ought never to have thought of in the first place, or which, once you had thought of it, you should have kept to yourself in silence. Because dissension broke out among you, communion was refused, and the most holy people, split between the two of you, was cut off from the harmony of the common body. Let each of you, then, show equal consideration and accept the just advice that your fellow servant gives you. And what is this advice? It was not right to ask about such matters in the first place, nor to answer when asked. No law makes such inquiries necessary. They are put forward by the idle quibbling of useless leisure. Even if they arise as a kind of natural mental exercise, we ought still to keep them shut up within our minds, and not readily bring them out into public assemblies or carelessly entrust them to everyone's ears. For how great is any one of us, that he could either understand precisely the meaning of matters so great and so very difficult, or explain them worthily? And shortly afterwards: Therefore in such matters we must avoid much talk. Our natural weakness may leave us unable to explain what has been proposed, or the slower understanding of the hearers being taught may fail to grasp precisely what was said. Either way the people may then be driven to blasphemy or to schism. And after other things: For dissension is held to be neither fitting nor in any way permissible. To remind your understanding with a small example, you surely know that even the philosophers all agree in one doctrine. Often, when they disagree on some part of their propositions, the excellence of their learning divides them, yet the unity of their doctrine brings them back into harmony with one another. If this is so, is it not far more right that you, who have been appointed servants of the great God, should be of one mind with one another in such a choice of religion? Let us consider what has been said with deeper reflection and greater understanding. Is it right that, because of a few petty quarrels among you over empty words, brothers should be set against brothers and children against fathers, and that the honorable fellowship of communion should be torn apart by you through impious dissension? Let us willingly turn away from the temptations of the devil. Our great God, the Savior of all, has spread out his light for all alike. Under his providence, allow me, the servant of the Supreme Being, to carry this endeavor through to its end, so that by my appeal, my service and the earnestness of my admonition I may lead you, his peoples, back to the holy fellowship of communion. And after other things: Concerning divine providence, then, let there be among you one faith, one understanding, one agreement about the Supreme Being. As for the hairsplitting you carry on with one another about these trivial questions, even if you do not come to one opinion, it ought to stay within your thoughts, kept in the secret place of the mind. But let the special bond of common friendship, faith in the truth, and the worship of God and honor for the law remain unshaken among you. Return, then, to friendship and goodwill toward one another. Give back to the whole people their own embraces. And you yourselves, having cleansed your own souls, as it were, recognize one another once more. For friendship is often sweeter when it returns to reconciliation after a time of enmity. Give me back, then, peaceful days and nights free from care, so that I too may keep some pleasure in pure light and the joy of a quiet life for the rest of my days. Otherwise I must groan, be overcome by tears all the time, and not even bear the span of my life calmly. For while the peoples of God, my fellow servants I mean, are divided from one another by such unjust and harmful contention, how can I stay composed in mind any longer? Listen, so that you may understand the depth of my grief over this. Recently, when I arrived at the city of Nicomedia, I meant to press on at once to the East. But just as I was hurrying toward you and was already with you for the most part, the news of this affair reined my thoughts back. I did not want to be forced to see with my own eyes what I thought I could not even bear to hear with my ears. Open for me, then, by your concord the road to the East, which you have closed to me by your quarrels with one another. Allow me soon to see you and all the other peoples rejoicing together, and to confess to the Supreme Being, in auspicious words of praise, the thanks we owe for the common concord and freedom of all.” Such were the wonderful counsels, full of wisdom, that the emperor's letter offered. But the evil proved stronger than both the emperor's zeal and the standing of the man who served as bearer of the letter.

So when the emperor saw the church in turmoil, he convened an ecumenical council and sent letters summoning bishops from everywhere to meet at Nicaea in Bithynia. He was in the sixteenth year and sixth month of his reign when he undertook this for the peace of the church. Bishops came from many provinces and cities. Eusebius, son of Pamphilus, speaks of them word for word as follows in the third book of his Life of Constantine: “From all the churches that filled the whole of Europe, Libya and Asia, the very choicest of God's ministers were gathered together. One house of prayer, as though enlarged by God, held within it at the same time Syrians and Cilicians, Phoenicians, Arabs and Palestinians, and besides these Egyptians, Thebans, Libyans, and those who came from Mesopotamia. A Persian bishop too was present at the council, and a Scythian was not missing from the company. Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia provided their choicest men. Thracians and Macedonians, Achaeans and Epirotes, who live still farther away, also came. The renowned Hosius of Spain himself was there as well. He also held the place of Sylvester, bishop of great Rome, and sat with the rest together with the Roman presbyters Vito and Vincentius. The bishop of the city that is now the imperial capital, Metrophanes by name, stayed away because of his old age. But his presbyters attended and filled his place, and one of them was Alexander, who became bishop of the same city after him. Constantine alone of all emperors since the beginning of time bound together such a crown with the bond of peace. He dedicated it to Christ his Savior as a thank-offering worthy of God for his victory over his enemies and foes, and established in our day this image of the apostolic company. For in the apostles' time too, it is said, devout men were gathered from every nation under heaven, as told in the Acts of the Apostles, and among them were Parthians, Medes and Elamites. Yet that gathering fell short in that not all of them were ministers of God. In the present company, by contrast, the bishops numbered more than three hundred, and the presbyters and deacons who followed them, along with very many other attendants, were too many to count. Among these ministers of God, some stood out for the word of wisdom, others for the austerity of their life and their patient endurance, while others were adorned with a balance between the two. Some of them were honored for their great age, others shone with youth and vigor of soul, and others had only just set out on the course of ministry. For all of these the emperor ordered generous provisions to be supplied every day.”

This is what Eusebius, son of Pamphilus, related about those who assembled there. 6. After celebrating the festival of his victory over Licinius, the emperor himself also came to Nicaea. On the following day all the bishops met together in one place. The emperor came in after them. Once he had entered, he stood in the middle and would not sit down until the bishops had nodded their consent, so great was the reverence and respect the emperor had for these men. The all-praised emperor then addressed them with words of exhortation and instruction, praising, glorifying and giving thanks to the God of all, who had granted him so many blessings. He spoke roughly as follows:

“The nurturing justice of almighty God has laid down many paths, most plain to see, by which the human race may be blessed. Not least among them is that more distinguished and most brilliantly shining one which he prepared for all of us, greater than any wonder, as the chief point of the most holy law of the catholic Church: the Lord’s dwelling-place of faith. We see that its summit has reached to the light of the stars, and we know that its foundations, even when the work was only beginning, were rooted so deeply and faithfully by the divine will that the whole world has become aware of it. From that summit, then, which rises wholly above all the rest, right to the end of the way out, there appears a smooth and level road that enjoys the brightness of light. Its front is adorned with a star-like seal, and twelve columns, brighter than snow and immovable in their position of faith, support it for ever by the power of the divinity of our Saviour. The craftsman of so great a work has given us the majesty of his immortal law to understand, as we also take up a righteous faith from the soul. To its gates whoever wishes may approach, urged by nothing else than pure and pious desire, with only the confidence of a clean mind. To this same house a saving purpose has added a wonderful splendour of adornment. I mean that within, throughout the whole enclosure of the Lord’s house, the faith of human beings, honoured with flowering crowns, gathers the fruit of immortality, brings the pure offspring of human life into the open, and makes them illustrious. Then, in turn, the heavenly glory outside, itself crowned, inscribes the prizes of the contest that is ever being born, or rather ever growing; and these, inscribed with fitting praise, adorn the whole completion of the work. This same house of the Lord is guarded by only two guards. Divine fear comes to the minds of some as a means of correction, while praise toward God is always present to the right-minded as the prize of their understanding. With these two stationed at the porch of the most holy place, the doors stand open to receive righteousness, and righteousness, once settled within, remains undefiled; but unrighteousness may not even approach the doors, and is shut out and banished from this place. These things, most honoured brothers, worthy of all praise, being so clear, have led me into the brightness of the eternal and immortal light, so that I should not stand far off and perhaps be made out of tune with the truth by some wavering faith of soul.

“But what shall I declare first? The form of the happiness that lies hidden, enclosed within my breast, or the divine benefits that almighty God has bestowed upon me? From these, the number of his many works would already seem enough to show that our God himself, the Father of all things, has rightly made my humble self his servant. Believe me, most honoured brothers, giving unreserved credence to what I say: even though my mind, filled to the full with divine benefits, seems to be blessed, and seems able on that account to render surpassing praises, nevertheless, as the faithfulness of truth plainly shows, neither voice nor tongue is adequate to carry out the mind’s command—and quite rightly so. For since the greatness of the benefits is beyond measure, the mind, being something lofty, reaches the regions above the body, while the course of the tongue, shut up in a very narrow place and almost untried, falls entirely silent. Who among us is so rash in his thinking as to throw out a word of such presumption, daring to claim quite easily that he can fully utter glorious and worthy praises to God who can do all things, the creator of all that is most beautiful? For if anyone were to consider only the magnificence of him who ordained that he should be born, he would see with understanding that nothing can be found that could be said worthily of God. What, then, ought my humble devotion to say, except what the divine word of truth reveals? Let even the greatest worship consider wisely whether it can attain to his greatness in the very things said about him, without any error making it slip. Would that I, your fellow servant, had abundant resources of speech, so that I might praise as they deserve to be proclaimed those things which our divine Saviour, the guardian of all things, displayed by the gentle will of his divinity at the outset of his coming, when for our benefit he deigned to take from a virgin the dwelling of a pure body, making known to all people the lesson of his compassion.

“Where then shall I begin? With his teaching and majesty? With the divine teachings of which he, by himself and taught by no one, showed himself the only teacher? Or with how, by his providence, multitudes too many to be counted were revived with a little food, the scantiest bread and only two fish? By his divine providence he also raised Lazarus after his death with a short rod and brought him back again into the brightness of light. How might I speak of his pure divinity, by which, seeing a woman suffering from a most secret ailment, and granting her only the favour of speaking with him, he made her well again and free from all disease? Who could worthily describe his immortal work, by which a man consumed by the long and unbroken wasting of disease, lying there with all his limbs loosened and racked, was suddenly strengthened by divine healing, put on his shoulders the very pallet on which he had lain, and ran through his homeland and district pouring out praises of thanksgiving? Or his divine and steady walking, when he stepped onto the wild sea, trod it underfoot and went across on foot, made the liquid of the deepest sea firm beneath his divine footsteps, and made his way through the midst of an ocean bounded by no measure of depth as if over dry land? Or his gentle forbearance, by which, victorious in all things, he tamed the insolence of senseless multitudes and, removing their savagery far from them once it was tamed, subjected it to the law? Or those most brilliant and greatest works of his divinity, by which we live, in which we delight, and through which we not only look forward to the hope of future happiness but in a way already possess it? What more do I dare to say, with so slight a preparation of speech, except only this, which the purity of my consecrated soul ought to understand: what kind of God almighty is, who dwells in heaven, toward the whole human race, and most especially and above all toward righteousness, which is most beautiful and greater than any praise—since he deigned to take, as befitted his own divine Spirit, a most holy body, to dwell in it, and so to bring salvation to human bodies.

“Since, then, the boundless madness of his enemies, confused as if by a kind of mist, does not hesitate to put a destructively perverse interpretation on this most holy and saving ordinance of God who can do all things, I will try to give a brief account of it, so far as the faith and devotion of my soul supply me with abundance of speech. For their malice, like that of the pagans, introduces such a kind of shamelessness that they are not afraid to say with impious mouth that God who can do all things neither did nor wished to do all that is declared in the divine law. O impious voice, which rightly calls down upon itself every extreme of punishment! Truly, in madness and recklessness it seeks to obscure the glory of this divine benefaction, which no human being can comprehend. For what is more worthy of God than purity? It came forth from the most holy communion with the fountain of righteousness, flooded through the whole circuit of the world, and displayed to mankind the powers of the most holy virtues. Those who at first thought these virtues hostile to themselves suffered the fate of the Assyrians, and since the Assyrians led the way in this evil example, the other nations too were persuaded to side with them. Yet among them, as we confirm by our own observation, we see the divine compassion of God our Saviour at work, since he himself has commanded those of them who for many years, day after day, were driven by the goad of fiery madness to come to the forbearance of saving healing. And even so the greatness of such a benefaction cannot win the gratitude of the rest, because men do not know that divine power is able to raise up any people, to establish it once raised on high, and then again to pull it down and dissolve it. Indeed, human affairs would have turned out the opposite way, had not God who can do all things resolved to accomplish everything by the silent will of his divinity. For human madness would have run rampant, human insolence without limit would have laid waste every soul, and the many other things that fulfil their proper order in the course of the world could never have appeared. All would quickly have perished together with ignorance of God. The injustice of envy and malice would not have remained confined to a few; no one would have been found free of this malice, since the kinds of religious cults had spread so greatly and widely into men’s souls that, through their shamefulness, the light of this brightness of ours would undeservedly have been darkened for them and they would have been deprived of it for ever.

“No argument of those I have mentioned, therefore, will be able to drag my faith out of my soul. For there accompanies it, with nothing evil standing in the way, a perfect power: the living Word of truth, the one who can do all things, the guardian of all things, the protector of our salvation. So in a certain way he seems to lavish upon us the converse of his most holy Word, to preserve [?] the one who sets free, and to grant us the brightness of light. Why then, even now, do the peoples of all the nations, failing to perceive the heavenly light and despising what is most glorious and holy, seek after what is earthly, which has no substance of truth, no radiance of pure brightness, no sovereignty of heavenly divinity? O unworthy spectacle! Even now, falling short in no impiety and paying no heed to what is right, they fall into wretched error and do not see, and they never cease defiling the brightness of the world with these filthy works: setting up wood and stone and bronze and silver and gold and such earthly materials to be worshipped, promising themselves the hope of life from them, building temples for them with conspicuous adornment, and thus adding ever more to their worship, because the size of the buildings they have raised offers a marvel worthy of their own eyes. When they think they are doing these things, it is plainly evident—even though in their arrogance they themselves neither perceive nor see it—that, while they imagine they are glorying in their own works, they are caught. Do we not see how great and how mighty God is, the ruler of all, who is also master and judge of all, and whom some, without realizing it, insult by their very confidence in what they suppose to be their own virtue? For by his design the form of our body too received its proper shape. And so that we might have harmony in its full vigour, he bound together the joining of all the limbs with the strongest sinews, so that in every action of our endeavour we might possess the untiring vigour of our own harmony. When these things had been completed by his saving design, he also breathed a spirit into us, so that all of them could move and flourish; he granted sight to our eyes, gave understanding to our head, and enclosed reason within this whole region of our mind. Therefore, if anyone of sound mind considers the reasoning of this design, and leaves aside the rest, which can be grasped neither by word nor by number, he will be able with quick reflection both to see and to understand the eternal and saving authority of the immortal God. No man will be able to bind him in the snares of any error, since it is clearly open to him to see that all things that have come to be exist by the power of God, as he himself has willed all these things to be.

“And so that it may be seen that a lawless way of life in the world produced in men their ignorance of God—when the thought of a first sin was born in the wretched souls of perverse men from the deceit of the enemy—we may take clear proof of this from the divine law. For from the time when the divine and holy command was not kept with fitting care by those two who were set there in the beginning, the flower of this name [?] sprang up afterwards; and it continued and grew all the more from the time when those two were cast out by the divine will. This evil, together with men’s perversity, advanced so far that it passed sentence on the foundations of both east and west, and the very excess of the opposing power seized men’s minds and darkened them. In this matter, however, the untiring compassion of God who can do all things is eternal and immortal. For through all the days and times that have passed, God sets free countless multitudes of peoples enslaved under this burden, through me, his own servant, and will lead them out into the full brightness of eternal light. From all this, therefore, most beloved brothers, I am confident that through a more intimate providence and the glorious benefits of our immortal God I shall henceforth be the more distinguished for my most pure faith toward him.

“Let the most pure synod of your holiness, then, receive me, and do not allow the doors of the most chaste Church, the pure and common mother of us all, to be shut against me.
