Even though the thought of my soul, seeking the perfect purity of the catholic faith, does not even now consider itself worthy to obtain this very easily, it nevertheless urges and reminds, has borne on the brow of its own modesty the seal of all the noblest virtues, and has begun to lay hold of the gates of immortality and to knock at them, so that you too may deign at once to grant the goodwill of your brotherhood, looking toward the one concord and peace of the catholic faith. For this is fitting to God, in keeping with the faith of the catholic Church, and beneficial to the common good: that all of us together should offer a worthy return to the one who has bestowed on us the most precious peace granted us by God.”

"It would be a terrible thing, truly terrible, if now that our enemies have been destroyed and no one dares to resist any longer, we should turn our weapons on one another and give our enemies pleasure and cause for laughter. This would be all the worse since we are discussing divine matters and have the teaching of the all-holy Spirit in writing. The books of the Gospels and of the apostles, and the oracles of the ancient prophets, clearly teach us what we must believe about God. So let us drive out this warlike strife and find the answer to our questions in the divinely inspired words."

The all-wise emperor set these words and others like them before the priests, as a son who loves his father speaks to his fathers, for he was working to bring about agreement on the apostolic doctrines. Three hundred and eighteen bishops had come together to the synod. Three hundred of them accepted what was said and welcomed both harmony with one another and soundness of doctrine. The rest, as we said earlier, fought against the apostolic doctrines. These men, seventeen in number, worked hard to strengthen the opinion of Arius. They were Eusebius of Nicomedia, as already mentioned, Theognis of Nicaea, Maris of Chalcedon, Theodore of Heraclea in Thrace, Menophantus of Ephesus, Patrophilus of Scythopolis, Narcissus of Neronias in Second Cilicia, which we now call Irenopolis, Theonas of Marmarica, Secundus of Ptolemais in Egypt, and eight others with them. They mixed themselves in with the choir of the three hundred saints as if they were orthodox, but they worked against the apostolic doctrines and pleaded on behalf of Arius. They were nobly opposed by our fathers among the saints Alexander of Constantinople, who was then a presbyter, and Athanasius, the archdeacon of the church of Alexandria. For this reason envy armed itself against them, as we shall relate later. Our holy bishops called Arius to the synod and allowed him to defend his own doctrines, at the bidding of the emperor, victorious in all things, since, as we have just said, he himself sat with the synod.

But a remarkable thing done at the synod by the emperor, victorious in all things, should not be passed over in silence. When all the bishops had assembled, inquiries and comparisons of views were taking place, as is customary, and some of the bishops had petty quarrels with one another. They handed in petitions and drew up accusations before the pious emperor. He received the petitions, sealed them with his ring, and ordered them to be kept safe. Seeing how these bishops were at odds with one another, he said that they must all come together on a single day to deal with these matters. When the appointed day arrived, the emperor took his seat in the midst of them. Once there was a silence suited to the occasion, he ordered everyone's petitions to be brought. He received them and put them in the fold of his robe, refusing even to glance at their contents. Then he said: "God has appointed you priests and rulers to judge and decide for the multitudes. He has declared you to be gods, since you are above all other people, according to the sayings 'I said, You are gods, all of you sons of the Most High,' and 'God has taken his stand in the assembly of the gods.' You must therefore pay little attention to common affairs and devote all your effort to divine things." He ordered fire to be brought and commanded that the petitions be burned. He was anxious that no outsider should learn of the unseemly undertakings of such bishops. So great was the emperor's reverence for the priests of God, a reverence that all right-thinking people would admire.

I think it would also be wrong to pass over in silence another thing of the same kind that he did. Some quarrelsome and abusive laymen had brought charges against certain bishops and handed their written accusations to the emperor, and this was before the agreement had been reached. He received these too, tied them up, sealed them with his ring and ordered them to be kept. Then, once he had brought about the settlement and agreement, he ordered them to be brought, and in the presence of all the bishops he burned these too, swearing that he had not read any of what was written in them. He said that the faults of priests must not become known to the multitude, so that people would not take this as an occasion of stumbling and sin without fear. They say he also added that if he had seen with his own eyes a bishop breaking into another man's marriage, he would have covered the unlawful deed with his purple robe, so that the sight of what was being done would not harm those who saw it. So great was the emperor's godly and admirable wisdom.

For many days, indeed for a long stretch of time, the emperor met with the bishops, discussing questions of the faith with them and sorting through their different opinions. For, as we have said many times, there were some among them who were mixed up with the lawless doctrines of Arius and who worked against the great number of holy bishops who were fighting for the truth. But our fathers, the best and in every way most holy of men, were protected by the armor of truth and boldly proclaimed the splendid and blameless faith. With them was also a great number of confessors, who stood against those who wanted to promote the wicked doctrines of Arius.

Among them was also the great and holy Paphnutius, an ornament to the choir of confessors and bishops. He was an Egyptian and a man of God, one of that company whose right eye the emperor Maximian had gouged out, and whose left leg he had hamstrung before handing him over to be held in the mines. So great was the grace of God in him that he performed signs no less than those done long ago by the apostles. He drove out demons by a word alone, and by prayer he healed people of various illnesses. He asked God to give the blind their sight, and he restored paralyzed people to their natural strength, making their limbs work soundly again. The emperor held him in the highest honor, often summoned him to the palace, and kissed the eye that had been gouged out. Such was the pious emperor's faith in the saints.

There was also Spyridon, a Cypriot man distinguished in the Lord, who had dedicated to the flock of Christ the experience as a shepherd that he had gained since boyhood. He was known for living the life of a prophet. Even while he administered his see, he did not stop tending his own sheep. He was so kind and forbearing that once, when robbers made a stealthy attack on his flock, they were held fast by invisible bonds and could not move until morning. The blessed man came to them and by his prayer had them released from their bonds. More than that, as they were leaving he gave them the best of his rams, saying, "Take this for your needs, young men, so that you do not go away empty-handed tonight and blame me for your want." We have heard many other wonderful things about this saint, but we shall set down one out of many.

This blessed and celebrated man of God had a daughter named Irene, who served the old man faithfully and departed this human life as a virgin. After her death a merchant returned from abroad and asked the old man for a deposit that he had left in the keeping of his daughter, the virgin. The blessed Spyridon knew nothing at all about the matter. Since the man kept pressing him hard, the old man searched the house up and down many times. When he found nothing he was greatly distressed, and he told the man that he knew of nothing and that there was nothing in the house. But the merchant cried out, overcome with tears and lamenting, and demanded his deposit. He said he would kill himself over the loss if he did not receive what he had entrusted, explaining that he had kept this as a comfort for his old age by depositing it with the virgin. So the holy old man was compelled to go with the merchant to his daughter's tomb to inquire into the matter. When he arrived he called his daughter by name and said to her, "My child Irene." She answered from the tomb and said to him, "What do you want, father?" The old man said to her, "Where did you put this man's deposit, daughter?" She said to him, "It lies in such and such a place, father," and she pointed out the place clearly to her father. He said to her, "Go in peace, my child Irene." So the old man returned home, found the deposit where the virgin had said it lay, and gave it back to the man. Many other wonders of this man are celebrated, and many miracles, which the local people still show to visitors even today, to confirm our true faith in Christ. Such were the holy men who adorned the church in those times, and many of them were present at the synod in Nicaea. Athanasius too, of whom we have already spoken and who was then a deacon, was acknowledged by all to have a share in that choir of saints. He was at the side of Alexander, bishop of the church of Alexandria, and was his very best helper. Day after day, for a long time, our holy bishops raised a great many questions about the faith, believing that nothing should be done hastily or rashly in so great an inquiry. They often summoned Arius and, through close questioning, opened up his propositions and refuted them. They took the greatest care and thought over how they ought to vote and define the faith so as to overthrow his lawless doctrines. So they deliberated over these matters with much reflection and prayer to God. That is why they set out, very wisely and most fittingly, their refutations of the lawless doctrines of Arius and his followers, tearing out by the roots their foul blasphemies against the Son of God and destroying them. To their claim that the Son is not from God, our bishops opposed the phrase "God from God." To their claim that he is not true God, our bishops wrote in answer "true God from true God." To their claim that he is a creature, our bishops responded with the definition "begotten, not made." And against the "of a different essence" that they put forward, our bishops set the statement that the Son is "of one essence" with the Father, that is, "begotten from the essence of the Father." They proclaimed him creator and maker "of things visible and invisible," according to the apostolic faith handed down to his church from the beginning, and they supplied proofs from the testimony of Scripture, as the course of our account will show. Having overturned the deadly poisons with this antidote, they now unanimously set down in writing the apostolic faith in a clearer form.

"The holy, great and ecumenical synod of our holy fathers gathered at Nicaea, through the blessed and holy Hosius, bishop of the city of Córdoba in the province of Spain, who also held the place of the bishop of Rome together with the presbyters from that see already named, spoke as follows, another man interpreting for him: The Godhead is not one person, as the Jews suppose, but three persons in true subsistence, not in mere name, and this is proclaimed by many testimonies from both the Old and the New Testament. The Old Testament, which still speaks in a more bodily manner, presented the Word as something spoken. The New Testament showed that the Word is God, according to the words 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,' and that he is a perfect person from a perfect person. For the Son is not a part of God; he is perfect God just as the Father is, being of the same essence as the Father who begot him in a way beyond words. In the same way the Holy Spirit also exists together with the Father and the Son, being of the same essence and the same substance as the Father and the Son. Therefore we must confess one will, one kingdom, one authority, one lordship over all created natures, both visible and intelligible, and one Godhead and the same essence of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. We do not proclaim a confusion or a division of the persons of that ineffable and blessed Trinity. We believe that the Father is always truly the Father of a true Son, existing and subsisting forever; that the Son is truly the Son of a true Father, existing and subsisting forever; and that the Holy Spirit is truly the Holy Spirit, existing and subsisting forever: a Trinity undivided, ineffable, truly incomprehensible and inexpressible, whose Godhead is one and whose essence is the same. And we confess this as the true and exact doctrine of the same faith, handed down to us from the beginning by the Lord through his holy apostles and through our ancient holy fathers who kept their holy faith spotless. With the good pleasure of the Holy Spirit, we are ready to show by a great many testimonies from the divine Scriptures that these things are so."

When these words were spoken by them, or rather by the Holy Spirit through them, those who championed the impiety of Arius grumbled under their breath, greatly distressed. These were Eusebius of Nicomedia, Theognis of Nicaea and their party, whom we have already described. Even so, they looked to Arius's hired men, certain philosophers of great learning, whom Arius had hired as advocates of his own wickedness and brought with him to that holy and ecumenical synod. A great many philosophers were present, and the enemies of the truth, having placed their hopes in them, as we have just said, were rightly brought down together with the teacher of their blasphemy. In him and in them the holy Scripture was fulfilled, which says, "Cursed is everyone who puts his hope in a human being and whose heart has turned away from the Lord." For truly the blasphemous heart of Arius, the enemy of God, and of those who shared his impiety had turned away from the Lord, since they dared to call the Son of God a creature and a thing made, he who is the creator of all things and maker of created natures visible and invisible.

One of the philosophers hired by Arius, who was admired far above all the others, argued at great length on behalf of Arius against our bishops for a great many days. Each day the debate drew a large audience, as crowds of people came running together. Against what the holy synod said, the philosopher put forward the impious blasphemies of Arius, saying of the Son of God that "there was a time when he was not," and that he is a creature and a thing made from nothing, and of a different essence and subsistence. He fought hard for these foul doctrines of Arius, with words falling like snowstorms, raging against the Son of God and attacking that choir of holy priests, while the enemy of human salvation spoke in him and through him. But the champions of the truth, our bishops, calmly offered the philosopher the replies that were due and fitting in defense of the apostolic doctrines. They imitated David, the great prophet and king, who says, "I was ready and was not troubled." They burned up all the philosopher's intricate propositions with the divine word as fire burns tow. Yet even so the philosopher, trusting in his diabolical skill with words, persisted in shooting back arrows at the truth the bishops proclaimed. He met every argument brought against him with great ease, or so he thought, and he forced himself to answer every point raised. But like an eel he slipped out of the arguments that pressed him harder, in which he thought he was holding his ground, and he was caught by his own words and fell. Even so, he went on attacking the most peaceable synod in a boastful frenzy, hoping to defeat the invincible power of Christ's unconquerable Spirit that was in them. But God, who catches the wise in their own craftiness, wished to show that his kingdom does not consist in talk but in power, and through one of his servants who was there he forcefully silenced the evil demon speaking in the philosopher, and more than that, drove it out. For one of the holy confessors present at the synod was a man of simple nature, more so than any of the other saints, who knew nothing but Jesus Christ and him crucified in the flesh, according to the Scriptures. He was there with the bishops, and when he saw the philosopher exalting himself over our holy bishops and boasting in his wicked disputation, he asked the bishops, the priests of God, to give him a chance to talk with the philosopher. Our holy bishops, seeing the man's simplicity and that he had no education, urged him not to put himself forward, in case he should become a laughingstock to the wicked enemies of the truth. But he would not hold back. He went up to the philosopher and said to him, "In the name of Jesus Christ, God the Word, who is forever with the Father, hear the doctrines of the truth, philosopher." The philosopher said to him, "Speak, if you like." And the saint said to him, "There is one God, who made heaven and earth and the sea and everything in them. He formed man from the earth, and brought all things into being by his Word and by the Holy Spirit. This Word, philosopher, we know to be the Son of God and we worship him. We believe that for our redemption he became flesh from a virgin, was born and became man, and that through the suffering of his flesh on the cross and through his death he set us free from eternal condemnation, and through his resurrection he won eternal life for us. We hope that he who ascended into heaven will come again and be the judge of everything we have done. Do you believe these things, philosopher?" The philosopher, as though he had never had any experience in arguing back, was struck dumb and fell silent like a deaf or mute man. He said only this to him, in a very pitiful voice: "I too think that these things are so, and that it is nothing other than everything just as you have said." The old man said to him, "If you believe that these things are so, philosopher, get up and follow me, and let us hurry to the church, where you will receive the seal of this faith." The philosopher turned himself wholly to true reverence for the God of all things. He got up and followed the old man, and turning around he said to his disciples and to all who had come to listen, "Listen, gentlemen. As long as my contest was one of words, I set words against words and overturned what was put to me by the art of speaking. But when, instead of words, a divine power came out of the mouth of the one debating with me, words could no longer stand against that power, for no human being can resist God. So if any of you is able to understand, as I have come to understand, let him believe in Christ and follow this old man, in whom God has spoken."

In this way the philosopher took up the faith, was enlightened and became a Christian, and he rejoiced to have been defeated by the old man. When this philosopher had been baptized and joined to the church of God, and was at rest and rejoicing over the mighty works of God, the synod rejoiced. The debate with another philosopher named Phaedo, who also spoke on behalf of Arius, the enemy of God, and of the blasphemy he had invented.

The philosopher's question to the holy synod on "Let us make man": "And God said, 'Let us make man in our image and likeness.' If then one were led by what the words indicate, or by their sense, one would say that God has human form. But we know that God is simple and without shape. So tell me, what do the meanings of these terms intend? Surely the divine does not have human form?" The reply of the holy fathers through Eustathius, bishop of Antioch: "Not so, philosopher. Rather, God's saying 'Let them rule over all the earth' and 'Let them have dominion over it and over everything in it': this is the proper sense of making man in the image of God and of his ruling over all the earth. Just as God rules over all the earth and everything in it, so he appointed man as a second ruler over all the earth and what is in it. This, I say, is what it means that man was made in the image and likeness of God." A further reply of the holy fathers on the same point, through the same bishop Eustathius: "'And God said, Let us make man in our image and likeness.' But let us ask, philosopher, to whom he said this. For in saying 'And God said, Let us make man in our image and likeness,' Scripture has set us a question to consider: to whom did he say 'Let us make'? For after saying 'And God said, Let us make man,' it goes on to say, 'And God made man; in the image of God he made him; male and female he made them.' So the meaning of 'Let us make' signifies a person who is a fellow creator, and introduces one who shares the same name equally. For just as the Father who said 'Let us make man' is God, so the one to whom he said 'Let us make' is also God, since the Godhead of both persons is one: the one who said 'Let us make man in our image and likeness' and the one who made man. For the expression 'Let us make' presents the fixed and unchanging Godhead of the Father and the Son. For the image of God is simple and uncompounded, being fire by nature."
The unanimous reply of the holy fathers: "The essence of the holy Trinity is unapproachable light, a nature that cannot be endured. This is the meaning of 'Let us make.'

The philosopher's objection on behalf of Arius: I will say again that God is simple, without form and without composition. How, then, are we to understand "in our image and likeness", and how can it be that the one who spoke did not exist before the one to whom he said, "Let us make man", and the rest? Give us a clear proof on these matters, if you can.

The holy bishops spoke through Hosius, bishop of the city of Córdoba, with another man interpreting for him: If, as you claim, the Father existed before the Son, and the Son came later, created by God after some period of time and afterwards proclaimed his Son by the Father himself; if, as you impiously and blasphemously say, he was created by him beforehand for the making of created natures, then, by your impious reasoning, the uncreated God would have said to the one you call a created god: "Make me a man in my image and likeness." But God has always been Father, as we have already shown, and the Son always coexists with the Father. He is not later in time, not lesser in power, not bounded by place. He always and equally coexists with the Father eternally, begotten from him in a way beyond understanding and beyond words, as we said before. He is true God, existing always from the ever-existing true God and Father. He is without beginning together with the Father, eternal together with the Father, always reigning together with the Father, of one substance with the Father, equal in power to the Father, a fellow-creator with the Father. The divine voice of the Gospels does say that all things came into being through the Son, and that "without him not one thing came into being that has come into being"; yet he did not create apart from the Father, since there is one Godhead and one will of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, the Father being always inseparable from the Son and the Son from the Father. So you must understand, philosopher, that the Father and the Son are one in the substance of the Godhead, as the Son himself cries out in the Gospels, "I and the Father are one"; and it was to him that the Father said, "Let us make man in our image and likeness."

The philosopher's objection: In our earlier questions we already said that God does not have human form. So tell us what this saying means: "in our image and likeness." The phrase gives us no small struggle; for the moment, this is what must be discussed.

Answer of the holy synod through the same Hosius, bishop of the city of Córdoba: The phrase "in the image", philosopher, must be understood not in terms of the composition of bodies. Rather, the word of truth presents it as something stamped on the intellect. Listen, then, and understand. God, being good by nature, implanted his image and likeness in the intellectual being of man: goodness, simplicity, holiness, purity, generosity, kindness, blessedness, and the like. He did this so that what God is by nature, the man created by him, that is, his intellect, might be able to have by God's grace. Skilled painters, when they paint likenesses on panels, do not paint their images from a single colour but from many, leaving nothing out. In the same way God has granted the man he created to have, through the virtues, his image and likeness in the intellectual storehouse of the soul, that is, in the mind. So the image is found in man complete, through the divine qualities we have mentioned, which God placed in him when he said, "Let us make man in our image and likeness."

The philosopher's objection: Let me set these matters aside for the present. What needs to be asked instead concerns the one through whom God made man and all things, visible and invisible. What you have said does not seem right to me: that the Father and the Son are one in the same respect, eternally and together, and that the Son, being God, always existed together with the Father beforehand. I would say that he was brought into being by God as an assistant in the works of creation. For God needed an assistant to fashion man and the world. Therefore, when God the Creator was about to create the created natures, he brought into existence for himself an instrument through which he would create all natures. Just as a carpenter first provides himself with tools for fashioning the things he means to make, so we can understand it in the case of God: he brought the Son into existence for himself as an instrument and created the world through him. When the apostles say that "all things came into being through him", it means that the natures made through him were created as through an instrument. And when God said that man was to be created "in our image and likeness" through the instrument, that is, through the Son, God was speaking of his own image and likeness.

Reply of the holy fathers through Leontius, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, and Eupsychius, bishop of Tyana: If, as you say, the Son was created by the Father as an instrument for making the created natures, then you are refuted by your own words, philosopher. For the voice of the Gospel says, as you yourself just recalled, "All things came into being through him", and it adds, "and without him not one thing came into being that has come into being." So if everything created came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being, and the Son too is a creature, as you say, then he created himself, and not the Father.

The philosopher's objection: I have said once and for all that God made all things through him as through an instrument, having made him for this very purpose before all creation, preparing him as an instrument for making the created natures.

Reply of the holy fathers through the same bishops, Leontius and Eupsychius: Tell us, my good man, where did anyone ever proclaim to you that the Son of God, or his Holy Spirit, is an instrument? Give us the testimonies for your propositions. Which Spirit-bearing writer's signature can you produce who declared the Son of God to be an instrument, the Son who is the Creator of all the ages, of all the heavenly hosts, and of everything on earth? Listen, then, philosopher, to the testimonies from the divine Scriptures, which have set forth that his Son is God, coeternal with the Father, and the Creator and Maker of all created natures. In the book of Genesis you have the prophet Moses, who declared the Son to be a fellow-creator with God the Father. He says, as we told you before, my good man, "God said, 'Let us make man in our image and likeness'"; [?] this naturally calls the Son a person and a fellow-creator, not an instrument. For the words "And God made man; in the image of God he made him; male and female he made them" signify the authority of persons. By saying "Let us make man" he does away with the notion of instruments. Now receive a still clearer and more authoritative testimony, set forth about the person of the Son alone, which shows him to be the Maker of all the natures that have come into being. As it is written in the book of Baruch, from the mouth of the prophet Jeremiah, who says: "He who prepared the earth for all time filled it with four-footed creatures; he who sends out the light, and it goes; he called it, and it obeyed him with trembling. The stars shone in their watches and rejoiced; he called them, and they said, 'Here we are'; they shone with gladness for the one who made them. This is our God; no other shall be compared with him. He found out the whole way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel whom he loved. Afterwards he appeared on earth and lived among men." And Isaiah says to Israel: "And now, have you not known? Have you not heard? The everlasting God, the God who prepared the ends of the earth." Who, then, is this everlasting God, philosopher, who prepared the ends of the earth, who also appeared on earth and lived among men? Do you say it was the Son who lived among men, or the Father?

Answer of the philosopher: "It was the Son," he said, "who lived among them, as the divine Scriptures have said, and I have accepted this, being persuaded by them. But I still have a very strong and unanswerable objection concerning him: that God created him before all creation, so that he might create all things through him. And I will prove this as the debate goes on."

Answer of the holy fathers through the same most holy bishops, Leontius and Eupsychius: Not so, philosopher. You cannot prove what you claim. For he is God's offspring, not his handiwork, as we have shown at length. Indeed, philosopher, which man rich in piety and understanding is not amazed at the many workings of the natures he fashioned, fashioned as by God, that is, created by him, when Scripture cries out, "God made man", and, "God saw all the things that he had made, and behold, they were very good"? John the Evangelist shows most clearly that he always coexists with the Father, coeternal with the Father and without beginning together with him. For he says, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being that has come into being." See, philosopher, it has been shown most clearly that the Son is the Maker of every nature that has come into being. If, then, he is the Maker of all created things, visible and intelligible, as indeed he is, it is plain that he is truly God by nature, and not an instrument, as you say, nor a creature, nor a handiwork, nor later than the Father. For the word "was", spoken four times by the Evangelist, admits of nothing existing before it. And so that you may know most fully that he is not subject to another's authority but has authority in his own right, as the Father does, receive another very clear testimony. Listen to the inspired Isaiah crying out. "And they will wish," he says, "that they had been burned with fire", foretelling this of the Jews, "for a child has been born, a son has also been given to us, whose rule is upon his shoulder, and his name is called Messenger of Great Counsel, Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God, Sovereign." Hear, philosopher: he is proclaimed beforehand as Sovereign, and not as subject to another's authority, as you people say. But let us repeat the words again: "Mighty God, Sovereign, Prince of Peace, Father of the age to come." And in one of his acts of kindness the only-begotten Son of God himself shows that he has authority in his own right and is the creator of man: in the restoring of the man blind from birth, which was done by the Son of God himself. For he is the coeternal radiance of the Father and the exact imprint of his whole being, as the apostle Paul, the chosen vessel, says. See, philosopher, how many [?] have shown the Son of God to be without beginning, since he is also uncreated together with the Father, and the Creator of all created natures, both visible and intelligible, as we have said many times. But where are the witnesses for your instruments? Tell us, if you have any. Perhaps, then, you were baptized believing in instruments, if indeed, as you say, you are a believer in God.

The philosopher's objection concerning "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works", from the Proverbs of Solomon: "Since you do such violence to the truth," he said, "what are we to say about this plain statement: 'The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works'?"

Reply of the holy fathers through Eusebius, son of Pamphilus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine: Why do you run through the depths so plausibly and so easily, as you suppose? Do not, philosopher, heap up cowardly pretexts for yourself. Take care that you do not step carelessly onto cliffs that are hard to climb and fall headlong. But now we will speak about “The Lord created me.” Those before us have published many explanations of this saying, “The Lord created me,” and among others they have applied it to the economy in the flesh of the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ. You surely know their expositions and how they understood it. But we will now set out an exposition on other grounds as well, with the Lord Jesus Christ working with us. And if you wish, philosopher, let us put forward the whole passage together with its beginning. Its beginning says: “If I declare to you the things that happen day by day, I will remember to recount the things from the beginning of the age.” Then it goes on: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works; before the age he founded me in the beginning, before he made the earth, before the springs of water came forth, before the mountains were settled, and before all the hills he begets me.” So, to establish the words “The Lord created me,” he added: “The Lord made lands and uninhabited places.” Let us then seek the Lord who created it, the one who also made lands and uninhabited places. Solomon was stung by the words of the one who said to Job, “Where were you when I founded the earth?” and said, “The Lord made lands and uninhabited places.” And in the book of Baruch, from the mouth of Jeremiah the prophet, as we showed earlier, it says concerning the one who made lands and uninhabited places: “The sons of Hagar, who seek understanding on the earth, the merchants and the seekers of understanding, did not know the way of wisdom, nor did they remember her paths.” And a little later: “But he who knows all things knows her; he found her out by his understanding.” Having spoken of the one who found out wisdom by his understanding, it goes on to his works as well, saying: “He who prepared the earth for all time filled it with four-footed beasts; he who sends forth the light, and it goes.” We must not neglect, philosopher, to repeat the same words again for a clear proof of the matter before us. “He who sends forth the light,” it says, “and it goes; he called it, and it obeyed him with trembling. The stars shone in their watches and rejoiced; he called them, and they said, ‘Here we are’; they shone with gladness for the one who made them. This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him. He found out the whole way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel whom he loved. After this he appeared on earth and lived among men.” We have added these two passages, which properly concern the one who made lands and uninhabited places and which Solomon and Baruch, that is, Jeremiah, spoke. (For having said “The Lord created me,” he went on to his works as well, saying, “The Lord made lands and uninhabited places.”) So let us reason out, my good sir, who is the Lord who made lands and uninhabited places. We will understand that it is none other than the one who prepared the earth for all time (for in preparing the earth he made lands and uninhabited places), who also filled it with four-footed beasts, who also called the light and it obeyed him with trembling, and so on, and of whom it says that “he appeared on earth and lived among men.” We must understand, then, that this is the Lord who created the rational wisdom as the beginning of his ways. He who made lands and uninhabited places and prepared the earth for all time made this wisdom ready for the man made in his image. But let us look again at the beginning of the passage: “If I declare to you the things that happen day by day.” He did not say “the things to come.” And again he says, “I will remember to recount the things from the beginning of the age,” but not the things before the age. We have come to know that the Son of God is the one who also created the rational wisdom, who prepared the earth for all time, who made lands and uninhabited places, and who also said to Job, “When the stars were made, all my angels praised me.” And Moses says of the one who made the light: “And God said, ‘Let there be light,’” and he goes on: “And God made the two great lights and the stars,” and so on. What has been said seems to me sufficient, philosopher, and the proofs have established it: the Son of God created both the rational wisdom in Solomon and all created things, and he is not an instrument. But to set before you a clearer proof of the truth of the matter, and to come more quickly to its meaning and to its contemplation, let us cite the words of scripture. When the prophet Moses was about to depart this life, as is written in the book of the Assumption of Moses, he summoned Joshua son of Nun and, speaking with him, said: “And God foresaw me before the foundation of the world to be the mediator of his covenant.” And in the book of the Mystical Words of Moses, Moses himself foretold things about David and Solomon. About Solomon he foretold this: “And God will make wisdom and righteousness and full knowledge shine upon him like a torch; he will build the house of God,” and so on. And to make what I say clearer, let us examine the meaning this way: Is man for the sake of the world, or the world for the sake of man? The philosopher: Certainly the world is for the sake of man.

Our holy bishops said through the same bishop, Eusebius son of Pamphilus: If the world is for the sake of man, then man was surely prior in God’s thought, and the world came after man and after the rational wisdom in God’s thought. Man, therefore, is prior to the world, and so is wisdom. Whatever is prior to the world also exists before the natures of the world, such as heaven and earth, day, night, clouds, winds, deeps, springs, mountains and hills. Wisdom is prior to all these, and so is man, for whose sake the world exists, in God’s thought. Man, then, being older than the natures of the world, and wisdom as well, already existed before the world in God’s thought. Yet man, though created later, was brought in during the course of creation, while the world, which in God’s thought came after man, was brought forth earlier in the course of creation. The same is true of wisdom, which the Son of God found out by his understanding and gave to the man made in his image: it too existed before the world and its natures in God’s thought. Solomon knew this within himself, taught by the wisdom God had given him: man and wisdom existed before the world and its natures in God’s thought. He also examined closely how the Lord, who had found out by his understanding what already existed before the world in God’s thought, before the foundation of the world, then created it later than the world and its natures. So Solomon speaks as if in the person of the wisdom in man, which existed before the world in God’s thought: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works.” It was fitting for the wisdom in man, the rational wisdom made ready for the man who came to be in the image of God, to utter these words. So he applied “The Lord created” to what existed before the world in God’s thought; to that he attached it. And “he begets me” he said understanding it, in turn, of what is brought forth afterwards by natural procreation. Understand “he begets me,” then, philosopher, of the same nature growing old and being renewed until the end. So “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works” must be taken to refer to the rational wisdom given to man. “He begets me” refers to what comes from that nature itself, according to God’s foreknowledge, from images, rolling like a wheel back around to the turning-post, returning from the beginning: from the first-created man, created in the image of God, in whom God placed the created rational wisdom and on whom he imprinted his pure love. The Savior, accomplishing the re-creation of that man in himself, said to the Father, in keeping with the economy: “You loved me,” he says, “before the foundation of the world.” And Solomon set down “before the age he founded me in the beginning” knowing that the ages in this world take their substance from the cycle of day and night, and that to exist before day and night is to exist before this age. Having contemplated these matters, Solomon interpreted the words in a way that fits both man and wisdom. Therefore, speaking in her person, he says: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works; before the age he founded me in the beginning.” He reasoned within himself again that when God was about to bring these natures of the world into being, though they were earlier in creation than man and wisdom, those who were prior in God’s thought had to be present, so that as the natures were brought forth they might record them in order as they came forth; and he reasoned that man and wisdom were appointed to rule over the works. So the rational and discerning wisdom given to man by God, which shone upon Solomon like a torch, as the great Moses says, speaks in Solomon: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works,” and so on. In the person of this wisdom, which together with man is prior to the world, the same writer recounts the works of God as he brought forth the natures in the world, and says: “The Lord made lands and uninhabited places, the inhabited heights of the land under heaven. When he prepared the heaven, I was present with him, when he marked out his own throne upon the winds; when he made strong the clouds above, and when he set firm the springs of the land under heaven; when he set his decree for the sea, and the waters shall not pass beyond the word of his mouth; and when he made strong the foundations of the earth, I was beside him, setting things in order; I was the one in whom he delighted.” These things are spoken in the person of wisdom, and they show beyond doubt that the one who existed before the world in God’s thought, for whose sake the world was prepared, clearly existed before the natures of the world as well. Having become a witness to the coming forth of the natures, the one who was prior to them, wisdom, which he found out by his understanding and made ready for man, recounts their order. Who, then, is the one who prepared this wisdom beforehand and gave it to man, and who explained the works to him? None other than the one who prepared the earth for all time, who also filled it with four-footed beasts, who called the light and it obeyed him with trembling, who appeared on earth and lived among men. To him belong the active comings forth of the natures. It has been shown most clearly at every point that “The Lord created me” was said in the person of wisdom: not of the Son of God, but of the rational wisdom made ready by the Lord himself and given to man, for whose sake the world came to be. It was said in the person of the rational wisdom. And the Lord confirms what has been said in the Gospel, saying: “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.” He personified the world as the Sabbath, as if to say: the world was made for man, and not man for the world.
Another objection of the philosopher: “But,” he says, “the wisdom in Solomon is the Son of God, that is, the wisdom of God, who said, ‘The Lord created me,’ and so on.”
Reply of the holy bishops to the philosopher through the bishop Eusebius, son of Pamphilus: Tell me, philosopher, is the wisdom in Solomon, as you say, the wisdom of God?
The philosopher: “Yes,” he says, “that is so.”
The bishop: Tell me, does the wisdom of God have foreknowledge or not?
The philosopher: Yes, it does.
The bishop: Is the wisdom of God, which you say is in Solomon, the Son of God?
The philosopher: “Yes,” he says.
The bishop: How does the judge judge? According to foreknowledge or not?
The philosopher: “Yes,” he says, “but how?”
The bishop: So does the judge judge according to foreknowledge, and according to works, as one who knows beforehand?
The philosopher: Yes, I said so.

The bishop: How, then, does the wisdom in Solomon say, “There are three things impossible for me to understand, and the fourth I do not know”? The wisdom in Solomon named the three things and said it could not understand them, and of the fourth it said that it did not know “the ways of a man in his youth.” If, then, the wisdom in Solomon is the wisdom of God, how does it judge the world when it does not know the ways of a man in his youth? And how can it be true that the one who made man in the image of God, that is, the Son of God, does not know the ways of a man in his youth? For Moses the prophet says that he made man, and so does John the evangelist: “All things,” he says, “came into being through him.” He fashioned their hearts one by one; he understands all their works; he tests hearts and minds, according to the prophet who said: “You knew my sitting down and my rising up; you understood all my thoughts,” he says, “from afar. You searched out my path and my portion, and you foresaw all my ways.” And again elsewhere: “He who disciplines the nations, shall he not rebuke, he who teaches man knowledge? The Lord knows the thoughts of men, that they are futile.” Does the one who knows these things and foreknows all things not know the ways of a man in his youth? Much can be found in the scriptures that exposes the folly of those who have misunderstood this saying. For how could the one who teaches man knowledge not know the ways of a man in his youth? Know well, then, philosopher, that Solomon received a discerning wisdom, a reasoning wisdom, which the Son of God found out by his understanding and made ready for the man made in his image. Indeed, the Lord confirms what has been said in the Gospels. By saying, “And behold, something greater than Solomon is here,” he refuted those who say that he is the wisdom in Solomon. For even if the two share the name “wisdom” in the sound of the word, the wisdom of God, the Son of God, knows beforehand and judges according to foreknowledge and according to works, as creator and maker of all things. So Paul too, the chosen vessel, writing to the Hebrews, says something like this about him: “For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and spirit, and able to judge the thoughts and intentions of the heart. No creature is hidden before him, but all things are naked and laid bare to his eyes, to whom we must give account.” And the same apostle writes to the Romans: “To them belong the fathers, and from them, according to the flesh, comes the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.” Here he shows that the wisdom of God the Father is truly God from God himself, eternal from eternal and true from true, being by nature forever the Son of the God and Father who forever is.
Rejoinder of the philosopher: What, then, does it mean when it says, “They did not know the way of wisdom, nor did they remember her paths,” and so on?

Reply of the holy bishops through the same Eusebius Pamphili: Often, philosopher, when you have looked at the words of wisdom, you have marveled at the power of wisdom, because in it one can find the greatest truth of thought in the briefest words. One might perhaps rightly compare the words of Scripture to the Gospel parable which says that the kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed. It is smaller than all the seeds on the earth, but when it has sprung up and grown to its full size, it gives ample shelter to the birds. In the same way we see the power of the divine words sown in brief words. But when their meanings are filled out and stretch out like branches toward the understanding of the birds, that is, of human beings, so great a power is found in them that they give ample shelter not only to the farmers but also to the birds that come near. What, then, moved me to this thought, if not the word of holy Scripture spoken by the sacred psalmist David? It demonstrates and establishes not the reasoning wisdom, as you yourself supposed, but the incomprehensible Wisdom, uncreated and without beginning, which fashioned both that wisdom and everything that has come into being. That Wisdom is Christ, since Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God in the manner of his ineffable and inconceivable Godhead, the true God the Word of God. For he says, "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host." You have heard "the word of the Lord"; you have heard "the Spirit of his mouth." Listen once more, then, to the establishment of the true faith, which the pious understand and proclaim piously. For I think you have not grasped the sense of anything that so great a spiritual choir of holy high priests has already declared to you. Listen, then, piously, and do not try to search out the ineffable by human reasoning. What is perfect neither diminishes nor increases. One is unbegotten: God the Father. One also is begotten from him: the only-begotten Son, God the Word. Just as there is no other God unbegotten together with God the Father, so there is no other Son of God begotten together with his only-begotten Son, God the Word, or begotten before him or after him. Truly one is God the Father; truly one also is the Son, God the Word, ineffably begotten from him. Just as God is not Father in name only, so the Son is not Son in name only, but truly Son. The Father is genuine; the Son is genuine. The Father is God; the Son begotten from him is also God. The Father is perfect; his Son is also perfect. The Father is incorporeal; the Son is also incorporeal, for the stamp and image of the incorporeal is clearly incorporeal. Do you believe this, philosopher, that his only-begotten Son was begotten from the substance of the Father, as we demonstrated from the beginning of our discussion with a great many scriptural testimonies, or not? Counter-question of the philosopher: How, and in what manner? Tell me.

The holy bishops said through the same Eusebius Pamphili: Do not ask how, philosopher. If you do, you are bent on throwing yourself over a cliff by trying to search out what cannot be searched out. We have already told you this at length, and we solemnly warned you of it at the beginning of the debate. If it is possible to ask how the Unbegotten is, then it is also possible to ask how the Begotten is. But if the Unbegotten leaves no room to ask how he is unbegotten, so neither does the Begotten leave room to ask how he was begotten. Do not seek what cannot be searched out, for you will not find it; seek what can be found, and you will find it. If you do inquire, from whom can you learn? From the earth? It did not yet exist. From the sea? The waters had not yet been created. From heaven? It had not been made. From the sun and moon and stars? They had not yet been fashioned. From angels and archangels? They did not yet exist, since the Son is their maker too. From the ages, then? The Only-begotten is before the ages. Do not question things that have not always existed about the one who always exists. The Father is ineffable and unbegotten; the Son is ineffable and was ineffably begotten from him. Keep silent about the "how," and leave it to the one who begot and the one who was begotten. For only the Father knows who the Son is, and the Son the Father, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him, as his Gospel says. But if you will not stop asking how, and insist on searching out the unsearchable, we laugh at your audacity. Or rather, we mourn for you, because you will not understand by faith that God is always the Father of his Son, and that his only-begotten Son is always his Son. The Son always coexists with the Father and is not later than him, as you impiously claim. Understand by faith instead, and confess, as you have often heard, that the Son is perfect from perfect, eternal light from eternal light, true God from the true God and Father, uncreated from uncreated, uncompounded from uncompounded, always with the Father. For "In the beginning was the Word," as John the Evangelist says, "and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." Nothing exists before the "was," philosopher. The "was," philosopher, rules out "was not," as we showed earlier, and "God" rules out "not God." Believe what is written; do not imagine or seek what is not written. Believe that the Son himself fashioned all things that have come into being at the Father's nod. This was not a glance of the eyes, for God is uncompounded, as we said before. It was a nod, in a way that he alone knows. We understand this by faith and proclaim it, following the teaching of the holy Scriptures. By the will of the Father and his own will he fashioned the whole creation, heavenly and earthly, visible and intelligible. He did not use instruments or machines or the help of any other. He acted by the will of the Father, as we said just now, who said to him and to the Holy Spirit, "Let us make man in our image and likeness." He did not say "You make" or "You all make," but "Let us make," showing that the substance and the honor are one and equal in that blessed and ineffable Trinity. Do not grumble under your breath, philosopher, and roll your eyes. Look instead with the eye of the mind at the precision of the apostolic doctrines and receive them faithfully: be unbelieving no longer, but believing. Listen, then, and understand. The Word of God, his Son before the ages, to whom he said "Let us make man" and the rest, himself became man in the last days by the Father's will and his own. He became incarnate from a virgin for the sake of Adam, the man who had fallen. The incorporeal one emptied himself in a body, as the apostle Paul said, for the sake of the body. God the Word took the body as a cloud, so that he would not burn up the created natures in the world, for no one has ever seen God. He was held by flesh, so that the flesh too might be freed from death through its unchangeable union with him. He was invisible in the visible, so that he might endure what is visible. As man he was subject to time, but in truth he was in both respects God and man, one and the same man and God. For Christ is one from both, while the difference between the substances, his Godhead and his flesh, is understood and recognized. He was and is God; he became man by the divine plan. Because of him there are prophets, because of him apostles, because of him martyrs: prophets because of the one they prophesied, apostles because of the one sent according to the divine plan, martyrs because of the first martyr. The Son, being God, came upon earth, hiding the greatness of his Godhead in flesh as he willed, without leaving the heavens empty. Nor, even before he became incarnate, was the world empty of him. He was and is God, and he also became man by the divine plan, incarnate and born of a virgin out of his own love for humankind. The Father begot a Son worthy of himself and equal to him, in a way that only God the Father who begot him and the Son begotten from him know, philosopher.

Objection of the philosopher: Do not keep forcing the truth any longer, and do not try to cover the undimmed light of Scripture like a cloud with the skill of your words. Come instead to the plain sense of the Scripture set before you. Do not run away from "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works," or from "The Lord made lands and uninhabited places, the inhabited heights of the land under heaven." Both passages have one and the same meaning about the one Lord. These are the works of God. He created a first-created being as the beginning of his ways for his works, and he also called this being his Son. Through him, as through an instrument, he also created lands and uninhabited places. For even if the created wisdom of God, that is, the Son, did the work, it was still God who created the things that did not exist, through him, as through an instrument.

Reply of the holy bishops through the same Eusebius Pamphili: You have strayed far from the royal highway, that is, the apostolic faith, and you somehow tolerate being carried off outside it, having once chosen to throw yourself over the cliff. Yet you lifted your head a little out of the abyss of impiety that engulfs you when you heard from this holy synod the prophecy of the great Jeremiah. He points with his finger, so to speak, and says, "This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him," and the rest. After this he adds, "He appeared on earth and lived among men." And you know, philosopher, that when the holy bishops asked you who it was who appeared on earth and lived among men, the Father or the Son, you confessed that it was the Son, as the divine Scriptures say. Did you not say this? How, then, are you again hurling yourself, or rather sinking yourself, into the abyss of Arius's wickedness? You have not broken away and separated yourself from the man to whom you had yoked yourself. Wretched man, you prefer the blasphemous words of Arius to the apostolic doctrines, calling the Son of God a creature and an instrument. Listen to us, then, philosopher, if you really are a philosopher. Be persuaded that the Son of God is not himself the created reasoning wisdom that was given to man by the Son himself, the one who created lands and uninhabited places. Fix your mind on this, looking not to hostility but to truth, and the truth itself will guide you. You will know that the only-begotten Son of God is not a creature. He is himself the Creator and Fashioner of all created natures. You yourself understood this when you looked a little more closely, and you will understand it, or so at least I trust, if you long to be saved.

Objection of the philosopher against the Holy Spirit: Granted, he says, that what you say about the Son is credible and indisputable. He created, or created together with God the Father, as the testimonies show. He is not something made but the offspring of God, begotten from him by nature. Look, we accept it. But you surely have nothing to say about the Spirit as well? Who would dare to say that the Holy Spirit is the creator of any natures that have come into being? Where do testimonies say of him that he fashioned any of the visible and invisible creatures? And who has written anything at all about him, as they have about the Son? Let any of you speak up, if he can.

Rejoinder of the fathers through Protogenes, bishop of Serdica: It is not difficult, philosopher, to show you the testimonies to the works of the Holy Spirit that our fathers set out about him, showing that he created. Let us quote again what was said about creation: "And God said, 'Let us make man in our image and likeness,'" and it goes on to say, "And God made man; in the image of God he made him; male and female he made them." The Father, who said to the Son "Let us make," is God, and the Son, being God, made man. If, then, we call both the one who spoke and the one who made Adam and Eve God, hear next about the Holy Spirit. Was the one who made Adam God, or not?

The philosopher: Yes, he is God. The bishop: In the book of Job, Elihu the Buzite says to Job, "The divine Spirit is what made me." If, then, the one who made Adam is God, what would you call the one who made Elihu? Or do you think Elihu is of a different substance from Adam? When craftsmen have equal skill, the equal workmanship of the finished product naturally shows in the human person. What, then, will you call the one who made Elihu, philosopher? Surely God, and the maker of man? Scripture said of the one who made Adam, "And God made Adam." In the same way it is right for us to say of the one who made Elihu that the Holy Spirit is God. When the fashioning of the work is equal, the title of the makers is also equal, since one Godhead of the holy Trinity is understood in three perfect and equal hypostases. And in the book of the Assumption of Moses, Michael the archangel, in his dispute with the devil, says, "For we were all created from his Holy Spirit." And again he says, "His Spirit went forth from the face of God, and the world came to be." This is equivalent to "All things came to be through him." For the divine and ineffable Trinity, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, is always inseparable, and together they fashioned the whole creation, both intelligible and sensible. It also says in Psalm 32, "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host." Hear God saying in Isaiah, "I am the Lord your God; I, the God of Israel, will hear you." Having spoken of his kindnesses to the people, he goes on to say, "so that they may see and understand and know together that the hand of the Lord has done all these things, and the Holy One of Israel has displayed them." Here he calls the Holy Spirit of God the "hand," and his Son the "Holy One of Israel." And again he said to Jacob, "My hand laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand made firm the heaven." Ezekiel likewise says, "The hand of the Lord came upon me." Scripture usually calls the Holy Spirit of God either the hand or the arm, philosopher, and calls his Son the right hand.

The holy fathers spoke further through Leontius, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia: What has been said about the works of the Holy Spirit is enough to persuade you, philosopher, that he is co-creator with the Father and the Son of all created natures, and of the same Godhead and substance as the Father and the Son. So fix your mind on what has already been said to you, and now hear clearer proofs about him from the holy Scriptures. The prophet David says in Psalm 77, "Sing to the Lord a new song." Why? "Because the Lord has done marvelous things; his right hand has saved him," meaning his Son, "and his holy arm," meaning the Holy Spirit. In the Catholic Epistles, too, John the Evangelist cries out about the Holy Spirit and, like all the others, declares him God: "It is the Spirit who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth." A little later he says, "Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony of God in himself," that is, the Spirit of God, "but whoever does not believe God has made him a liar." And the divine Peter, the great champion of the apostles, says to Ananias, "Why has Satan filled your heart, so that you lied to the Holy Spirit?" A little later he says, "You have not lied to men but to God." Again, in the Old Testament it says, "I fill heaven and earth, says the Lord," and Solomon shows who it is that fills them when he says, "The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world." Be persuaded, then, about the lordship of the Holy Spirit as well, and accept the testimonies about him. Believe that the Holy Spirit is of the same Godhead, the same substance and the same reality as the Father and the Son, and always coexists with the Father and the Son. Do you hear, philosopher?

Reply of the philosopher to our holy fathers: So then, as you say, and as the testimonies of the Scriptures that you have brought forward show, the Holy Spirit too must be called God. The idea would have seemed forced to me if you had not brought forward these passages of Scripture. Still, while the proof about Elihu the Buzite is clear, I had never heard of the so-called Assumption of Moses that you mentioned just now until today. So I ask you to set out a clearer basis for what you have said. What you have said so far is not enough to give me complete assurance about the Spirit. The subject requires plainer and nobler language, for this inquiry is not about trivial matters.

Reply of our holy fathers to the philosopher through the same bishop Leontius: The proof presented to you is abundant, philosopher, and the testimonies from the divine Scriptures are perfectly clear and able to persuade you on the matter before us. So we wonder how you, who seem to be full of so much understanding, still have doubts. But since we want you to look toward the truth, and pray for this, we urge your intelligence to begin to understand that uncreated and unchangeable nature by faith. Do not dare to pry into things beyond the mind by human reasoning, as we have often said. You are a philosopher, as you say, philosopher, so do not put up any longer with being mixed up in the heterodox and impious notions of Arius. Instead, receive faithfully, as we said just now, both what has now been said to you and what will be said. Accept one Godhead: of the Father, who inexpressibly begot the Son; of the Son, who was begotten from him; and of the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father himself and is the Son's own. As the apostle Paul says, "If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him." Elsewhere the same apostle says, "Now the Lord is the Spirit." And again: "There are different kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit; there are different kinds of service, but the same Lord; and there are different kinds of working, but it is the same God who works all things in all." Not long after, he says, "All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each one individually as he wills." See, philosopher, a most clear and distinct proof that declares the Holy Spirit God and shows his sovereign freedom. See how he says here, "There are different kinds of working, but the same God who works all things in all," and "All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each one individually as he wills." And what does the Lord say in the Gospels, as you know, when he speaks plainly with the Samaritan woman? "God is spirit." If, then, God is spirit, the Spirit is certainly God too. Yet these are not one God and another God; there is one Godhead of the distinct persons, according to the concept of the hypostases. But when we hear the word "person" (prosopon), let us not suppose that the divine has human form. For it is uncompounded and without shape, as you yourself confessed with us at the beginning of the discussion. Indeed, heaven and earth are also said in Scripture to have a face (prosopon). The Lord himself, speaking with the scribes and Pharisees in the Gospels, said, "Hypocrites, you know how to interpret the face of the sky and the earth," and so on. For everything that subsists is said, insofar as it subsists, to have a face, that is, a form, belonging to its own nature. Heaven and earth, however, are created, as is the whole nature of things that have come into being. The divine and ineffable substance is uncreated, since it is simple, uncompounded and without shape, eternal and immortal. But let us return to the matter at hand. We have shown through many testimonies from the divine Scriptures that the Holy Spirit is co-creator with the Father and the Son of all creation, both visible and intelligible. For he is always inseparable from the Father and the Son, just as the Son is inseparable from the Father and the Father from the Son. Come now, if you please, and take some sound guidance from illustrations too, even if they are weaker. Your word, like every human being's, is spoken aloud, yet it is born from your mind without being divided from it. Likewise your spirit also proceeds from you, and you would not call either your word or your spirit foreign to you. You would not refuse to think this about human beings. But what of that ineffable, inconceivable and incomprehensible substance of God? His Word is not a spoken word but one always living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword. It is the judge of all things, since it is also their creator; no creature is hidden from it, and all things are naked and laid bare before its eyes. His Holy Spirit searches even the depths of God. Does anyone dare to say that the Word or the Spirit of God is foreign to him, or to accept those who say such things? Yes, philosopher?

Reply of the philosopher to the assembly of the holy bishops: You have led me to a loftier idea by saying that one Godhead of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit must be understood and believed. I remember what you said earlier: that the Father is God, the Son is God and the Holy Spirit is God. But now you say that there is one Godhead of the three perfect hypostases of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. Please explain your statements to me more plainly.

Reply of the holy fathers to the philosopher, through the same bishop Leontius: That divine and ineffable essence, which transcends all things and contains all things, cannot be expressed, since it is also beyond conception, beyond reckoning and wholly unsearchable. But hear us. We have not told you of one God and then another, as the impious Arius blasphemously did when he spoke of one uncreated God and another created one, and proclaimed that the Spirit of God was likewise created. God forbid! What we have said is that one Godhead is to be conceived and believed: one essence, one lordship and one will of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. We have said that the hypostases of the Holy Trinity are not separated from one another, nor located in places, but that by faith alone one Godhead is to be conceived and believed, as we have often said, of the holy, consubstantial and worshipful Trinity. See how the true faith has shown at every point that we must not conceive of any difference within the Holy Trinity. Now be willing to give us your attention here for a little, and you will be still more fully convinced, as you receive saving counsel from the Holy Spirit through us. Then you will know that the one Godhead of the Holy Trinity always is and subsists. It is a Trinity, truly a Trinity, and nothing in it ever existed before the rest. It always is, and always in the same way, an undivided and consubstantial Trinity.

Reply of the philosopher: Do not think that I am turning away from the doctrines of the truth. If I were, I would have rejected your words at the very beginning of our discussion. I am examining the meaning of your ideas so that the substance of what you are saying may become clearer and more distinct to me.

Reply of the holy fathers to the philosopher, by way of illustration, concerning fire, radiance and light, through the same bishop Leontius: Listen now, listen, O philosopher. We have already set before your mind, through a great many passages of the divine Scriptures, that the Godhead is something simple and uncompounded, as you yourself agreed at the start of your propositions. By nature it is immortal, eternal and uncreated fire, and light that cannot be contained or comprehended. It is not conceived as being in one person, as the Jews suppose. Rather, all Christians believe in it and proclaim it as a Trinity of persons who are always inseparable, the inseparable Trinity of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, as has been demonstrated. Learn now as well, O philosopher. What we are doing may be bold, but may the divine majesty be gracious to us, for we undertake this labour for your salvation and that of others. Learn, then, about intelligible things from things perceived by the senses, about what is beyond the mind from what lies within its reach, and about what is beyond speech from what can be spoken. It is true that all things, seen and conceived, all creatures in heaven, on earth and under the earth, are beyond comparison with that uncreated, incomprehensible and immortal essence of God. Nevertheless, let us state the example that has occurred to us. It is of no small benefit to those who receive it in faith, and it offers a sufficient image of true religion to those who wish to understand it reverently. This fire that our senses perceive is one nature or essence, and yet it is a triad: at one and the same time fire, radiance and light. None of these is found to exist before another. The three, the fire, the radiance that comes from it, and the light, exist inseparably from one another. So separate the three, O philosopher, if you can, and show us one existing before another. Show us the fire existing by itself before the radiance, with the radiance coming into being some time after the fire. Or show us the light coming later or after the fire and the radiance, or else before them. Show us, if you can, by separating the three from one another, that the fire is not at once fire, radiance and light, though the nature of the fire is one. Take these things into your mind, things perceived by the senses and created, even though, as we have just said, they cannot be compared with the eternal and unbearable essence of God. Nevertheless, draw saving starting points from them, give wings of faith to the eye of your understanding, and rise up to the lofty knowledge of God. Then, as we pray and believe, the grace of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit will meet you and shine upon you. It will show you one Godhead, which is immortal fire, radiance and light: simple and uncompounded, inseparable, undivided, inconceivable and ineffable, the truly consubstantial Trinity of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.

How the philosopher came to believe in the Holy Trinity. When the philosopher heard this, he was as though in a trance and stood speechless for a very long time. His thoughts threw him into turmoil, and great fear fell upon him. Then he came to himself and cried out with a loud voice: "Glory to you, O God, who inspired these holy ones of yours with the mystery, beyond all understanding, of the spotless, inseparable and uncreated Godhead! But I beg you, O Christ, all-good Son of an all-good Father, forgive the sins I committed against you when I was led astray by the impious opinions of Arius. Do not exact punishment from me, you who are the just Judge, for those impious words which I, wretch that I am, uttered against you. Woe to Arius and his impious faction, who blasphemed against the Son of God! They said, 'There was a time when he was not,' and that the Son of God and the Holy Spirit are a creature, a thing made and of another essence. They said that the Son of God and the Holy Spirit are not of the same essence as the Father. I anathematize, now and for ever, Arius and his impious opinions, all who share his views, and all who blaspheme against the Father, against the Son and against the Holy Spirit. For whoever does not have the Son does not have the Father either, and whoever has blasphemed against the Son and the Holy Spirit has blasphemed against the Father. I implore your sacred assembly of elders: help me with your prayers on my behalf to Christ, the Son of God, for I follow above all what the Holy Spirit has set forth and defined through you. I confess that these things are true and certain. For I believe this to be what the hierophant Paul spoke of: 'the mystery that was hidden from the ages and from the generations, which has now been revealed,' as it is said, 'to his holy apostles and prophets' and to you 'in the Spirit.' That mystery is that his Son and his Holy Spirit always exist, coexist and abide together with God the Father."

The holy fathers went on and spoke to the philosopher about a spring, a river and water, through bishop Leontius: There is something else to be understood as well, O philosopher, who are now a friend of the truth. Let us think of a spring that gives birth to a river of water. Every river, as you know, has a spring as its parent. The river comes forth from the spring of water, yet no one calls the river a spring or the spring a river. The spring is called a spring and the river a river, and both are one water. But when someone wants to draw water from the river or the spring, he changes the name. He will not say, "Go off and draw, and bring me the spring," or "the river," but "water." So we must speak of one nature but three persons: spring, river, water. The divine Scripture too is shown to say these things, for we are telling you nothing foreign to it, you who are now a true child of grace, even if we have presented the word of truth by way of examples, figures and images. The divine Scripture says of the Son: "He will turn toward them like a river of peace." He comes forth, clearly, from the true spring of life, the Godhead of the Father, as the Lord himself proclaims in the Gospels: "I came forth from the Father and have come." He also said most plainly, "I and the Father are one," and, "I am in the Father and the Father is in me." As for the Holy Spirit, all of us believers receive it from him. It is of the same essence as the Father and the Son: it proceeds from the Father, yet it belongs properly to the Son, as we demonstrated above. That it wells up for us from him the Lord himself taught most clearly in the Gospels when he said: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, out of his belly will flow rivers of living water." The evangelist, inspired by God, interprets the saying and adds: "Now he said this about the Spirit, which those who believed in him were to receive." And see what the prophet David proclaims about this spring of true life, the Holy Trinity: "With you is the spring of life; in your light we shall see light." He calls God the Father the spring of life, yet he speaks to the Son, since the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father. He calls the Son light, and in that light, he says, we shall see light, that is, the Holy Spirit. For he says, "In your light we shall see light." The Father is truly the spring of life and of light. The Son too is light, from the light of the Father, and the Holy Spirit too is light, from that same light. For, as we must say again and again, the Godhead of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit is one, as he himself proclaims through the words of the prophets: "I am God, and there is no other"; "I, God, am first, and I am hereafter, and for ever I am"; and again, "I am, and I have not changed," and so on, in accordance with the passages already cited. I think it necessary to repeat these sayings, if not all of them, because there are so many, then at least the clearer ones, so that what has been said may rest on a firmer foundation. So we will set out the words that came from the mouth of the prophet Jeremiah: "He who prepared the earth for all time filled it with four-footed beasts.
