He sends forth the light, and it goes; he called it, and it obeyed him with trembling. The stars shone in their watches and were glad. He called them, and they said, 'Here we are.' They shone with gladness for him who made them. This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him," and so on. Here, most God-beloved philosopher, we must fix our minds and unfold the sense of the Scripture. It has shown, as you yourself agreed, that these things were foretold about the Son. For after this it says, "He was seen on earth and lived among human beings." Now suppose that, as Arius in his impious wickedness holds, the Son is some other, created essence and a God who came into being later than the Father. Yet Scripture says of him, "This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him." Then, by Arius' impiety, the Father is not God, since Scripture says of the Son, "No other shall be reckoned beside him." So the impious Ariomaniacs, together with the author of their blasphemy, stand convicted of having cast the Father himself out of the Godhead even before they deny the Son, and these enemies of the truth are found to be utterly godless. For whoever does not have the Son, as it says in the Catholic Epistles, does not have the Father either. But the catholic faith knows one Godhead, and upholds it as that of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and no other shall be reckoned beside it. This mystery of the holy, worshipful and consubstantial Trinity is inconceivable, ineffable and wholly incomprehensible, and can be grasped by faith alone.

The philosopher: Truly divine and full of light are the things the Holy Spirit has uttered through you. Since the sacred words of your teaching are dear to me, I beg you: lend me your holy ears and teach me about what I ask, so that you may receive from God the fullest reward for my salvation.

Reply of the holy fathers through the same bishop Leontius: Say what you wish. We long to satisfy you fully, since now above all, enlightened as you are by the Holy Spirit, you can readily accept the proofs drawn from the sayings of Scripture on every point.

Thanksgiving of the philosopher, and his question about the Lord's becoming man: Thanks to your sacred heads! But tell me, most holy men, how are we to understand that God the Word, the Son of God, was seen on earth and lived among human beings, when he cannot be seen by any created nature, whether visible or intelligible? And what was the reason he undertook these things? Teach me, I beg you.

Reply of the holy fathers to the philosopher through bishop Leontius: The reason for his coming, which he arranged in his providence, was the fall that befell the first-created human beings, Adam and Eve, in paradise, a fall that spread through their whole race. Since they transgressed the commandment and were stripped of the divine gift, the Creator wished to restore that gift to the human race. Here we should understand that just as God said, "Let us make man according to our image and likeness," and God made man, as the proofs given earlier show, so the same God said again, "Let us save the man who is lost, whom we made according to our image and likeness." And just as God the Father said "Let us make" and the Son, who is God from God, did the creating, so the same Son, by the Father's will, chose in turn to save man in himself.
Question of the philosopher on the same subject: And how was he seen on earth and how did he live as a man among human beings, when he is unchangeable God?

Reply of the holy fathers through Macarius, bishop of Jerusalem: In the words of the inspired Paul, "great is the mystery of godliness: he who was manifested in the flesh," that is, the Son of God, and only then was he "seen" even "by angels." For the Only-begotten could not be seen by angels or archangels or any of the heavenly powers, since "no one has ever seen God." When you hear of his coming down from heaven, do not suppose that his uncontainable Godhead moved from one place to another. Understand this whole matter as a dispensation of providence, the truly great mystery of godliness, in which we have been renewed. For renewal is the recovery of newness. That is why the Word of God himself, restoring to us our likeness to himself, came down into likeness with us. But it was impossible for God to become like us without taking flesh. For what was added to him was not an incorporeal form of incorporeal essence, which is what he himself was, but something bodily, and he could not have a bodily essence without assuming it. So he truly assumed a body. We had fallen from our original kinship with him through the loss of the incorporeal form, that is, the grace of the Spirit, which we lost through the first human beings, Adam and Eve. He assumed a body so that through this bodily assumption we might be brought back into kinship and receive again the divine, incorporeal form. He takes flesh from a woman. In this way he becomes of one race with us, so that he may share his own glory with us as his kin, and also so that through his birth he may save woman. For it says, "the woman will be saved through childbearing." The flesh he assumed had its natural life-principle, for there is no flesh without that which gives life, which Scripture properly calls the soul.
The philosopher: Who would not be amazed at these mighty works of God, as you have described them? But how does he take flesh from a woman, as you have just said?

Reply of the holy fathers through the same Macarius, bishop of Jerusalem: We have already told you, my good friend, never to ask "how" about the mysteries of God, for they are ineffable and beyond reasoning. But we will tell you as much as words can convey, according to what we have been taught from the sacred Scriptures. No human being and no angel knows how that mystery of the Lord's dispensation in the flesh came about, so as to comprehend it completely. Not even Gabriel, who ministered to that mystery, nor the all-pure, spotless and holy Virgin Mary, could set out a full understanding of the incarnation of God the Word. Only the only-begotten Son of God himself knows exactly how he became man for our sake. Those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word, as Luke says, have handed down to us these things about his dispensation in the flesh: that according to the flesh he was of the seed of David and Abraham; that "of her was born Jesus," that is, of the Virgin, "who is called Christ"; that "theirs are the fathers, and from them, according to the flesh, is Christ"; that "it was not angels he took hold of, but the seed of Abraham"; and that he was made like us in every respect except sin. These things we know. But the manner in which they came about surpasses the understanding of every rational nature. On this point too the prophet Jeremiah says, "He is a man, and who will know him?"

The philosopher and the whole crowd that had gathered to listen were amazed, and the holy fathers continued, speaking through Macarius, bishop of Jerusalem: We have already shown at great length that the only-begotten Son of God, being God, became man out of love for humankind, taking flesh and being born of the Virgin Mary by an ineffable birth. Since he wished, as our discussion has already shown, to renew what had been undone through the fall of the first-formed, he entered into what is ours so that he might bring us into what is his, stooping down to our weakness like the best of physicians. Again we say that his stooping down, his descending and his being sent must be understood in terms of the manner of his becoming man, as we have already shown. For by his Godhead he always fills all things together with the Father, according to the ideas set out earlier. Listen, then. We are born of a woman; out of love for humankind he came to this too. But we are born from pleasure, sleep and a man's seed, while he alone was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. We are nursed with milk; he who by his Godhead gives food to all flesh came to this too in the flesh. We advance and grow in stature; he did not disdain to undergo this too in the body, as it is written, "Jesus advanced in wisdom and stature and in favour with God and men." When he had lived to his thirtieth year, so that he might bless every stage of life, he came to baptism. At that time John, the son of Zechariah, was preaching to the people a baptism of repentance. John did not give the gift of forgiveness of sins or of adoption as sons, for it did not belong to John to give these things, nor to any angel, but only to God the Word himself, who took flesh and became man. He submits to baptism for our sake, and though he is sinless God, he was baptized in the body as a man. He did not need baptism himself, but he did it to glorify our baptism, so that we might believe that just as the Holy Spirit came down upon him, so it comes down upon us who are baptized into him. Then, after living among human beings, handing down the teaching of his divine commandments and working miraculous signs for a period of three years and into the fourth, he came at last to his voluntary bodily suffering for our sake. For the punishment of the cross was owed by us. Yet even if all of us had been crucified, we would still not have had the strength to snatch ourselves from death. For "death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned." There were many saints, many prophets, many righteous men, and not one of them could ransom himself from the power of death. But the Saviour of all came himself, and in his sinless flesh, taken from us, he accepted in our place and on our behalf the punishments owed by us. After death we are carried down to Hades; he accepted this too and went down into it of his own will. He was not carried down as we are, but went down. For he was not subject to death; he was master over death. He went down alone and came up again with a multitude. He was the spiritual grain of wheat that fell into the earth for our sake and died in the flesh. By the power of his Godhead he raised up the temple of his body, according to the Scriptures, and it bore as its fruit the resurrection of the whole human race. After his three days in the tomb and his return to life from the dead, he appeared to the disciples and showed them the wounds his body had suffered on the cross, saying: "Touch me and see that it is I myself, the one who worked wonders, who also accepted in my flesh these sufferings for the sake of your race." Then for forty days he ate and stayed with them and gave them counsel in saving commandments. After that he ascended into the heavens while they watched, and the sacred Scriptures have taught that he has taken his seat at the right hand of the Father. We also await his coming at the end of the age to judge the living and the dead, as he reigns eternally and always with the Father for endless ages. This is the apostolic and blameless faith of the Church. It was handed down from on high, from the Lord himself, through the apostles, from forebears to descendants, and the Church upholds it and holds it fast to this day and for ever, for the Lord said to the disciples: "Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit."

When the Holy Spirit had uttered these things in this way through our holy fathers gathered at that holy council, the whole crowd that had assembled to listen magnified God. The most God-beloved emperor himself was also listening, for he attended most of the council's sessions, and he was filled with admiration and glorified God at hearing such divine doctrines. Rejoicing indeed at the agreement of our bishops, he exulted in spirit, for he was eager that no one, great or small, should dissent from this saving confession.

So, after this long and protracted examination of the worshipful question had been brought to completion, all our people together resolved that the term "consubstantial" must be laid down for the faith of the Church, in the way that our holy fathers after the apostles handed down this faith: that is, to confess that the Son and the Holy Spirit are of the same substance as the Father. All the holy bishops gathered at Nicaea confirmed this faith. The multitude of priests and holy confessors, the all-praised and most God-beloved emperor himself, and the whole multitude of the faithful who had come together there joyfully received this confession of faith, except for seventeen bishops, whom we mentioned above. Arius, who seemed to take delight in them, was caught along with them, since they were of one mind with him: together with him they said that the Son had been fashioned by God from outside, out of certain non-existent hypostases, and had not been begotten from the very Godhead of the Father.

Therefore all our holy fathers decreed by a unanimous vote that these men, together with Arius, should once again be expelled from the catholic Church. They anathematized both the men themselves and their impious opinion, and the blasphemous words and notions they had used against the Son of God, saying that he was from things that are not, that there was a time when he was not, that the Son of God was by his free will capable of vice and virtue, and calling him a creature and a thing made. The holy synod anathematized all these things and the men themselves, and would not even bear to hear their impious opinion, their madness and their blasphemous words.

Moreover, the bishops at once tore up the document, full of their impiety, which these men had dared to submit. Such was the end the holy synod brought to their affairs. As for the orthodox faith, all the bishops in agreement, embracing the whole of it in a few words for the sake of the simplicity of the faithful multitude of the people, set out in writing the creed of the catholic faith in more or less these words:

Exposition of the catholic and apostolic faith set forth by the synod at Nicaea under the most God-beloved emperor Constantine, in the consulship of the illustrious Paulinus and Julian, in the year 636 from Alexander, on the 19th of the month of Daisios, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the thirteenth indiction, at Nicaea, the metropolis of Bithynia: "We believe in one God, the Father Almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten of the Father, only-begotten, that is, of the substance of the Father, God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father, through whom all things came to be, those in heaven and those on earth; who for us men and for our salvation came down and was made flesh and became man, suffered, was buried, and rose on the third day, and ascended into the heavens, and sits at the right hand of the Father, and is coming again to judge the living and the dead; and in his Holy Spirit. But those who say, 'There was a time when he was not,' and 'Before he was begotten he was not,' and that he came to be from things that are not, or who assert that the Son of God is of another hypostasis or substance, or is created, or changeable, or alterable — such people the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes."

This is the faith which our holy fathers at Nicaea, the orthodox bishops, set forth, first of all against Arius, who blasphemed and said that the Son of God is a creature, and also against Sabellius, Photinus, Paul of Samosata, Mani, Valentinus and Marcion, and against every heresy that has risen up against the catholic and apostolic Church. These the synod of holy orthodox men gathered in the city of Nicaea condemned; their names and their provinces are listed below.

The decisions of the synod were then referred to the pious and all-praised emperor: both the sentence against those who fought against God and the exposition of the orthodox faith. He gladly received the latter with the greatest possible reverence, as something brought forth from God. Those who opposed it he decreed should go into exile, as men who set themselves against God. Six of the bishops who sided with Arius accepted being driven out together with Arius himself and his associates. But the other eleven, fearing the presence of the God-loving emperor and the great number of bishops at the synod, lest they be banished, feigned agreement and signed the "consubstantial" with their hand, not with their intention. The ringleader of this deceit was Eusebius of Nicomedia, who is shown to have held a double-minded opinion to the very end, as Eustathius of Antioch, Eusebius son of Pamphilus, Athanasius the Great and all who have written the history of the synod relate: through hypocrisy the man seemed to be on our side, while he stoutly championed the faction of our opponents.

Hosius, bishop of the city of Cordoba, to the holy churches of God throughout Rome, Spain and all Italy, and in the remaining nations beyond, on my side, as far as the Ocean, through the presbyters of Rome who were with him, Vito and Vincent.
Alexander of Alexandria, together with Athanasius, who was then archdeacon, to those throughout all Egypt, Libya and the Pentapolis, and the regions bordering them as far as the provinces of India.
Eustathius of Antioch the Great, to those throughout Coele-Syria, all Mesopotamia, and both Cilicias.
John the Persian, to those in all Persia and in Greater India.

Leontius of Caesarea in Cappadocia, the ornament of the Lord's Church, to those throughout Cappadocia itself, Galatia, Pontus Diospontus, Paphlagonia, Pontus Polemoniacus, and Lesser and Greater Armenia.
Theonas of Cyzicus, to those throughout Asia and the Hellespont, Lydia and Caria, through the bishops under him, Eutychius of Smyrna and Marinus of Troas.
Macarius of Jerusalem, together with Eusebius son of Pamphilus, bishop of Caesarea, to those throughout Palestine, Arabia and Phoenicia.

Alexander of Thessalonica, through those subject to him, to those throughout First and Second Macedonia together with Hellas, all of Europe, both Scythias, and all those throughout Illyricum, Thessaly and Achaea.
Nunechius of Laodicea, to those throughout First and Second Phrygia.
The admirable Protogenes of the city of Serdica, to those in Dacia, Calabria and Dardania, and the regions bordering them.
Caecilian of Carthage, to the holy churches of God throughout all the provinces, the Africas and both the Numidias and the Mauretanias.
Pistus of Marcianopolis, to those throughout Moesia, the nations of the Athenians [?] and of the Gauls, and the cities neighboring them.

Alexander of Constantinople, who was then still a presbyter but later obtained the episcopal priesthood of the church there, together with Paul, who was then still a reader and his notary, to those in all the islands of the Cyclades."
All these holy and apostolic men carried the decisions of the holy, great and ecumenical synod of Nicaea to all the holy churches of God under heaven, and delivered them everywhere on earth.

The emperor Constantine, delighted at the exposition of the right and apostolic faith, which had been uttered from the Holy Spirit by our three hundred holy fathers as if through one mouth, and ratified by all, rose from his throne in the presence of the whole multitude of the holy high priests and of all who had flocked together to that holy hearing of the faith. Stretching out his hands and lifting his eyes to heaven toward God, he sang praises in words of blessing to God, the Savior and benefactor of us all, because he had granted him the concord among the bishops that he longed for and their unanimity concerning the right and saving faith. So great was that altogether excellent and God-loving emperor's care for the churches of God and for the most peaceful concord of their shepherds.

I think it not out of place to include in this work what Eusebius son of Pamphilus well set down about these matters — I mean what was transacted at the synod — when he began to speak of them in the third book of his Life of Constantine, the God-loving emperor. It runs as follows:

"When a great many proposals were put forward by each party, and at first much dispute arose from some of them, the all-praised emperor listened to them all with patient attention and received the proposals of both sides with the utmost diligence. Taking up in turn what was said by each party, he gently drew together those who were contentiously opposed, conversing mildly with each and speaking in Greek, since he was not unacquainted with that language either. He was sweet and pleasant, persuading some, shaming others by his words, praising those who spoke well, and urging all toward concord, until he had brought them to be of one mind and one opinion on the matters before him. Thus the pious confession of praise prevailed unanimously, and the saving faith, truly uttered from the Holy Spirit by all our holy fathers mentioned above, was confirmed. At the same time he also laid down by law that a single time should be agreed upon by all for the saving feast of Easter. Then he decreed that what had been resolved in common should be ratified in writing by the signature of each, and he urged the bishops to set out in writing their particular ecclesiastical regulations and canons."

The emperor's faith moves us to recall another matter as well, for he applied such zeal and forethought to the peace of the Church that he neglected not even the smallest things. He had invited to the synod Acesius, bishop of the Novatian sect, and those with him, since they too glorified the "consubstantial" and the Trinity. So after the definition of faith had been set forth and signed by the synod and by the emperor, the emperor Constantine asked Acesius whether he too assented to the faith and to the decree on the feast of Easter. Acesius said to him, "The synod has decreed nothing new, O emperor. For this is how we have all received from of old, from the apostolic times, both the definition of faith and the time of the feast of Easter." And the emperor said to him, "Why then do you separate yourself from our communion?" Acesius related what had happened in the persecution under Decius concerning those who had not been able to endure the contest of martyrdom but had denied the faith, and he put forward the strictness of a severe canon, saying that those who had sinned after baptism ought not to be received when they repented, nor be deemed worthy any longer of communion in the mysteries. When Acesius had said this, the emperor said to him, "Set up a ladder, Acesius, and climb up to heaven by yourself."
After this all the bishops set out various ecclesiastical regulations.

Let us converse with the light, which is Christ, as people standing near him; as those who see him, so let us conduct our lives by sanctifying prayers. For prayers sanctify if we pray with the divine Word, and the divine Word is present wherever a pure heart and a pure life are preserved with humility. Israel toiled in offering sacrifices; the prophets cried out to God, "Send out your light and your truth." They cried out, and we have received. "Others have labored," as the Lord said, "and we have entered into their labor." For the Lord himself came to us, saying, "I am the light; I am the truth." We received grace without toil, but we must guard grace with toil.

On those who say that Christians ought not to work. Since some, not wishing to work but to be busybodies, wrongly take the sacred words of the Lord when he said, "Do not be anxious for your life, what you will eat," as though he were saying that Christians who follow this saying ought not to work the land, we must show that the Lord did not say it in that sense. For it is possible both to work and not to be anxious, since we know and believe that the Lord himself gives the increase and the fruits of our labors, as he said: "The kingdom of God is as if a man should cast his seed upon the ground, and should sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should sprout and grow, he knows not how."

On those in holy orders. Those in holy orders should be a type and image of the heavenly beings. The bishop holds the throne of the Lord himself, being, after him, the head of the church he has received; the presbyter holds the throne of the seraphim, and the deacon that of the cherubim; and it is fitting that the attendant be for the service of these.
That laypeople should not go up into the ambo. That laypeople should not go up into the ambo, except those appointed to read or to chant from the parchments.

On holy baptism. Our baptism is to be perceived not with the eyes of sense but with the eyes of the mind. You see water: consider the power of God hidden in the waters. For the sacred words teach that we are baptized in the Holy Spirit and in fire. Through the faith of the one baptizing and the faith of the one being baptized, by means of the sacred invocation, understand the waters to be filled with the sanctification of the Spirit and with divine fire. For it says, "He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire." The one being baptized goes down liable for sins and held in bondage to corruption, but comes up freed from that bondage and from sin, having become by his grace a son of God and an heir, and a fellow heir with Christ, having put on Christ himself, as it is written: "As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ."

On the divine table and the mystery of the body and blood of Christ upon it. Here again, at the divine table, let us not look in a lowly way at the bread and the cup set before us, but, lifting up our minds, let us understand by faith that there lies upon that holy table the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, sacrificed by the priests without being slain; and, truly receiving his precious body and blood, let us believe that these are the tokens of our resurrection. This is why we do not receive much but only a little: so that we may know that it is not for satiety but for sanctification.

On the resurrection of the dead. The Lord did not hand over his own flesh to suffering and death for us without purpose, but in order to accomplish our salvation, although he was free from death, as our argument has shown above. And the prophet cries out as if in his person, foretelling the coming mystery of his dispensation in the flesh: "I have become," he says, "like a man without help, free among the dead." Who is free from death except God? Yet, according to the proofs already given, having become flesh out of love for humankind he became like a man without help, humbling his own flesh to death, even death on a cross; and that flesh is proclaimed to have been raised, so that, having made us immortal, he might grant to us who had been despaired of, through that very firstfruits of ours, the hope of our resurrection, so that we might no longer be slaves to eternal death but free, just as Christ our firstfruits is, as the blessed apostle Paul says: "Christ the firstfruits, then those who belong to Christ at his coming." He testifies that we await from heaven as Savior this very one, our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God the Father, who will raise our bodies from the tombs, saying: "Our citizenship is in heaven, from which we also await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory." For our body must be glorified in this way, like the Master's: incapable of evil and of all the passions of the present life, free from death and from sin, holy, so that we may be able to walk with him in newness of life in heavenly light, reigning forever with Christ himself. For it is in this hope that we have received holy baptism and that we partake of the saving share in his holy members. These are the doctrines of the catholic Church.

That the Church of God is one. The Church in heaven is one, and the same Church is also on earth. On it the Holy Spirit rests. The heresies outside it, which people hold, are not the teachings of our Savior or of the apostles, but of Satan and of their father the devil. For they teach the doctrines of the Jews and the Greeks in another guise, in order to rob people of the life that truly is life.

On God's foreknowledge and on the world. The world was made smaller because of foreknowledge, for God foreknew that man would sin. That is why, according to the sacred Scriptures, we look for new heavens and a new earth, when the appearing and kingdom of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ is revealed to us. Then, as Daniel says, the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom, and the earth will be pure and holy, a land of the living and not of the dead. David foresaw it with the eye of faith and cries out, "I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living" — the land of the meek and humble. For he says, "Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth." And the prophet says, "The feet of the meek and humble shall tread upon it."

These few, out of many, are the ecclesiastical regulations worked out by our holy fathers that we have gathered into this work. At that same synod of Nicaea they also set forth twenty ecclesiastical canons, which I thought it necessary to include in this writing as well.

On eunuchs who have castrated themselves. If anyone has been operated on by a physician because of illness, or has been castrated by barbarians, let him remain in the clergy. But if anyone who is in good health has castrated himself, he should be suspended even if he is enrolled in the clergy, and from now on none of this kind should be admitted. Just as it is plain that this has been said of those who deliberately do this and dare to castrate themselves, so, if any have been made eunuchs by barbarians or by their masters, but are otherwise found worthy, the canon admits them to the clergy.

On those advanced to ordination from among the pagans. Many things have been done contrary to the church's canon, whether through necessity or because people were pressing for them in some other way. Men who had only just come to the faith from a pagan life, and had been instructed for a short time, were brought straight to the spiritual washing, and as soon as they were baptized they were advanced to the office of bishop or presbyter. It has therefore seemed right that nothing of this kind should happen in future. A catechumen needs time, and after baptism he needs further testing. For the apostle's writing is clear when it says, "Not a recent convert, lest he become puffed up and fall into condemnation and the snare of the devil." But if, as time goes on, some sin of the soul is found in the person, and he is convicted by two or three witnesses, such a man shall be removed from the clergy. Whoever acts against these rules, boldly defying the great synod, will himself put his own clerical standing at risk.

On those who keep women living with them. The great synod has entirely forbidden any bishop, presbyter or deacon, or indeed anyone in the clergy, to have a woman living with him, unless she is his mother, sister or aunt, or one of those persons who alone are beyond all suspicion. Whoever acts against this will put his own rank at risk.

On the appointment of bishops. It is most fitting that a bishop be appointed by all the bishops of the province. But if this is difficult, whether because of pressing necessity or because of the length of the journey, then at the very least three should gather in one place, with the absent bishops also giving their vote and their consent in writing, and then they should perform the ordination. In each province the ratification of what is done is to be given to the metropolitan bishop.

On those who are excommunicated. As for those who have been excommunicated by the bishops of each province, whether clergy or members of the lay order, let the ruling be upheld according to the canon that those cast out by some are not to be received by others. But let it be examined whether they were expelled from the congregation through the bishop's pettiness, contentiousness or some other such ill feeling. So that this may receive proper examination, it has seemed right that synods be held in each province twice every year. In this way all the bishops of the province will gather in one place and examine such questions together, and those who have admittedly offended against their bishop will be seen, with good reason, to be excommunicated by all, until it seems good to the assembly or to the bishop to pass a more lenient sentence on them. Let one of the synods be held before Lent, so that, all pettiness being removed, the gift may be offered pure to God, and the second around the season of autumn.

On the special honours that the church has assigned by canon to those who govern the greater sees. Let the ancient customs prevail in Egypt, Libya and the Pentapolis, so that the bishop in Alexandria has authority over all these, since this is also customary for the bishop in Rome. Likewise in Antioch and in the other provinces, let the churches keep their privileges. In general this much is plain: if anyone becomes a bishop without the consent of the metropolitan, the great synod has decreed that such a man ought not to be a bishop. If, however, two or three object out of personal contentiousness to the common vote of all, when that vote is reasonable and in accordance with the church's canon, let the vote of the majority prevail.

On the bishop in Aelia. Since custom and ancient tradition have prevailed that the bishop in Aelia should be honoured, let him have the honour that follows from this, while the metropolis keeps its own proper dignity.

On those called Cathars. As for those who once called themselves Cathars but are now coming over to the most holy catholic and apostolic church, the holy and great synod has decided that they are to receive the laying on of hands and so remain in the clergy. Before all this, however, they must confess in writing that they will agree with and follow the teachings of the catholic and apostolic church: that is, that they will hold communion both with those who have married twice and with those who lapsed in the persecution, for whom a period has been fixed and a time appointed, so that they follow the catholic church in all its teachings. Wherever, then, whether in villages or in cities, all those found to be ordained are of their party alone, those found in the clergy shall remain in the same rank. But where some come over in a place where there is already a bishop or presbyter of the catholic church, it is plain that the bishop of the church will keep the dignity of bishop, while the one called bishop among the Cathars will have the honour of a presbyter, unless the bishop sees fit to let him share in the honour of the title. If this does not please him, he shall find him a place either as a country bishop or as a presbyter, so that he may clearly be seen to belong to the clergy, and so that there may not be two bishops in the city.

On the ordination of presbyters. If any have been advanced as presbyters without examination, or confessed their sins when examined, and men acting against the canon laid hands on them even after they confessed, the canon does not admit such men. For the catholic church insists on what is above reproach.

On those who have fallen and were promoted through ignorance. If any of the lapsed have been promoted through ignorance, or even with the foreknowledge of those who promoted them, this does not override the church's canon; for once they are discovered they are deposed.

On those who transgressed without necessity. As for those who transgressed without necessity, without the confiscation of their property, without danger or anything of that kind, as happened under the tyranny of Licinius, the synod has decided that, although they were unworthy of mercy, kindness should nevertheless be shown them. Those who sincerely repent shall therefore spend three years among the hearers and seven years among the kneelers, and for two years they shall share with the people in the prayers, but without the offering.

On those who renounced the world and ran back to it again. Some were called by grace, showed their first zeal and laid aside their belts, but afterwards ran back to their own vomit, so that some even paid money and used favours to get back into military service. Let these spend ten years among the kneelers after their three years as hearers. In all these cases, however, it is proper to examine their intention and the kind of repentance they show. Those who show their conversion in deed and not in outward show, by fear and tears and patience and good works, shall share in the prayers once they have completed the appointed time as hearers, and the bishop may also decide something more lenient about them. But those who took it indifferently, and thought that the outward form of entering the church was enough for their conversion, must complete the full time.

On those who seek communion when they are dying. As for those who are departing this life, the ancient law of the canons shall be kept now as well: if anyone is departing, let him not be deprived of the Lord's provision for the journey. But if, having been given up for dead, receiving communion and sharing in the offering, he is found again among the living, let him be placed with those who share in the prayer only. And in general, for anyone at all who is departing and asks to receive the eucharist, let the bishop, after examination, give him a share of the offering.

On catechumens who have lapsed. As for catechumens who lapsed during their instruction, the holy and great synod has decided that they are to be hearers only for three years, and after that to pray with the catechumens.

That no one should move from one city to another. Because of the great disturbance and the factions that have arisen, it has been decided that the custom found in some places contrary to the canon should be abolished entirely, so that neither bishop nor presbyter nor deacon may move from city to city. If anyone, after this decree of the holy synod, attempts anything of the kind, or lends himself to such a thing, the arrangement shall be wholly annulled, and he shall be restored to the church for which he was ordained bishop, presbyter or deacon.

On those who do not remain in the churches for which they were appointed. If any presbyters or deacons, or any who are enrolled in the clergy at all, rashly withdraw from their church, having neither the fear of God before their eyes nor any knowledge of the church's canon, they are by no means to be received in another church. Every pressure must be brought to bear on them to return to their own dioceses, and if they persist, it is proper that they be excommunicated. And if anyone should dare to steal away a man who belongs to another and ordain him in his own church without the consent of the bishop whom the man enrolled in the canon has left, let the ordination be void.

On clergy who lend at interest. Many who are enrolled in the canon, pursuing greed and shameful gain, have forgotten the divine Scripture that says, "He did not lend his money at interest," and they lend and demand one percent a month. The holy and great synod has therefore ruled that if anyone after this decree is found taking interest on a transaction, or going about the business in some other way, or demanding fifty percent, or devising anything else for the sake of shameful gain, he shall be deposed from the clergy and shall be a stranger to the canon.

On presbyters who receive the eucharist from deacons. It has come to the attention of the holy and great synod that in some places and cities deacons give the eucharist to presbyters. Neither canon nor custom has handed down that those who have no authority to offer should give the body of Christ to those who do offer. It has also become known that some deacons now touch the eucharist even before the bishops. Let all these practices be abolished, and let the deacons keep within their own bounds, knowing that they are the servants of the bishop and rank below the presbyters. Let them receive the eucharist in their proper order after the presbyters, with either the bishop or the presbyter giving it to them. Nor may deacons sit among the presbyters, for this is done against the canon and against good order. If anyone will not obey even after these decrees, let him be removed from the diaconate.

On those who have come over or are coming over to the catholic church from Paul of Samosata. As for those who were Paulianists and then took refuge in the catholic church, the rule has been laid down that they must in every case be rebaptized. If any of them were enrolled in the clergy in the past, then if they prove blameless and above reproach, let them be rebaptized and ordained by the bishop of the catholic church; but if on examination they are found unfit, it is proper that they be deposed. The same rule shall likewise be observed for deaconesses and in general for all those enrolled in the same canon. We have mentioned the deaconesses who have been enrolled in that status, since they have no laying on of hands at all, and so they are in every case to be counted among the laity.

On those who kneel on the Lord's Day. Since there are some who kneel on the Lord's Day and during the days of Pentecost, the holy synod has decided, so that everything may be kept alike and with one mind in every diocese, that prayers are to be offered to the Lord standing.
These twenty laws concerning the order of the church were written down by that same holy council of theirs in the presence of the most God-beloved and all-praised Emperor Constantine.

Some of the bishops also wanted to lay down another law, but the godly Paphnutius prevented it. About this I have thought it necessary to tell a story worthy of the greatest wonder. Some of the bishops wanted to bring a new law into the church at the synod and to make a ruling on this matter as they had on the other affairs of the church.

They were therefore drafting a rule that those in holy orders, whether bishops, presbyters, deacons, subdeacons or anyone else on the priestly roll, should not sleep with the wives they had married while they were still laymen. While this was being drawn up, the godly Paphnutius stood up in the middle of the crowd of bishops and cried out in a loud voice: "Do not make the yoke of those in holy orders heavier. For marriage, it says, is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled. Do not by excessive strictness do the church harm instead. For not everyone, he said, can bear the discipline of passionlessness. No one, I think, will be kept in chastity if each man's wife is deprived of her husband. And I call it good chastity for each man to have intercourse with his own lawful wife. Surely she should not be separated whom God has joined, and whom he married once and for all while he was a reader or a cantor or a layman." Paphnutius said this though he himself had no experience of marriage, since he had been brought up in monasteries from childhood. So the whole assembly of bishops, persuaded by the man's advice, fell silent on this question, leaving it to the judgement of those who wished, by mutual agreement, to abstain from their own wives. These things were done at the holy, great and ecumenical synod gathered at Nicaea in Bithynia. But Eusebius and Theognis and the Arians with them could not bear the firm confirmation of the true faith, and still would not bring themselves to anathematize Arius. They were found out, and for this they were again sent into exile by decree of the most God-beloved emperor and by judgement of the holy synod of bishops. Others were appointed in their place in their dioceses by vote of that same synod and of the clergy and people of each diocese. Amphion took over the leadership of the church of Nicomedia, Chrestus that of Nicaea itself, and others the sees of those who shared their views. But once again Eusebius and Theognis used their usual schemes, and finding in the emperor's kindness a means for deceit, they tried to get back into the fight and recover their former power. Their wicked schemes were very many and full of every impiety, and I would refer those who wish to learn about them to Theodoret and the others who have written ecclesiastical history. For my part, I shall go on from here in my account to what follows: to what the synod of bishops wrote to the bishops who had stayed away and to their own dioceses, and also what the victorious and most faithful emperor wrote, to support the most holy faith that had been set out and the holy feast of Easter, and to refute the champions of impiety. When the synod had been splendidly convened for all these purposes and the faith had been proclaimed in a manner worthy of God, and the holy fathers had settled everything concerning the good order of the church, they were eager to make known all that had been decreed by letters to all the holy churches of God under heaven, adding also what concerned Melitius.

For a certain Melitius had been made a bishop not long before the madness of Arius. He was convicted by the most godly Peter, bishop of Alexandria, who also won the crown of martyrdom. But although he was deposed, this same Melitius did not accept the sentence of deposition. Instead, he filled the Thebaid and the neighbouring parts of Egypt with turmoil and storm, acting like a tyrant against the authority of Alexander the bishop. The assembly of the synod therefore wrote to the church of the Alexandrians what it had enacted about his innovation:

Synodal letter written by the holy synod at Nicaea to the clergy and people of the orthodox faith in Alexandria, Egypt, the Pentapolis and Libya, and to the holy churches of God throughout all the world under heaven. "To the church of the Alexandrians, holy and great by the grace of God, and to our beloved brothers, the orthodox clergy and people in Egypt, the Pentapolis and Libya and throughout the world under heaven: the bishops who gathered at Nicaea and formed the holy and great synod send greetings in the Lord. By the grace of God, and with the most God-beloved Emperor Constantine bringing us together from various provinces and cities, the great and holy synod convened at Nicaea has dealt with matters concerning the faith of the church. It has seemed necessary to us to send you a letter about these things, so that you may know what was raised and examined, and what was decided and confirmed. First of all, then, the impiety and lawlessness of Arius and his followers were examined in the presence of our most God-beloved Emperor Constantine. It was unanimously decided that he should be anathematized, together with his impious opinion and the blasphemous words and ideas he had used in blaspheming the Son of God: saying that he is from nothing, that before he was begotten he did not exist, and that there was a time when he was not, and saying that the Son of God is capable of vice and virtue by his own free will, and calling him a creature and a thing made. The holy synod anathematized all these things, unwilling even to listen to his impious opinion, his folly and his blasphemous words. What end his affairs have come to you have certainly either heard or will hear; we say no more, lest we seem to trample on a man who has received the reward his own sin deserved. Yet his impiety was so powerful that it also brought ruin on Theonas of Marmarica and Secundus of Ptolemais, for they too have suffered the same fate as the others. But since the grace of God has freed Egypt from that false teaching and blasphemy, and from the persons who dared to cause dissension and division among a people that had long been at peace, there remained the matter of the rashness of Melitius and of those ordained by him. On this part too we make known to you, beloved brothers, what the synod decided. The synod, moved to greater leniency (for by strict reckoning he deserved no pardon at all), decided that Melitius should remain in his own city and have no authority to ordain or to put forward candidates or to lay on hands, and that he should not appear in the countryside or in any other city for this purpose, but should keep the bare name of his rank. Those whom he appointed, once confirmed by a more sacred ordination, are to be admitted to communion on these terms: they shall keep their rank and minister, but shall in every case be second to all those enrolled in each diocese and church who were promoted under our most honoured fellow minister Alexander. They shall have no authority to promote whomever they please, or to put forward names, or to do anything at all without the consent of the bishop of the catholic and apostolic church who is one of those subject to Alexander, our most holy fellow minister. But those who by the grace of God and your prayers have been found in no schism, and are without stain in the catholic and apostolic church, shall have authority both to promote and to put forward the names of those worthy of the clergy, and in general to do everything in accordance with the law and ordinance of the church. If any of those in the church should happen to die, then those recently received shall go up to the rank of the deceased, provided only that they appear worthy and the people choose them, with the bishop of Alexandria adding his vote and setting his seal on it. This was granted to all the others, but in the case of Melitius himself the same was not decided, because of his long-standing disorderliness and the hasty and reckless temper of his mind, so that no authority or power should be given to a man capable of causing the same disorders again. These are the matters that particularly concern Egypt and the most holy church of the Alexandrians. If anything else was laid down by canon or defined as doctrine in the presence of our lord and most honoured fellow minister and brother Alexander, he will report it to you more precisely when he is with you, since he was both a leader in and a partaker of what was done. We also bring you the good news about agreement on the most holy Easter: that by your prayers this matter too has been set right, so that all the brothers in the East, who formerly kept it with the Jews, will from now on celebrate the same most holy feast of Easter in agreement with the Romans and with you and with all of us who have kept Easter with you from of old. Rejoicing, then, in these achievements, in the common peace and harmony, and in the cutting off of every heresy, receive with greater honour and more abundant love our fellow minister and your bishop Alexander. He has gladdened us by his presence, and at his age has endured such great labour so that peace might come about among you and among all. Pray also for all of us, that what has seemed good may remain firm, having been done, as we believe, according to the good pleasure of Almighty God and of his only-begotten Son Jesus Christ our Lord and of the Holy Spirit, to whom be glory forever. Amen."

"You have probably learned already from other sources, beloved, what was done concerning the faith of the church at the great synod convened at Nicaea, since rumour usually runs ahead of the true account of events. But so that the truth may not be reported to you differently through such hearsay, we have thought it necessary to send you, first, the statement of faith that we put forward, and then the second, which they issued after making additions to our words. Our own document, then, which was read in the presence of our most God-beloved emperor and was declared sound and acceptable, runs as follows.

The faith set forth by us. We received it from the bishops before us, both in our first catechesis and when we received baptism; we learned it from the divine Scriptures; and we believed and taught it as presbyters and in our office as bishop. Believing it still, we now lay our faith before you. It is as follows:

We believe in one God, the Father Almighty, the maker of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Word of God, God from God, light from light, life from life, the only-begotten Son, the firstborn of all creation, begotten of the Father before all ages, through whom also all things came into being; who for our salvation was made flesh and lived among men, and suffered, and rose again on the third day, and ascended to the Father, and will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead. We believe also in one Holy Spirit, [?] truly the Holy Spirit, just as our Lord also said when he sent his disciples out to preach: "Go and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." Concerning these things we affirm that this is so, that we think thus, that we have long held this, and that we will stand firm for this faith until death, anathematizing every godless heresy. We testify before God Almighty and our Lord Jesus Christ that we have always held these things from heart and soul, ever since we have known ourselves, and that we now think and say them in truth. We are able to show you by proofs, and to persuade you, that in times past too we believed and preached in this way.

When we had set forth this faith, no one had any ground for objection. Rather, our most God-beloved emperor himself was the first to testify that it was entirely orthodox. He confessed that he himself held the same views, and he urged everyone to agree to it, to sign its doctrines, and to be of one mind with them, with the addition of only one word, "of one substance." He himself interpreted this word, saying that the Son is not called "of one substance" with the Father in the sense of the affections of bodies, and that he did not come to exist from the Father by division or by any kind of severing; for an immaterial, intellectual and bodiless nature cannot undergo any bodily affection, and such things must be understood in divine and ineffable terms. Our most wise and most pious emperor reasoned in this philosophical way; but they, taking the addition of "of one substance" as their occasion, produced the following formula:

The faith dictated at the council. We believe in one God, the Father Almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten of the Father as only-begotten, that is, from the substance of the Father, God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father, through whom all things came into being, both those in heaven and those on earth; who for us men and for our salvation came down and was made flesh, became man, suffered, was buried, and rose again on the third day, ascended into the heavens, and is coming to judge the living and the dead; and in the Holy Spirit. As for those who say, "There was once when he was not," and "Before he was begotten he was not," and that he came into being from things that are not, or who claim that the Son of God is of another hypostasis or substance, or is created, or changeable, or alterable, the apostolic and catholic Church anathematizes them.

When they had dictated this formula, we did not let pass unexamined the sense in which they used the phrases "from the substance of the Father" and "of one substance with the Father." Questions and answers were raised on this point, and argument tested the meaning of what had been said. They acknowledged that "from the substance of the Father" indicated that the Son is from the Father, but not that he exists as a part of the Father. We too thought it right to assent to this meaning, since pious teaching declares that the Son is from the Father, yet is not a part of his substance. Therefore we ourselves agreed to this sense, and did not reject even the expression, keeping before our eyes the goal of peace and the aim of not falling away from right understanding. In the same way we also accepted "begotten, not made," since they said that "made" is a term common to the other creatures that came into being through the Son, to which the Son bears no likeness. He is therefore not a thing made, like those that came into being through him, but is of a substance higher than anything made; and the divine oracles teach that this substance was begotten from the Father, the manner of the begetting being inexpressible and beyond the reckoning of every originated nature. So too, when the statement that the Son is "of one substance" with the Father was examined, the argument established that this is not meant in the manner of bodies or like mortal living creatures. For it is not by division of the substance, nor by severing, nor by any affection, change or alteration of the Father's power, since the unbegotten nature of the Father is foreign to all these things. Rather, "of one substance with the Father" signifies that the Son of God bears no resemblance to originated creatures, but is in every way made like the Father alone, who begot him, and is not from any other hypostasis or substance, but from the Father. When the term was interpreted in this way, it seemed right to assent to it as well, since we knew that some of the ancients, learned and illustrious bishops and writers, had used the term "of one substance" in their teaching about the Father and the Son. Let this much be said, then, about the faith that was set forth. We all agreed to it, not without examination, but according to the meanings given, which were examined in the presence of the most God-beloved emperor himself and accepted on the grounds stated. We also judged the anathema they set forth after the creed to be unobjectionable, because it forbids the use of unscriptural expressions, through which almost all the confusion and disorder of the Church has come about. Since no divinely inspired Scripture uses "from things that are not," "there was once when he was not," and the phrases that follow, it did not seem reasonable to say and teach these things. We agreed with this decision too, as well made, since even before this time we were not accustomed to use these expressions. Further, anathematizing "before he was begotten he was not" was not thought absurd, since all confess that he was Son of God before his birth according to the flesh. Indeed, our most God-beloved emperor himself argued that he existed even according to his divine generation before all ages, since even before he was begotten in actuality, he was in the Father in potentiality, unbegottenly; for the Father is always Father, just as he is always King and Savior, being all things in potentiality and remaining always the same and unchanging. We have felt bound to send you this, beloved, to make clear to you how carefully we examined and gave our assent, and how reasonably we resisted, even to the last hour, while statements worded differently offended us, and then accepted without contention what was unobjectionable, once a fair examination of the meaning of the words showed us that it agreed with what we ourselves had confessed in the faith we had set forth earlier. We greet you together with the brotherhood among you. We pray that you may fare well in the Lord, most honored brothers."

"Victor Constantine Maximus Augustus to the bishops and peoples. Since Arius has imitated wicked and impious men, it is just that he should suffer the same disgrace as they. Porphyry, the enemy of godliness, composed certain lawless treatises against religion and received a fitting reward: he became a byword for all time to come, was covered with the worst of reputations, and his impious writings were destroyed. In the same way it has now been decided that Arius and those who share his views shall be called Porphyrians, so that they may bear the name of those whose ways they have imitated. In addition, if any treatise written by Arius is found, it is to be handed over to the fire, so that not only may the evil of his teaching be destroyed, but no memorial of him at all may remain. And I give this public warning: if anyone is caught having hidden a treatise written by Arius, and not having brought it forward at once and burned it, his penalty shall be death. As soon as he is convicted of this, he shall suffer capital punishment. God will keep you, beloved brothers."
The emperor also wrote other letters, in a more solemn style, against Arius and those who shared his opinions, and had them posted publicly in every city.

"Constantine Augustus to the catholic Church of the Alexandrians and of all the orthodox. Greetings, beloved brothers. We have received perfect grace from divine providence, so that, freed from all error, we may acknowledge one and the same faith. The devil no longer has any power against us; everything he attempted through his evil schemes has been torn up by the roots. The splendor of truth, at God's command, has conquered the dissensions, the schisms, those tumults, and the deadly poisons, so to speak, of discord. We all, therefore, worship one God in name, and believe that he is one. To bring this about, by the will of God I summoned most of the bishops to the city of Nicaea, and with them I myself, as one of you—rejoicing exceedingly to be your fellow servant—also took part in the examination of the truth. Everything that seemed to give rise to doubt and dissension was tested and carefully examined. And may the divine majesty forgive us [for speaking of them]: how great and how terrible were the blasphemies some unfittingly uttered about our Savior, about our hope and life, saying things contrary to the divinely inspired Scriptures and the holy faith, and confessing that they believed them! More than three hundred bishops, admired for their sobriety and insight, confirmed one and the same faith, which according to the truth is the exact faith of the divine law; Arius alone was found to have been overcome by the working of the devil, and to have spread this evil with impious intent, first among you and then among others as well. Let us therefore embrace the faith that Almighty God has given; let us return to our beloved brothers, from whom a certain shameless servant of the devil separated us; let us go back to our common body and our true members with all eagerness. This befits your insight, your faith and your holiness: that now the error of that man, who has been shown to be an enemy of the truth, has been exposed, you should return to the divine grace. For what pleased the three hundred holy bishops is nothing other than the judgment of the Son of God alone, especially since the Holy Spirit, dwelling in the minds of such great men, has brought the divine will to light. Therefore let no one doubt, let no one delay, but all of you return eagerly to the truest path, so that when I come to you, as I shall very soon, I may join with you in giving due thanks to the all-seeing God, because by revealing the pure faith he has restored to us the love we prayed for. God will keep you, beloved brothers."

"Constantine Augustus to the churches and to the bishops who were absent from the holy and great council at Nicaea, greetings. Having learned from the prosperity of public affairs how great is the grace of the divine power, I judged that my first aim, above all else, should be that among the most blessed multitudes of the catholic Church one faith, sincere love, and a single-minded piety toward Almighty God should be preserved.

But this could not be given a firm and settled order in any other way than by all the bishops, or at least most of them, coming together in one place and reaching a decision on each matter concerning our most holy religion. For this reason as many God-beloved bishops as possible assembled in this city of Nicaea—and I myself was present with them as one of you, for I would not deny what gives me the greatest joy, that I am your fellow servant—and every matter received due examination, until the judgment pleasing to the all-seeing God was brought to light, leading to harmony and unity, so that nothing further remained to cause dissension or dispute about the faith.

There, when a question was also raised about the most holy day of Easter, it was decided by common judgment that it would be good for all Christians everywhere to celebrate the saving feast of most holy Easter on one day. For what could be finer or more dignified for us than that this feast, from which we have received the hope of immortality [?], should be kept by all without fail in one order and on a clear principle? First of all, it seemed unworthy to observe that most holy feast by following the custom of the Jews, who, having stained their hands with a lawless crime, are rightly blinded in their souls, defiled as they are. For once their custom has been rejected, we may carry the fulfillment of this observance into future ages by a truer order, which we have kept from the first day of the Passion until now. Let us therefore have nothing in common with the most hostile crowd of the Jews. We have received another way from the Savior; a course lies open to our most sacred religion, and a fitting law. Holding to this with one accord, let us tear ourselves away from that shameful complicity, most honored brothers. For it is truly most absurd for them to boast against us that we would be unable to keep these things without their teaching. How can they think rightly, who after that murder of the Lord, having lost their minds, are driven not by any reason but by uncontrollable impulse, wherever their innate madness may lead them? That is why in this matter too they do not see the truth, so that, constantly erring to the greatest degree, instead of making the proper correction they celebrate the Passover a second time in the same year. Why then should we follow those who are admittedly in grievous error? For we would never consent to keep Passover twice in one year. But even if these things were not so, your wisdom ought always to take care [?] that the purity of our soul should not seem, through any resemblance, to share in the ways of utterly wicked men. Besides this, one can also see that in so great a matter and in a feast of such a religion it is unlawful for there to be disagreement. For our Savior handed down to us one day of our liberation, that is, of his most holy Passion, and he willed that his catholic Church be one. Even if its members are gathered in many different places, nevertheless they are cherished by one Spirit, that is, by the divine will. Let the wisdom of your holiness consider how terrible and unseemly it is that on the same days some should be devoting themselves to fasting while others are holding banquets, and that after the days of Easter some should be found in festivals and relaxation while others are given over to the appointed fasts. For this reason divine providence wills that this should receive due correction and be brought to one rule, as I think you all see. Since, then, this had to be corrected so that we have nothing in common with those murderers of their fathers and of the Lord; and since there is a seemly order, which all the churches of the western, southern and northern parts of the world observe, but which some in the regions of the East do not accept; for these reasons everyone judged it good for the present—and I myself promised that it would please your wisdom—that what is observed with one and the same harmonious judgment in the city of the Romans, in Italy and all Africa, in Spain, Gaul and the Britains, in Egypt and the Libyas, in all Greece, in the diocese of Asia, in Pontus and in Cilicia, your understanding should also gladly accept. Consider that not only is the number of churches in the places just mentioned greater, but also that it is most holy for all to resolve in common on what sound reason seems to demand: to have no fellowship with the perjury of the Jews. To put the main point briefly: it pleased the common judgment of all that the most holy feast of Easter should be celebrated on one and the same day. For it is not fitting that there should be any difference in so holy a matter, and it is better to follow this judgment, in which there is no admixture of alien error and sin. Since these things have thus been settled by divine judgment through so many great and holy bishops, receive gladly this heavenly grace and this truly divine command. For whatever is done in the holy councils of the bishops is to be referred to the divine will. Therefore, having made known to all our beloved brothers what has been written above, you must accept and put into effect both the aforementioned statement of the catholic faith and the observance of the most holy day of Easter, so that when I come to see you, as I have long desired, I may be able to celebrate the holy feast with you on one and the same day, and may rejoice with you in all things, seeing the devil's cruelty destroyed by divine power through our actions, while our faith, peace and concord flourish everywhere, and I may send up hymns of thanksgiving with you to God, the benefactor of all and Savior. God will keep you, beloved brothers."

This is what he wrote to those who had been absent from the council. Those who had come together he treated kindly with words and with gifts. He ordered many couches to be prepared and entertained them all at once, taking the more distinguished to his own table and distributing the others among the other tables. When he saw some whose right eyes had not been left to them but had been gouged out, and learned that their steadfastness in piety toward Christ had been the cause of this suffering, he pressed his lips to their wounds, believing that by his kiss he would draw a blessing from them. When the banquet came to an end, he presented them with further gifts. He also gave letters to the governors in charge of the provinces, instructing them to provide annual allowances of grain in every city to consecrated virgins, widows, and those dedicated to the divine service, measuring these by his generosity rather than by need.

Eusebius, son of Pamphilus, treating of these things, speaks somewhat as follows: "Thus, after the all-praised and most faithful Emperor Constantine had refreshed the holy bishops with the greatest reverence, he took leave of them and dismissed them all to return home. They went back with great joy, and from then on a single judgment prevailed among all, agreed upon in the presence of the emperor himself, those who had long been divided being joined together as one body. The emperor, rejoicing at this success, bestowed its flourishing fruit by letters on the bishops who had not been present at the council, and he ordered generous distributions of money to be made to all the people, both those in the countryside and those in the cities, honoring in this way the feast of the twentieth year of his reign." He had assembled the holy council of bishops in the sixteenth year and sixth month of his reign, as the account above has shown from the ancient narratives; and in the twentieth year, when they had dissolved the assembly of the council, each departed to his own diocese, as was related earlier.

As for me, having included in this ecclesiastical history, as far as I was able, what was judged and defined at that holy council concerning the catholic and orthodox faith, the venerable feast of holy Easter, the ordering of the Church's divine liturgy, and the canons for good order within it, for the fullest assurance of those who read this work, I shall here bring my account to a close. I have decided to set out the remaining pious efforts of the all-praised and most faithful emperor on behalf of the faith in a third book, to the glory of Christ, the Savior of us all, and as the clearest proof of the most faithful emperor's piety.

I thought it necessary to add only this here, regarding it not as superfluous but as quite fitting: the names of the bishops sent by the common body of all the bishops to the provinces throughout the earth, through whom the council sent what it had decided, by means of synodal letters and the letters of the all-praised emperor, to all the holy churches of God under heaven, to the glory of God the Father and of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

"Hosius, bishop of the city of Cordoba: to the holy churches of God in Rome, Spain and all Italy, and in the remaining nations beyond, in my region, as far as the Ocean, through the presbyters of Rome who were with him, Vitus and Vincent."

Alexander of Alexandria, together with Athanasius, who was then archdeacon, to the churches throughout all Egypt, Libya and the Pentapolis, and the regions bordering them as far as the provinces of India.
Macarius of Jerusalem, together with Eusebius son of Pamphilus, bishop of Caesarea, to those throughout Palestine, Arabia and Phoenicia.
Eustathius of Antioch the Great, to those throughout Coele-Syria, all Mesopotamia, and both Cilicias.
John the Persian, to those in all Persia and in Greater India.
Leontius of Caesarea in Cappadocia, the ornament of the Lord's church, to those in Cappadocia itself, Galatia, Pontus Diospontus, Paphlagonia, Pontus Polemoniacus, and Lesser and Greater Armenia.
Theonas of Cyzicus, to those throughout Asia and the Hellespont, Lydia and Caria, through the bishops under him, Eutychius of Smyrna and Marinus of Troas.

Alexander of Thessalonica, through those under his jurisdiction, to those throughout First and Second Macedonia together with all Greece, and all Europe, both Scythias, and all those throughout Illyricum, Thessaly and Achaea.
Nunechius of Laodicea, to those throughout First and Second Phrygia.
The admirable Protogenes of the city of Sardica, to those in Dacia, Calabria and Dardania, and in the regions bordering them.

Alexander of Constantinople, who was then still a presbyter but later was allotted the episcopal priesthood of the church there, together with Paul, who was then still a reader and his notary, to those in all the islands of the Cyclades."

All these holy and apostolic men carried the decisions of the holy, great and ecumenical synod of Nicaea to all the holy churches of God under heaven and delivered them in every part of the earth, as our account has just shown.

Another letter of the emperor Constantine to the same bishop

In the first and second books of the Ecclesiastical History our account has proceeded in order. Beginning from the times of the reign of the Christ-bearing and victorious emperor Constantine, and passing through everything in between up to the full conclusion of the proceedings of the holy synod of Nicaea, it has set forth an image of what took place: the siege raised against the churches of God by the God-hating tyrants, and the most shameful overthrow of those same impious tyrants; how Christ, the bridegroom of the church, most nobly armed his worthy servant Constantine with the weapons of his precious cross and roused him against those impious men; how he granted him the trophies of victory over those tyrants, slaying them all, root and branch, beneath the feet of the most God-beloved Constantine, and through him bestowed from above a deep peace on his churches throughout the whole world; and the scheme that was afterwards set in motion against the church once more by the demon, the enemy who hates the good, through the utterly abominable Arius; and how, on account of him and the impious blasphemies he uttered against the Son of God, the holy, great and ecumenical synod at Nicaea was convened at God's command through his servant, the most God-beloved emperor Constantine. All that was done at that synod by the Holy Spirit, through the holy and orthodox high priests gathered there, three hundred in number, on behalf of the apostolic and orthodox faith, our account has set forth clearly, as far as we were able, by the grace of Christ our God. From here I shall proceed next to the narrative of the emperor's piety, and of how unceasing was his care for the churches of God.

Great and inexpressible was the flame of zeal for Christianity within him, to lead everyone, even those outside, to the true knowledge of the living God. He wrote to all the peoples under Roman rule, urging them to rid themselves of their former error, exhorting them to turn to the teaching of our Saviour God, and appealing to all to come over to this truth, following an apostolic rather than an imperial aim. He also roused the bishops in each city to build churches, not only encouraging them to this by letters but also generously giving money and supplying all the costs of construction. This is shown by what he wrote, which runs as follows.

"Victor Constantine, Maximus Augustus, to Eusebius. Until the present time, while an unholy will and tyranny persecuted the servants of God our Saviour, I have believed, and have fully convinced myself, most beloved brother, that the sacred buildings of all the churches had either fallen into ruin through neglect or, from fear of the injustice that threatened them, had become less than befitting. But now that liberty has been restored, and that dragon has been driven from the government of public affairs by the providence of the all-working God and by our service, I think the divine power has become manifest to all, and that those who through fear or unbelief or certain sins have fallen away will recognize the God who truly is and will come to the true and right faith and way of life. Therefore, for all the churches over which you yourself preside, or whose bishops, presbyters or deacons presiding in each place you know, remind them to be diligent about the work of building churches, whether by repairing those that exist, or enlarging them, or building new ones wherever need requires. You yourself, and through you the others, will request what is necessary from the governors and the prefectural staff; for they have been instructed to carry out with all diligence whatever your holiness tells them. May God preserve you, beloved brother." This, then, is what he wrote about the building of churches to this same Eusebius son of Pamphilus and to the bishops presiding in each province. What he also wrote to the same Eusebius of Palestine about the preparation of the sacred books can easily be learned from the letter itself.

"Victor Constantine, Maximus Augustus, to Bishop Eusebius. In the city that bears our name, with the assistance of God's providence, a very great multitude of people has devoted itself to the most holy church, since everything there is growing greatly. It therefore seems entirely fitting that more churches also be built in it. Accept, then, with the greatest readiness what our resolve has decided. It has seemed proper to us to make this known to your wisdom: that you should order fifty copies to be written on well-prepared parchment, easy to read and convenient to carry for use, by skilled calligraphers who know their craft exactly—copies, that is, of the divine Scriptures, whose provision and use you know to be necessary for the purposes of the church. Letters have been sent from our clemency to the financial officer of the diocese, so that he may take care to supply everything needed for their preparation. It will be the task of your diligence to see that the written copies are completed as quickly as possible; and you are entitled, by the authority of our letter, to the use of two public carriages for their transport.
