In this way the finely written copies may most easily be brought even before our eyes, one of the deacons of your church, naturally, carrying out this task; and when he reaches us, he will experience our generosity. May God preserve you, beloved brother."

These things are sufficient to prove, or rather to teach clearly, how the all-praised emperor, as we said above, devoted all his zeal to divine things. Nevertheless I shall add to what has been said his achievements concerning the Saviour's tomb. For he learned that people in a Corybantic frenzy, raving in the service of idols, had buried the Lord's tomb, striving to consign to oblivion the memory of humanity's salvation, and had built over it a temple of the licentious demon Aphrodite. The most faithful emperor therefore ordered that loathsome building to be demolished as quickly as possible, and the soil defiled by accursed sacrifices to be carried away and thrown somewhere far from the city; then he commanded that a church of our Saviour God be built, very great and very beautiful. The letter of the most God-beloved emperor which he sent to the president of that church—I mean the church in Jerusalem—shows this more clearly. At that time it was Macarius, whom we mentioned earlier, who had also taken part in the great synod at Nicaea and with the others had put out the flame of Arius' blasphemy.

"Victor Constantine, Maximus Augustus, to Macarius, bishop of Jerusalem. So great is the grace of our Saviour that no wealth of words, I think, could seem worthy of the present wonder. For the token of that most holy tomb, long hidden beneath the earth through so many cycles of years, could not remain concealed, until, through the grace of our Saviour God, the tyranny of the common enemy of us all was destroyed. Christ, King of all, having granted his servants freedom from that tyranny, has made the knowledge of that most holy place shine forth, so that it truly surpasses all amazement. For if all those throughout the whole world who are reputed wise were to gather into one place and wish to say something worthy of this event, they would not be able to compete with it in even the smallest degree; for belief in this wonder surpasses every nature capable of human reasoning as far as heavenly things are by nature more powerful than human ones. For this reason, then, this is always my first and only aim: that just as the faith of the truth displays itself daily in ever newer wonders, so too the souls of all of us may become more zealous for the holy law, in sobriety and unanimous eagerness. Since I think this is clear to all, I want you above all to be convinced that nothing concerns me more than to adorn with beautiful buildings that sacred place which, by God's command, I ordered to be relieved of the most shameful error of idolatry, as of some weight lying upon it—a place holy from the beginning by God's judgment, but shown to be still holier since it brought to light the faith in the saving passion. It is fitting, therefore, that your sagacity should so arrange matters and make provision for every necessity that not only the basilica of this most holy place may be better than those everywhere else, but that the rest also may be such that all the finest buildings in every city are surpassed by the splendour of this edifice. And know that we have entrusted the care of raising and finishing the walls to our friend Dracilianus, who acts as deputy of the most illustrious prefects, and to the governor of the province. For my piety has ordered that craftsmen and workmen and everything necessary for the building, whatever they learn from your sagacity, be sent at once through their provision. As for the columns or the marbles, whatever you consider most useful and valuable, make a survey and be diligent to write to us, so that once we learn from your letter how many and what kind are needed, these may be brought from every quarter for the splendour of this house. For it is right that the most wonderful place in the world should be adorned as it deserves. As for the vault of the basilica of this house, I wish to learn from you whether you think it should be coffered or done in some other most splendid kind of work. For if it is to be coffered, it can also be decorated with gold. For the rest, your holiness will quickly inform the aforementioned officials how many workmen and craftsmen and what expenses are needed. Be diligent to report these to me at once as well, not only concerning the marbles and columns but also concerning the coffered ceilings, if you judge this to be the better choice. May God preserve you, beloved brother."

The one who served this letter was none other than the emperor's own mother, that woman blessed in her child and praised by all the pious, who bore this great luminary for the world and nourished him in piety from childhood. For she, no less than the boy's father, her husband Constantius, brought him up in the divine laws of piety towards Christ. She endured the toils of the journey and took no account of the infirmities of old age—for she undertook this journey shortly before her death, reaching the end of this life at eighty years of age—
and, filled with longing and burning in her heart like fire to reach the holy places and to search for the Saviour's tomb and the precious wood of the cross of Christ, she arrived in Jerusalem.

When she saw the place that had received the sufferings of our common salvation, she at once ordered that loathsome temple to be razed to the ground and the accursed soil to be thrown somewhere far away. When the hidden place had been laid bare, three crosses were seen buried beside the Lord's tomb. Everyone believed without question that one of them was that of our Lord and Saviour, and the others those of the robbers crucified with him; yet they did not know which one had touched that holy body of the Lord and received the stream of his precious blood. But that most wise and truly divine Macarius, the president of that church, resolved the difficulty by the following means. He decided to bring the pieces of wood to a most distinguished woman of the city, who was gripped by a long illness and was near death, and so came to know the power of the saving cross, using the following prayer to God. Kneeling beside the woman's pallet, with the most God-beloved Helena and a great crowd of people present with him, he cried out in a loud voice: "You, Lord God Almighty, who through your only-begotten Son Jesus Christ wrought salvation for the human race on the wood of the cross; who now also, in these last times, inspired your handmaid, together with her son, your servant, to seek out the blessed wood on which Christ, the Saviour of all people, especially of believers, was nailed in the flesh: show us, Lord, which of these three pieces of wood is the cross of Christ, so that by its touch, applied through us to this sick and half-dead woman, it may lead her by the hand to health and to rising up." When he had finished praying, he brought the first piece of wood and laid it on the sick woman, but it did her no good. Then he brought the second as well, but it too proved ineffective. But when he stretched out his hand to the third, at once, as soon as its shadow fell on her, the wood drew near the sick woman, and a very great miracle took place. Suddenly the half-dead woman opened her eyes; then, when the precious cross of the Lord was laid on her, she immediately leapt up, and standing on her feet she sent up glory to God. Having become so much better than she had been, she went about the whole house rejoicing with all her household and proclaiming in a loud voice the good news of the power of the divine cross. So the most pious empress, mother of the all-praised and most God-beloved emperor Constantine, having given her sincere attention to the matter and having been assured concerning the Saviour's tomb and the precious cross of Christ, at once raised a house of prayer on that very spot, in accordance with the orders of her most pious son Constantine; and calling it the Martyrium, she advanced still more and more in faith. Having thus obtained what she longed for, she next devoted herself without hesitation to searching for the nails with which the Lord's body had been nailed to the wood of the cross. When she found them, she set some into the imperial helmet, taking forethought for her son's head, so that it might ward off the missiles of the enemy; and this helmet she sent to her son as a divine gift. The rest of the nails she had forged and worked into the bridle of the emperor's horse, contriving safety for the emperor and at the same time bringing an ancient prophecy to fulfilment. For long ago the prophet Zechariah cried out: "And what is on the bridle shall be holy to the Lord Almighty." Of the saving cross she assigned a portion to the palace; for the remainder she made a case of silver and gave it to the bishop of that city, the divine Macarius whom we mentioned above, charging him to keep these memorials of salvation for future generations. Gathering craftsmen skilled in every kind of material from everywhere, together with Macarius, president of the church there, and in accordance with the orders of the emperor Constantine her son, she built those very great and most splendid churches in wonderful fashion. I have thought it quite superfluous to describe their beauty and size in this work, since practically all the lovers of Christ who stream there from every land under heaven behold the magnificence of the works. That all-praised and admirable empress, mother of the most faithful emperor, did another thing worthy of remembrance. She gathered all the women who practise lifelong virginity, had them recline on many couches, and herself performed the work of a servant, waiting on them, setting food before them, handing them cups and pouring wine, carrying the jug over the basin and pouring water over their hands. Having done these and similar things, she returned rejoicing to her son, and not long afterwards, in all cheerfulness, passed over to the imperishable life, after giving her son many instructions about a pious way of life and crowning him with her parting blessings. Even after her death she received honour such as befitted one who had served the God of all so carefully and so fervently. She left a daughter named Constantia, who had become the wife of the impious Licinius.
These few things, then, out of the many great virtues of the most blessed, most pious and most God-beloved Helena according to God our Saviour, I have set down in this historical work.

But I will turn my account once more to the divine zeal of the Christ-bearing emperor Constantine, her son. He so far surpassed both his father and his mother in devotion to the saving wood of Christ that he took the sign of the saving cross of the Lord Christ's passion in the flesh, which his mother had brought to him, and hid it away. He believed that the city named after him would be kept safe forever if that relic were guarded within it, so he placed it inside his own statue, which stands on the great porphyry column in the market called the Forum of Constantine.

This most God-beloved emperor, bound so closely to God by such piety and faith, brought a great many other barbarian nations into peace with himself. God subjected to him peoples that had long been at odds with the Romans. The more he humbled himself before God in reverence, the more, indeed far more, did God direct all things for him. At that time many additions were made to the preaching of the apostles. Matthew had preached to the Parthians, Bartholomew to the Ethiopians, and Thomas to the Indians of Greater India; yet the word about Christ was not yet known to the Indians who live beyond the Parthians, or to certain nations bordering on them. Now a philosopher named Metrodorus had travelled through nearly every nation for the sake of inquiry. In imitation of him, a man of Tyre named Meropius, a distinguished philosopher, took up the same undertaking as Metrodorus for the sake of inquiry. He took with him two boys who were his kinsmen. They were well trained in every branch of letters and eager to learn about everything, and they had begged the philosopher Meropius to take them along with him. One of them was named Frumentius and the other Aedesius. Now the barbarians of that region had a custom and a law that, whenever the Romans failed to keep the treaty of peace with them, they would kill any of our people found among them. At that time the treaty between the two sides happened to have been broken for a short while, and it was just then that Meropius was exploring innermost India together with Frumentius and Aedesius. Hard pressed by a lack of necessities, and above all of water, they set out from that country, and as they sailed along the sea they put in at certain places belonging to those innermost Indians, since contrary winds kept them from going further. For some days they stayed there unnoticed, taking what their bodies needed from the land. But one day, while the boys were sitting under a tree going over their reading, the barbarians came upon them and slaughtered everyone along with Meropius except the two boys, Frumentius and Aedesius. When the barbarians saw them they were moved to pity and spared them because they were children, and they brought them as a gift to their own king. The king, perceiving Frumentius' natural ability, at once made him steward over the expenses of his household, and appointed Aedesius to be his cupbearer. While they were in these posts and advancing day by day, it came about that the king departed this human life, leaving a son who was still a very small child as successor to his kingdom, by the decree of the great king of the Indians. So Frumentius and his companion then became guardians of the boy's whole kingdom, for his mother put them in charge of everything because of their sincere character and their experience in practical affairs. Along with natural ability they had knowledge, having been well schooled above all by education and by life in a foreign land, the very things that give even the young the steadiness of their elders. Since they were also devout, distinguished for their faith in God and surpassing most people in every kind of kindness, they travelled over land and sea managing the affairs of the boy's kingdom. They instructed the neighbouring peoples to bring to them any Romans staying among them as foreigners, taking forethought to sow the knowledge of God among the Indians through these men. And the times were favourable to them. Having found some such men, they urged them to follow the customs of the Romans: to make places of prayer and to build churches where those who were receiving the knowledge of God could gather, even if they could not set up altars, since they had no authority of priesthood. From this the Indians in those further regions gained an occasion to come to know God, for Frumentius approached them with great zeal, with kindnesses, gentle persuasion and exhortations. When the royal child whose kingdom they had been governing as guardians reached manhood and had grown to his full stature, they asked him as a favour to grant them leave to return to their homes. The king and his mother urged them with many entreaties to stay, held on to them and would not release them. But Frumentius told them that he and his companion were greatly distressed about this, and so they compelled the king and his mother to agree to let them go. These consented with the greatest sorrow, for they did not wish to oppose Frumentius, whom they regarded as their master. The two handed over to the boy and his mother all the affairs of the kingdom that had been entrusted to them, and left India with great honour to make their way home. Then Aedesius went to Tyre, while Frumentius came to Alexandria, reasoning that it was right not to neglect the divine work that was under way among the barbarians. He went to Athanasius, bishop of the church of the Alexandrians, who at that time held the helm of the high priesthood there. Frumentius related to him everything that had happened and urged that a bishop be sent to them. Then the great Athanasius, considering what had been said very wisely and with great understanding, said to Frumentius: "And what other such man shall we find, one in whom is the Spirit of God as in you, brother, who is able to direct these things rightly and to govern the churches there as well as anyone could?" And he ordained him bishop and ordered him to journey back to the Indians, to consecrate the churches there and to care for the people of that land. After his ordination a very great grace from God was added to the man, and he sent forth apostolic rays. For when he reached the innermost India already mentioned, he confirmed the gospel of Christ with signs and mighty works and drew great multitudes of the Indians to the true faith of Christ, and they received the divine word through him with complete sincerity. Therefore churches and ordinations multiplied among those nations. Aedesius told us these things while he was living in Tyre, for he became a presbyter of the church there and remained in it until the end of his life.

At the same time the Iberians and the Lazi, who live in the region of Pontus, also received the word of God, having never believed in it before. The cause of this very great blessing was a woman who lived among them as a captive. She led a life of the highest discipline, and by her self-control and her other good works she filled them all with amazement. When they asked her the reason for such great asceticism, that holy woman said simply, "For the sake of Christ, the Son of God." Yet this brought none of them to faith in true religion; they only marvelled at the woman and, observing her strange way of life, pondered it a great deal. Now it was their custom, whenever they had a small child fall ill, to go round to all the local people and seek help from every quarter. So it happened that a certain woman, having gone round to everyone, came also to the captive. As the woman stood at the door with her little child, the captive said to her, "I can do nothing to help the child, but I know that Christ, of whom I have often told you, is able even to raise the dead and to grant healing to those who have been given up for lost." The child's mother implored the captive. Then, moved with pity for the woman's pleading, she wrapped the infant in her own sackcloth, prayed to God, and gave the child back to its mother healthy. What had happened spread to many people and reached even the queen, who lay gripped by a very severe illness; she had been sick for a long time and was now incurable of the grievous disease that had come upon her. She therefore sent members of her household to ask the captive to come to her. But the captive, out of fear and reverence, declined to go over to the queen, knowing how easily a person slips when human glory creeps in. So when the queen learned that she was firmly determined not to come, she ordered that she herself be carried to the captive on her couch. The blessed captive, put to shame by the queen's humility, wrapped the queen in her sackcloth in the same way, knelt down upon it, and offered her prayers to God with her usual prayer to Christ. Then she sent her home healthy, rejoicing and walking on her own feet, a new and strange wonder to the people of the land, confessing the grace of Christ as she had been taught by the captive woman. As she walked she cried out plainly, "Glory to you, O Christ, master of the captive! To you be thanks and to you all honour, our Saviour, who have counted us worthy to believe in you!" The queen also told her husband everything, and he was moved to want to reward the captive with money, as a fitting recompense for the kindness she had shown his wife. But the queen said to him, "This captive, O king, does not desire silver, nor does she seek to gain gold. The only gift she asks of us that is worthy of her is that we believe that Christ is the Son of the Most High God. For one whose whole life is fasting and self-control has no use for treasures of gold and silver. I have had experience of this devout woman, and I am telling you the truth, O king. But if you care at all for my salvation, let us repay the woman in a newer way, by accepting her Christ and worshipping him." For the time being, however, he was rather reluctant. Although his wife often reminded him, he kept putting it off, deflecting her request with promises and saying that he hoped a suitable time would come when this would be to his advantage. And that is what happened, by the providence of God, who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For it happened that while he was absorbed in hunting in a thickly wooded and very deep forest, he was overtaken in broad daylight by an unexpected night. Suddenly, at midday, a very deep darkness was poured over the whole forest where the king was. Since his companions had scattered this way and that in the hunt, the king was seized with the greatest fear and could not think at all how to escape what had come upon him. All his companions were suffering the same distress: the darkness had fixed each of those who were hurrying to reach him to the spot where it had overtaken him, like a pillar, and did not allow them to move forward to help one another. Then the king remembered his wife and the captive who had healed her when she was incurable, and he cried out, saying, "Christ, Lord of the captive, stand by me now, so that I may escape the distress that presses on me. For I have the clearest proof of your divine power in my own wife." As soon as he finished the prayer the darkness was immediately lifted, and the light of day was poured out over the whole forest where they had been fixed, brighter than before. When they came home, they found the king safe and sound, at once commanding that the captive be brought to him immediately, and promising that he would no longer worship any other god than Jesus Christ, whom the woman worshipped. So the captive woman came and became the king's teacher, setting out for him the whole pattern of the faith. He was overjoyed and felt no shame at learning godliness from a woman of humble station; on the contrary, he took pride in her and ordered that she be brought out into the midst of the people, speaking openly about her and saying, "My wife escaped death through this woman's prayer, by the grace of Christ, King of all." And he urged his subjects, if they wished to be saved, to share the same mind and to choose the worship of Christ, despising the idols. When he learned from the holy woman that churches must be founded for the worship of Christ, he at once set about the work eagerly. They built and raised the outer walls of the building, and next the columns had to be set up in the middle of the building to divide the men and women who would gather there. But God, wishing to plant a firm conviction in the king and in all his subjects concerning the gospel of Jesus Christ his Son that had been preached through the captive woman, caused the third column, as it was being raised in the middle and was still slanting, not to become fully upright like the other two. The builders laboured hard, until the ropes and all their machines had snapped and broken; then they withdrew and fled, afraid that they would be caught underneath the column and killed. For the column stood hanging slantwise in the air, and they could devise no remedy, as builders usually do. The captive heard of this and was seized with great fear that the people might turn back again to their idols. At sunset she came to the place, knelt before God, and by prayer lasting until morning raised the column. It did not stand on its base but hung upright, about one cubit above the base, for God arranged that the captive should not go home until the people arrived, so that they might know her faith in the true God whom she preached. So at dawn they came with the king, and when they saw so great a column hanging upright they were astounded. Then, when the captive had become known to everyone through what had happened, and as she rose from her prayer, the column immediately settled into place as perfectly as could be, as though craftsmen were fitting it to its base, and it stood far more firmly and handsomely than the columns before and after it. As a result the rest of the people came together and joined in confessing the king's faith, marvelling at Christ; for that holy captive woman had solemnly charged them to do this. She feared the simplicity of the people, lest, goaded by their ancestral superstition, they should transfer to her the reverence due to Christ, or form an opinion of her that did not lead to piety. That is why, when she caused the hanging column to be fitted to its proper place, she urged them to join in her prayer, thereby keeping her own reputation in the shade and declaring that the power of Christ the Saviour passes to all people who are devout toward him, in works beyond human power. When the church was finished, the captive advised the king and queen to send to the most God-beloved emperor Constantine, who had been brought up in true religion, asking him to send them someone to consecrate that church. Then envoys sent by the king and the commonwealth of the Iberians reached Constantinople. They reported to the emperor Constantine that the faith of Christ had been established in their land, and asked him to give them a bishop to consecrate and to order the churches among them. The pious and Christ-loving emperor Constantine received them kindly and, rejoicing in the Lord, granted their request. He urged Alexander, bishop of Constantinople, to ordain a bishop for the Iberians, seeing in this the will of God, who was subjecting foreign peoples to him. Our informant for these things was the most faithful Bacurius, a most devout man and a very distinguished member of the royal family of the Iberians in his country. He became a commander of the Romans and, campaigning on the frontier heights of Palestine against the Saracen barbarians, won a most complete victory over them.

But we must return to the subject we undertook, the history of the reign. The emperor Constantine, being very attentive to Christianity and burning with an apostolic longing for Christ, built yet more churches in various cities. He built one at the place called the Oak of Mamre, under which, as the sacred scriptures tell us, the angels were entertained by Abraham. For the emperor Constantine, excellent in all things and most beloved of God, learned that an altar had been set up under that oak and that pagan sacrifices were being performed on it. He rebuked Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, by letter for having overlooked so abominable an outrage, and ordered that the altar be overthrown and that a church of the living God be built beside the oak. Again, learning that the people of Heliopolis in Phoenicia lived impiously and followed a shameful way of life, he put an end to their shameful life by a solemn law. He built a church in that city, had a bishop ordained, and ordered that a sacred clergy be consecrated with him in that church; and in this way he made the evils of the Heliopolitans more moderate. Moreover, he selected Christians as civil magistrates, men attested for their upright life, and set them over the city and all the surrounding country, threatening the inhabitants with death unless they turned away as quickly as possible from their former shameful conduct and their superstition concerning the abominable idols. Further, he overthrew the [temple?] of Aphrodite at Aphaca [?] of unspeakable rites, and he drove out the Pythonic demon in Cilicia, ordering that the temple in which it lurked be torn down from its foundations.

Such were the good works that the most faithful emperor Constantine carried out everywhere on earth. I shall add to this ecclesiastical history another proof of the faith of the same most God-beloved emperor Constantine in the God of all. So great was his love and zeal for Christ that, when he was considering crossing into Persia on behalf of the Christians there, he ordered a tent to be made of embroidered linen in the form of a church, just as Moses had made in the wilderness. This was to be carried along on the march, so that in desert places he might have a place of prayer ready in which to offer his prayers to God. But it did not turn out as he intended that he should complete the expedition into Persia at that time, since he was taking thought for the peace of the churches of God. Still, he made provision for those nurtured in true religion who were subject to the king there, I mean the king of the Persians. He had learned that they were being persecuted by the impious people there, and that this very king, enslaved to error, was contriving all kinds of plots against them; his name was Sapor. So he wrote to him, urging him to embrace true religion and asking that the devout and the Christians be treated with honour. The letter itself will make the zeal of the Christ-loving emperor plain.

"By guarding the divine faith I share in the light of truth; guided by the light of truth I come to know the divine faith. Therefore, as events confirm, I acknowledge the most holy religion to be the teacher of the knowledge of the most holy God. This is the worship I confess that I hold. With the power of this God as my ally, I began from the farthest shores of the Ocean and roused the whole world, region by region, with sure hopes of salvation. So all the nations that had been enslaved under so many tyrants, worn down by daily calamities, and had almost faded away, have now received the vindication of the common cause. They have been rekindled as if by some great healing, and they exult and rejoice and celebrate festivals to God. This is the God I honour. His sign is carried on its shoulders by my army, which is dedicated to him, and it is directed wherever the cause of justice calls it. And from those very campaigns I at once receive his favour in splendid trophies. With a pure and unmixed mind I glory in proclaiming that this God dwells in the highest. I call upon this God on bended knee. I shun all abominable blood and all unpleasant and repulsive odours, and I turn away from all earthly glitter, the things in which that utterly foul and lawless error delights. That error has defiled many of the nations and whole peoples, cast them down and handed them over to the lowest depths. For the things that God, in his providence for humankind and out of his own love for humanity, brought into the open for our needs are wrongly turned to serve each person's desires. But he asks of people only a pure mind and an unstained soul, and by these he weighs their deeds of virtue and piety. He takes pleasure in works of fairness and gentleness. He loves the meek and hates the turbulent. He loves faith and punishes unbelief. He condemns and overthrows every power exercised with arrogance, punishes the insolence of the proud, and tears up from their foundations those who are puffed up with conceit. He also sets great value on a just kingship, strengthens it with his help, and preserves royal wisdom in the calm of peace. Therefore, brother, I rejoice and exult greatly. I confess this God to be the author and saviour of all. Many of those who reigned here, led astray by mad errors, tried to deny him. But such a punishing end consumed them all that the whole human race after them holds up their calamities, and no other example, as a warning to anyone who would imitate them. I consider that man to have been one of these whom divine justice drove from here like a thunderbolt and handed over to your regions, where he made the trophy over him famous among you for his shame. Yet it seems to have turned out for the good that in our own age, too, the punishment of such men has been plainly displayed. For I myself have seen the end of those who recently troubled the people dedicated to God with lawless decrees. Many thanks are therefore due to God, because by his perfect providence the whole human race that keeps his divine law has had peace restored to it, and it exults and rejoices. From this we too are persuaded that all things stand with us in the finest and safest state when, through the pure and approved religion of these people, I mean the peoples of God, and through their agreement concerning the divine, he deigns to gather all to himself. As for this company of men, my fellow servants, I mean the Christians, on whose behalf I say all this: how glad do you think I am to hear that the finest regions of Persia too are greatly adorned by them, just as I would wish? If you consent to treat them in the best way, as is fitting, then the best things will likewise be yours, since they too are yours. For in this way you will have the Lord and God of all gentle, merciful and kindly toward you. Therefore, since you are so great, I commend these people to you, because you are also renowned for piety, and I entrust their governance, I mean the Christians, to those among them who preside over the pious worship of God. Love them in a way that befits your humanity. For through your faith you will grant boundless favour both to yourself and to us."

Such was the care that Constantine, an emperor excellent in all things, took for those adorned with piety toward Christ. He looked after his own subjects, and he also provided as far as he could for those who lived under other sceptres. For this reason he himself enjoyed divine protection from above. He held the reins not only of the whole Roman world but also of the barbarians, and both rulers and ruled were well disposed toward him and gladly obeyed the bridle of his command. Even the barbarians, held in check by fear of war, now served him willingly, because they feared the God who stood beside Constantine. Trophies were set up everywhere, and the emperor showed himself victorious over all. But a great many others have written about these things more precisely, praising them to the glory of the God of all. Let us bring our account back to the sequence of the history before us.

The most faithful emperor Constantine, then, was concerned for the peace of the churches and, as we have often said, carried the care of them in his soul, as the apostle did. But those who were called priests only in appearance, all who had accepted the corruption of Arius, could not bear to keep quiet. They had taken up a war against the truth that admitted no truce, and they contrived all kinds of schemes against the orthodox faith. It happened that Constantia, sister of the God-loving emperor Constantine and wife of the impious Licinius, whom we have mentioned earlier, came into contact with a certain presbyter who shared the views of the partisans of Arius's blasphemy. He was a consummate flatterer named Eutocius. First he wormed his way in with some of Constantia's attendants, and soon he came into the presence of Constantia herself. He enjoyed a great deal of freedom of speech with her and of her favour, and through their frequent meetings his conversation with her about Arius also advanced. Growing bold, he then carried her away with his deceitful words. Envy alone, he said, was responsible for what had happened to Arius. With these and similar deceitful words he persuaded her that Arius held and taught the same things as Alexander and the bishops throughout the world. Constantia believed what he told her, especially when she heard from him that Arius was of one mind with Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, and that Pope Alexander opposed him for no reason, out of jealousy of his good standing with the many. So Constantia accepted the deceitful words of the presbyter of Arius's party. She was pleased with what he said, held that presbyter in greater honour and counted him among her closest intimates. Not long afterwards she fell into a very grave illness, from which she died. When the most pious emperor Constantine learned of it, he came in haste to visit her. After the death of her impious husband and the passing of their mother, the most God-loving and celebrated Helena, into the life free of grief, this all-praised and most faithful emperor had given her every care and had not let her experience the pains of widowhood or orphanhood. For this reason, even at her death, he gave her the attention that befitted her, both when absent and when present. After the emperor and Constantia had talked at length, Constantia, confident as she was with her own brother, said to him: "Grant me one favour, all-praised emperor, as I depart to God." The emperor said to her, "What is it?" Constantia replied: "I beg you, emperor, to order Arius to be released from exile. Put an end to the misfortune brought upon him by a plot, and do not stain your pious reign, even briefly, with innocent blood." The emperor Constantine granted his sister's request. He thought she was saying this out of sisterly affection and had not been talked into it by the presbyter of Arius's party, and he regarded his sister as a trustworthy counsellor. For the time being he forbade Arius to set foot in Alexandria and Egypt, but at the request of his sister Constantia he ordered him to be released from exile at once. Constantia also commended that presbyter of Arius's party to him. She urged the emperor to trust him and to take pleasure in what he said: "Since I have had experience of his orthodoxy, most pious emperor, I entrust him to you." Then Constantia departed this human life. That presbyter made his way into the palace, for the most gentle and God-loving emperor had promised Constantia at her request to do this, and afterwards he fulfilled the promise. The presbyter was ordered to visit him often, the emperor gave him the greatest freedom of speech, and he became one of the closest intimates of the Christ-bearing emperor Constantine.

When Eusebius of Nicomedia and Theognis of Nicaea, who were still in exile, heard of this, they took courage. They wrote a supposed document of repentance and sent it to the leading bishops, asking to be recalled from exile. They declared in word, though not in conduct, as they had done before, that they accepted and held the faith of Nicaea. The bishops who received this document of their feigned repentance treated them kindly, and at their request the two were recalled from exile by imperial order. They recovered the churches from which they had been driven and ejected the bishops ordained in their place: Eusebius drove out Amphion, and Theognis drove out Chrestus. It would be well to include in this work a copy of the document of their spurious repentance. It runs as follows:

"Since we have already been condemned by Your Holiness, we ought to bear in silence what your holy judgement has decided. But because by our silence we give grounds for accusation against ourselves, we report to Your Holiness that we agreed with your holy synod. After examining the meaning of the term homoousios, we were wholly for peace and in no way followed the heresy. For the safety of the churches we raised whatever points occurred to our minds. Having given and received full assurance, so as to satisfy those who were to be persuaded through us, we signed the faith. We did not, however, sign the anathema. This was not because we found fault with the faith, God forbid, but because we did not believe the accused to be such as he was charged with being. We had been fully assured that he was not such, both from his letters to us and from our conversations with him face to face. But if your holy synod has been convinced, we do not resist. We agree with what you have decided, and by this letter we confirm our assent. We are not complaining of exile; we are shedding the suspicion of heresy. If you will now at least see fit to receive us back into your presence, you will find us of one mind with you in everything, following what you have decided. For if Your Holiness saw fit that the very man charged with heresy should be treated kindly by our most pious emperor and granted clemency, and you pleaded for him to be freed from exile, how much more is it right that we, who are blameless, should be granted freedom from exile and a return to Your Holiness? It would be absurd for us to keep silent when the one thought guilty has been released, and so to supply clear evidence against ourselves through our silence, as we said before. We beg you, then, as befits your Christ-loving holiness, to remind our most God-beloved emperor about this, to place our petitions in his hands, and to decide quickly what is fitting for you to do in our case, most holy ones."

This is the document of recantation of Eusebius and Theognis, mentioned above. Their own words show that they signed the faith dictated at Nicaea by the holy synod there with their hand only, not with their intention, as has been shown before, and that they refused to join the holy synod in voting for the deposition of Arius and the anathema against him. Yet through the efforts of the bishops who received their petitions they were released from exile. They took possession of their former dioceses, as I said above, but had scarcely laid eyes on them, so to speak, before they hurried with all possible speed to the court. On reaching Constantinople they made bold to rush into the palace, relying on the patronage of that presbyter whom Constantia, as Constantine's own sister, had commended to the most God-beloved emperor, and who was treated with the greatest attention and honour by the emperor. Even so, as I said before, the presbyter did not dare to reveal the Arian heresy lodged within him, for he saw that the emperor's soul burned with zeal for divine things and for the exactness of the true faith. He did, however, bring Eusebius and Theognis in to the emperor, after advising them to conceal for the present the disease of the impious heresy of Arius. He pleaded with the emperor at length on their behalf to grant them freedom of speech, especially Eusebius, testifying that they held what had been stated at the synod. And indeed this true enemy of the truth was speaking the truth, for the flatterer said they held the very things they had muttered against with slanders there. The emperor had a natural nobility of character and great reverence for the clergy. He possessed the forgiving heart of David, the great king and prophet, and could not even bring himself to think of the plots Eusebius had dared to make against him in the time of the impious Licinius. So he received them kindly and reverently as priests of God, honoured them greatly, greeted them with a kiss, and told them to come to him often. As day by day they advanced in freedom of speech with Constantine, an emperor excellent in all things, they pressed that presbyter of Arius's party to begin pleading with the emperor on Arius's behalf and to ask that Arius be admitted to his presence, since Arius could commend himself and show that he held the views of the holy fathers at Nicaea. The presbyter gave way to the entreaties of Eusebius and Theognis and began to speak to the emperor on Arius's behalf. He presented most of what he said as coming from those men: that they declared Arius agreed with everything decided at the synod and approved of the faith proclaimed there. But what the presbyter said about Arius struck the emperor as strange. The presbyter kept this up for many days, sometimes in private and very often in the presence of Eusebius of Nicomedia. For the emperor sent for Eusebius quite often, since the most faithful emperor did not remember what this impious Eusebius had once staged against him. So with the skill of his deceitful words Eusebius, both through the presbyter and in person, persuaded the most humane and gentle emperor to order Arius summoned to him. He assured him that once Arius came into the presence of the pious emperor Constantine, he too would agree to everything to which "the synod and we," he said, "have agreed." These things seemed incredible to the emperor. Yet he was overcome by his God-loving gentleness and his zeal for the concord of the churches, and trusting them as priests, he said to them: "If Arius agrees with the synod and truly chooses to hold its views, I will receive him into my presence and send him back to Alexandria with honour." He said this and ordered by letter that Arius be summoned to court. Arius, having been honoured with the emperor's letter, hurried at once to reach Constantinople. With him was Euzoius, whom the divine Alexander, bishop of the church of Alexandria, had deposed along with him. Through the efforts of Eusebius of Nicomedia and his circle, word was brought to the pious emperor through the presbyter that Arius had arrived. So the emperor received him and Euzoius into his presence and asked them whether they agreed with the faith set forth at Nicaea by the three hundred holy fathers. Arius said on oath that he had always believed, and still believed, just as the holy fathers at Nicaea did, "and all who are with us believe the same." By this he meant Eusebius of Nicomedia and his circle and Theognis of Nicaea itself. He seemed to swear truly, but it was to deceive and win over the simplicity of the Christ-loving emperor. Arius's sworn statement so astonished the most God-beloved and gentle emperor that he immediately sent Arius off to Alexandria with honour. But when Arius reached Alexandria, Bishop Alexander would not receive him, at the urging of Athanasius, for he turned away from him as from a pollution. Then Eusebius and his circle wrote on Arius's behalf themselves, and they also induced the emperor to write rather sharply to Alexander and Athanasius. Athanasius refused absolutely to receive Arius and those with him. Writing together with the bishop, he explained to the emperor that it was impossible to take back again those who had once rejected the faith and had been anathematized and condemned by so great a holy synod "and by your God-loving Piety." Then the emperor took it badly. Stirred to anger by Eusebius of Nicomedia and his circle, he wrote to Athanasius with this threat:

"Now that you know my will, grant unhindered entry to all who wish to enter the church. For if I learn that you have hindered any who lay claim to the faith of the church, or have barred such people from entry, I will at once send someone to depose you by my order and remove you from your place."
In the same way he wrote similar things on Arius's behalf to Bishop Alexander:

"Victor Constantine Maximus Augustus to Father Alexander, bishop. Will most foul envy now, too, bark back with unholy sophistries of delay? What, then, of the present matter? Are we teaching doctrines different from those decided through you by the Holy Spirit, most honoured brother? Arius, that very Arius, I say, came to me, the Augustus, at the urging of a great many people. He professed to hold, concerning our catholic faith, those things that were defined and confirmed through you at the synod of Nicaea, when I, your fellow servant, was present and joined in the definition. He came to us at once together with Euzoius, since they clearly understood the intention of the imperial command. In the presence of a number of people I discussed the word of life with them. I am the man who has dedicated my mind to God with sincere faith; I am your fellow servant, who has taken upon myself the whole care for your peace and concord." And after other things: "I have therefore written not only to remind you but also to ask you to receive these men, who come as suppliants. If you find that they hold to the orthodox and ever-living apostolic faith set forth at Nicaea, for they affirmed in our presence that this is what they believe, then take thought for all, I beg you. For if you take thought for them, you will overcome hatreds with concord. Help concord, then, I beg you. Offer the blessings of friendship to those who have no doubts about the faith. Let me hear what I wish and long for: peace and concord among you all. May God keep you, most honoured father."
The emperor wrote this with an eye to the common good, not wishing the church to be torn apart, for he was eager to bring everyone to concord.

The divine Alexander received the emperor's letter and lived on only a short time. He then departed this life by a blessed end, having been bishop of God's church in Alexandria for sixteen years in all: nine years and one month before the Council of Nicaea, three years and six months in the time of the council, and three years and five months after the council, sixteen years altogether. Athanasius then took up the ministry of the priesthood. What sort of man he was in good sense, in piety, and in ordering the affairs of the church, what follows will show us. When the heretics learned that the divine Athanasius was at the head of the church, they were dismayed at first. But afterwards they joined against him with one mind, so as to wipe his memory from the earth, if one may put it so, just as the Jews plotted against Christ. For they at once set about persuading the most God-beloved emperor to issue imperial decrees against him. But first we must relate a little about the man's way of life from childhood. The blessed Alexander had been entrusted with the office of the priesthood after the blessed Achillas. After the assembly commemorating the contest of the holy Peter, bishop and martyr, he had invited the clergy to a meal and was waiting for them to gather. Standing apart, he saw from a distance some boys who had taken up a game that followed the order of the church. The house faced the sea, and the holy children were playing along its shore. Among them Athanasius was the bishop, and others of his age were presbyters and deacons. These brought him boys who were catechumens so that he might baptize them, and when Athanasius, as bishop, had baptized them all in the manner of the church, he wished to address them with a word of instruction. Astonished at what was happening, the divine Alexander ordered the boys brought to him. When he had learned everything just as it had taken place, he acted on the advice of the clergy with him. He perfected the boys who had been baptized, sealing them with the seal in Christ and anointing them with the holy symbols of saving baptism. Then he called Athanasius' parents and entrusted Athanasius to them. He ordered them to educate him in letters and to advance him in the Lord as far as they could, and when he had grown up, to give him back to him, or rather, as he directed, to the church, just as Hannah, he said, brought Samuel. So when time had passed, the parents brought Athanasius to Bishop Alexander, and the bishop at once put the priestly ephod on him, advancing him as a new Samuel for the church, to defend it against those who are truly Philistines. And indeed he endured many struggles at the hands of the heretics. They too formed a conspiracy, not merely forty men, as against the holy apostle Paul, but the whole multitude of heretics throughout the inhabited world, above all the Ariomaniacs. Meanwhile Athanasius sang with David, saying, "Though an army encamp against me, my heart shall not fear; though war rise up against me, in this will I hope": that is, hope to put on the crown of victory, which he longed to receive from the Lord, who said to him as well, "Take courage and do not fear, for I am with you, and no one shall lay hands on you to harm you." Most of what befell him we shall not recount, lest we weary those who will read this work by lengthening the account, for the things he suffered when persecuted by the most impious heretics are past counting. I shall be content with his more notable deeds, which are celebrated among all who knew the man. For as soon as he presided over the church, as we said, Eusebius of Nicomedia and his party, who were extremely hostile to Athanasius, saw a fitting opportunity for their own aim in what they took to be the emperor's displeasure with the great Athanasius. Daring everything, they stirred up every kind of trouble against him, striving to remove him from the episcopate and condemning the man as having entered the priesthood unworthily. For they hoped that the Arian doctrine could prevail only in this way, if they got Athanasius out of the way. So the aforementioned members of the impious Arian heresy, Ision, Eudaemon and Callinicus, banded together against him, and through them they set in motion various accusations against the divine Athanasius. First they claimed that Athanasius, on entering the episcopate, had ordered the Egyptians to pay a levy of linen garments to the church of the Alexandrians. To this they stitched on a second slander, worse than the first: that Athanasius, plotting against the emperor's government, had sent a certain Philumenus a casket full of gold to support resistance to the emperor Constantine. Third, a certain man called Ischyras had undertaken a deed deserving many deaths: although he had never received the priesthood, he took on the name of presbyter and dared to perform the functions of priests in the villages of the district called Mareotis. At that time the holy bishop Athanasius came to the Mareotis and was visiting the churches there. On learning about Ischyras, he sent the presbyter Macarius to find out whether what was said was true. Ischyras was found out, ran away from there in hasty flight, reached Nicomedia, and took refuge with Eusebius and his party. Out of hatred for Athanasius they received him as a presbyter, and they promised to honor him with the rank of bishop as well, if he would undertake to bring an accusation against Athanasius. He cobbled together the following story: "Macarius, Athanasius' presbyter, sent by Athanasius, made an assault on our church in the Mareotis, burst into the sanctuary, overturned the holy table, broke a mystical chalice, and burned the sacred books." These things and others like them the aforementioned accusers told the emperor through Eusebius of Nicomedia and his party. They stirred him to anger against Athanasius, adding that "when he received your divine letter he did not accept it, and he refused to receive Arius, who confessed the faith before your Piety." When the emperor heard what was said against Athanasius, he was so astounded that he at once ordered Athanasius the bishop to come to him in Constantinople with all speed. Athanasius came, met the emperor, refuted the slanderers' lie and fully satisfied the emperor. Fortified with imperial letters, he was sent back to Alexandria by the most faithful emperor with the very greatest honor, and he returned to the church entrusted to him by God. This is shown also by the letter of the pious emperor which he sent to the church of the Alexandrians, the last part of which I shall insert into this work. But let none of those who read this work blame me for not including the whole letter in the narrative of this ecclesiastical history. For I searched through all the writers on these matters and did not find it written out in full by any of them. Indeed, of very many other letters as well they recorded only some evident portion, in summary form, in the histories they labored over. Hence I grieve over this more than any of you. But let us return to our subject and inscribe in this history the end of the aforementioned letter, as the account promised. It was written as follows:

"The wicked have had no power against your bishop, believe me, brothers. They have aimed at nothing else than to waste our time and so leave themselves no room for repentance in this life. Help yourselves, therefore, I beg you: cherish your holy affection, love one another with all your strength, and receive your bishop Athanasius with boundless joy, beloved. Indeed, I know very well that his separation from you did not cause you as much grief as the overflowing joy you feel at his return to you. Drive away those who desire to destroy the grace of our concord, and looking to God, love one another, I beg you. For I gladly received your bishop Athanasius, and I spoke with him as one convinced that he is a man of God. May God preserve you, beloved brothers..."

Having received this letter from the emperor, the great Athanasius arrived at Alexandria. All the clergy and people welcomed him gladly and rejoiced to see their shepherd return to his flock with the very greatest honor. All glorified God and honored Constantine, that emperor excellent in every way, with acclamations. But while these things gave our side unspeakable joy, they brought endless pain and shame to the enemies and to those practiced in waging war against the Son of God. Even so, stripping all shame from their faces, having the form of piety but denying its power, the party of Eusebius of Nicomedia above all, who ought to have sunk into the earth, clothed themselves in the utmost shamelessness and turned their most grievous and wicked skill at evil plots against another tower of piety. The begetter and chief ringleader of all these wicked schemes was Eusebius of Nicomedia, very wise at doing evil, like his father the devil. For he held the reins not of God's church but of the impious workshop of the Arians. He lingered in Constantinople and saw the emperor quite often through the Arian presbyter, and he greatly increased his freedom of speech with him. Finding in the emperor's simplicity a resource for his own malicious craft, he easily contrived schemes against the champions of the truth. So, disappointed in his most wicked endeavor against the great Athanasius, he devised a plausible route for an attack on the divine Eustathius, president of the church of the Antiochenes. He approached the goodness-loving emperor Constantine as if he were most well-disposed and delighted with what the emperor was doing, asked leave to travel to Jerusalem, and professed a longing to see the sacred houses of God that the emperor had built there. With these deceitful words he beguiled the emperor's David-like soul and set out from Constantinople with the greatest honor, the emperor even assigning him carriages and every other service. Theognius of Nicaea set out with him, being, as we said before, his partner in his wicked and impious schemes. On their journey they reached Antioch and put on the mask of friendship, as Theodoret says. Theodoret, however, passed over a great many of the events and wrote his history with very brief attention. But I have consulted the writers before him, who narrated everything accurately, in order and sequence, and I set out the course of events from them. For, as I said before, we gather their labors from other writers and arrange them here.

But let us return to our subject. When the wretches reached the city of Antiochus, they were received spiritually and with the greatest joy by the president there, the great Eustathius. For he had heard of their feigned repentance as though it were genuine, it is said, and he rejoiced over them. Receiving them kindly for the sake of piety toward Christ, the great Eustathius showed them every possible attention. After this they left Antioch and reached the holy places of Jerusalem. There they found some men of like mind, by whom they were greatly encouraged in the drama they had concocted against the champion of the truth. This did not include Eusebius of Caesarea in Palestine, as Theodoret seems to suggest, slandering the man by writing falsehoods about him. All our holy fathers remember him as distinguished in the orthodox faith, and they celebrate the man's labors and contests at the Council of Nicaea on behalf of the holy and consubstantial Trinity. Just as they remember the divine Macarius, bishop in Jerusalem, the great Eustathius, Alexander of Alexandria, Leontius of Caesarea in Cappadocia, Eupsychius of Tyana, Protogenes of Serdica, and above all Hosius of Cordoba, Athanasius of Alexandria, Alexander of Constantinople, and all the rest who contended for the apostolic doctrines at that holy and sacred council, so too they remember the admirable Eusebius Pamphili, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine. Him, then, the party of Eusebius of Nicomedia did not find there. Instead they found men of like mind: Patrophilus of Scythopolis, Aetius of Lydda, Theodotus of Laodicea, and all the others they found who shared in Arius' impiety. They joined with them, revealed to them what they had concocted against the holy Eustathius, left Jerusalem together with them, and reached the city of Antiochus in their company.

The pretext for the others' coming was, supposedly, to do them the honor of an escort, but what they were really pursuing was war against piety toward Christ. They hired a harlot with gold and persuaded her to lend them her tongue for one hour. Then they convened a council with the great Eustathius and the holy bishops who were with him. After that, the authors of the drama against the high priest ordered everyone else to leave and commanded that the thrice-wretched woman be brought into the council as quickly as possible. The servants of their lawlessness brought the woman into their midst. She stood there showing a nursing infant and saying that she had conceived and borne it through intercourse with Eustathius, and she kept shouting this shamelessly. The great Eustathius, recognizing the slander for what it plainly was, ordered that if she had any witness to this, he should be brought forward. When she said she had none, those who had woven the slander tendered an oath to the harlot. Yet the divine apostolic rule declares that an accusation against a presbyter must not be received except on the evidence of two or three witnesses. But these men despised the divine laws and counted as nothing God's sentence decreed against slanderers. Through the harlot they wove an unwitnessed accusation against so great a man and accepted it, judges who were themselves condemned. And when the thrice-wretched woman also swore the oath they had imposed, crying out that the infant was Eustathius', those men, full of every disgrace, then passed sentence on him as an adulterer. There were many other bishops who defended the apostolic doctrines together with the great Eustathius. Knowing nothing of all that had been concocted, they openly opposed the lawless men and would not let Bishop Eustathius accept that unjust sentence. But the authors of the drama ran quickly to the emperor and persuaded him that the charges had been investigated and found true and that the sentence of deposition was just. So they arranged that the champion of piety and chastity be driven from the sacred precincts as at once an adulterer and a tyrant, and be led off into exile in a distant city of Illyricum, by way of Thrace.

Now the enemy of the apostolic doctrines, Eusebius of Nicomedia, skilled at staging slanders against the heralds of the true faith, stayed in Constantinople together with Theognius. But they had left behind in Antioch the partners of their own wickedness, who ordained Eulalius in place of the divine Eustathius. When he survived only a very short time, they put forward a certain Euphronius. When he too died very soon, for he lived only one year and a few months after his ordination, they arranged for the presidency of that church to be given to Flacillus. All these men alike held the impiety of Arius in secret. So all who held to the right and pious faith, clergy and laity alike, left the church assemblies and gathered by themselves. Everyone called them Eustathians, since they had formed after his departure. That thrice-wretched woman, however, fell not long afterward into a most grievous and prolonged illness. She then exposed the plot and laid bare the slander. She summoned not two or three but many of the priests and told them what had been concocted by that marvellous gang of the impious. She said she had dared to make that slander for money, but she claimed that her oath was not altogether false, for she cried out that the infant belonged to a certain Eustathius, a coppersmith. These, then, were the things dared at that time in Antioch by the impious Eusebius and his associates. But even so the impious were not put to shame, nor had they had their fill of slanders against the champions of truth. Seeing that their schemes against the great Eustathius had turned out as they wished, they stitched together yet another drama against the divine Athanasius, such as none of the worst of men had ever dared. Again they hired certain accusers from the same gang of Melitius and brought them before the emperor, crying out against Athanasius that the athlete of virtue had dared many shameful and unholy deeds. The leaders of these men were Eusebius, Theognius and Theodore of Heraclea in Thrace, who said that such things were intolerable and not to be borne by the ears. So they persuaded the emperor to order a synod to assemble at Antioch in Syria, where the enemies were more numerous, and Athanasius to be tried there. The emperor was persuaded, believing them as priests, for he was wholly ignorant of what they were concocting, and he ordered this to be done. But the champion of the truth, the great Athanasius, knowing the hostility of the impious men we have mentioned, did not come to the council. This gave them a still greater pretext for slander. Having once taken up war against the truth, they condemned him in letters to the emperor for tyranny and insolence. As a result the most gentle emperor was inflamed with anger against Athanasius. He wrote to him showing his anger and urging him to come to Tyre, for he had ordered the synod to be moved there and to assemble there, suspecting that Athanasius distrusted Antioch because many in the East had accepted the corruption of Arius. He also wrote to the synod what one adorned with piety ought to write. It reads as follows:

"Constantine, Victor, Greatest, Augustus, to the holy synod assembled at Tyre. It would perhaps have been fitting, and most suited to the prosperity of the times, for the catholic church to be free of strife and for the servants of Christ now to be free of all reproach. But some, driven by an unhealthy frenzy of contentiousness, for I could call it nothing else, and living in a manner unworthy of themselves, are trying to throw everything into confusion. This seems to me to go beyond every calamity. For this reason I urge you, already running, as the saying goes, to come together without any delay and fill up the synod. Make it a spiritual festival: give aid to those who need help, heal the brothers who are in danger, bring the members that are divided back to concord, and correct what is amiss while time allows. In this way you may restore to so many provinces the harmony that befits them, which, alas the absurdity of it, the arrogance of a very few men has destroyed. That this is pleasing to God the Master, more than all of us could pray for, and worthy of no ordinary glory for you yourselves, if you bring peace back, I believe everyone will agree. Do not delay any longer, then. From now on increase your zeal and strive to bring the matters before you to a fitting end, meeting, of course, with all sincerity and good faith. See to it that peace prevails in all things, for yourselves and for everyone. I have sent to those of the bishops whom you wished, so that they may come and share your concerns. I have sent Dionysius, the former consul, who will remind those who ought to attend the synod with you, and who will also be present as overseer of the proceedings, especially of their good order. If anyone, which for my part I do not expect, should try even now to evade our command and refuse to come to the synod, someone will be sent from us forthwith to expel him by imperial order and teach him that it is never proper to resist decisions of the emperor issued on behalf of the truth. For the rest, it will be the task of your holiness, with one mind in your judgment, acting neither from enmity nor from favor but rather in accordance with the ecclesiastical and apostolic rule, to devise the appropriate remedy for offenses and for whatever has happened through error. So you may free the church from all blasphemy, lighten my cares, and, by restoring the grace of peace to those now in strife, win the greatest good fortune for yourselves. May God preserve you, beloved brothers."

This, then, is what he wrote when he ordered the synod to be held at Tyre; for he trusted the slanderers as if they were priests. Though he kept the vigour of his piety unslackened, he thought that the opposing party had been wronged, and so, as a just judge, he put up even with this trouble. He ordered, however, that once the synod had finished and examined each matter thoroughly, the whole synod should go to Jerusalem for the dedication of the church he had built there. He also wrote another letter to the synod, directing that not only Athanasius but also Arius should appear before the synod, and that what each had done should be examined honestly. The aim was this: if, as Arius said, he had been cut off through envy while he was within the orthodox faith, [?] having first condemned himself for what he had dared against the truth, he should keep silent. That is, unless he had cunningly undertaken his recantation as a means of revenge against his own bishop Athanasius, weaving against him spewings of suspicion. If envy were found to be the cause, the bishops at the synod were to make every effort to bring the two together in peace; but if Arius had made use of a feigned repentance, he was to go back to Alexandria and be judged on this matter there.

The all-praised emperor wrote this out of concern for the concord of all, so that every wrangle there would be put out of the way and they could celebrate the dedication of the church in Jerusalem more peaceably as they consecrated it to God. The unholy Arius, however, could not bring himself to appear at the synod in Tyre. But the great Athanasius arrived at Tyre with great eagerness, together with Timothy and Macarius, his priests, and very many other clergy and respected men who accompanied him. So when the bishops had come together at Tyre, and all had assembled along with the consular Dionysius, the most eminent men with him who were honoured with high dignities, and the governor of the province, the former consul Dionysius delivered the emperor's letter to the synod of bishops. Some other bishops also arrived who were charged with corrupting doctrine, one of whom was Asclepas of Gaza. But I wish first to set down in this work the dramatic accusations against Saint Athanasius, and then to relate what happened at that notorious tribunal.

A certain Arsenius, formerly a reader of Athanasius, had been charged with certain crimes and was about to be killed by the mob. When the great Athanasius learned of this (for he had looked into the case), the man was saved in the following way. Having found out that Arsenius was the victim of slander, he came by night and rescued him, arranging for him to escape death by flight. Later the followers of Melitius found him in Egypt and arranged for him to be given the title of bishop. Some time afterwards, at the instigation of Eusebius of Nicomedia (for he was the one who everywhere contrived intricate slanders against the pious), the members of the Melitian faction hid this same Arsenius and saw to it that he stayed out of sight for a long time. Then they cut the right hand off a corpse, preserved it, placed it in a wooden box and carried it around everywhere, saying that Arsenius had been murdered and dismembered by Athanasius, and they called Athanasius a murderer. But the all-seeing eye of God did not allow Arsenius to stay hidden for very long. First it became known in Egypt and the Thebaid that he was alive. Then, as he himself later related, God put it into his mind to reflect on the rescue that Athanasius had arranged for him beyond all hope, and also that he would be doing wrong and committing the greatest crime if he allowed his benefactor to be put to death on his account rather than dying for him himself. So the Ruler of all brought him to Tyre, where the slanderers were displaying that theatrical hand before the judges. Athanasius's household saw him and took him to their lodging, and when they had learned from him both God's providential plan and his own willingness, they urged him to stay hidden for the time being. At dawn the great Athanasius came to the council with Timothy and Macarius, his priests, and those who had come there with him from Alexandria. First they brought in a woman who had lived a life of debauchery. She cried out shamelessly, saying that she had professed virginity, and that Athanasius, when he was lodging at her house, had raped her and violated her against her will. While she was saying this, the accused came in, and with him, among the others, the priest Timothy, an admirable man. When the judges ordered Athanasius to answer the accusation, Athanasius kept silent, as if he were not the one accused, while Timothy said to the woman, "Woman, have I ever met you? Have I ever entered your house?" She cried out all the more shamelessly, quarrelling with Timothy, stretching out her hand toward him, pointing at him and saying to Timothy himself, "You took my virginity, you stripped me of my chastity, you defiled the purity of my soul," and all the other things that women who have lost all shame through excess of debauchery are accustomed to say. What was happening was truly astonishing and beyond all wonder: Athanasius was the one accused, but it was Timothy who was being charged. So, since those who had composed the drama were put to shame, and those of the judges who were their accomplices blushed as well, they ordered the woman to be thrown out. Then the divine Athanasius said that the woman should not be let go, but that she should be questioned and they should learn [?]. But the slanderers cried out that there were other, more serious charges, which could in no way be dissolved by any art or cleverness: "for sight, not hearsay, will judge what is shown." With these words they displayed that notorious box and uncovered the preserved hand. When those in the council saw it, each of them cried out: the accomplices of the slanderers said that the abomination was real, while the others, who knew it was a lie, laughed, saying that Arsenius was hidden and still alive. The council was filled with the greatest uproar, and when a little quiet had barely been restored, the accused Athanasius asked the judges whether any among them knew Arsenius. Many said that they knew the man well, and Athanasius ordered him to be brought in. When he had come in and stood in the middle of the council, Athanasius asked again: "Is this Arsenius, whom I am said to have killed, and whom these men say was mutilated after his murder and deprived of his right hand?" Very many of those at the synod agreed that it was Arsenius himself. The divine Athanasius then pulled back his cloak and showed both of Arsenius's hands, right and left. "Let no one look for another," he said, "for each of us human beings has received two hands from the Maker of all." Yet even though this had been shown in this way by the judgement of the all-seeing God, and the accusers and the judges who were their accomplices ought to have hidden themselves and prayed that the very earth would gape open beneath them and swallow them whole, they did the opposite. They filled the council with uproar and riot, calling Athanasius a sorcerer and saying that he was deceiving people's eyes by some kind of witchcraft. They rose up against him and tried to tear the champion of piety apart and slaughter him, stirring up, so to speak, the very earth and throwing dust into the air, like those who once cried out against the divine apostle Paul, saying, "Away with him quickly; for it is not fitting that he should live." But those entrusted by the emperor with keeping order prevented the murder. They snatched the victor away, had him board a boat and so secured his safety. The divine Athanasius boarded the boat and set out for the imperial court, escaping the hands of the murderers. They, for their part, at once sent some bishops of their own mind to the Mareotis: Theognis of Nicaea, Maris of Chalcedon, Theodore of Heraclea in Thrace, Narcissus the Cilician, Ursacius and some others who shared their views, so that they might compile a one-sided record of proceedings there against Athanasius. (The Mareotis is in Alexandria, named after Lake Maria, being near it.) They instructed them also to send Arius, the author of the evils, to them as quickly as possible at Aelia, that is, Jerusalem, where they were going from Tyre with the bishops of the synod. For the emperor had again directed, as I said earlier, that the whole synod should go from Tyre to Jerusalem together with all the bishops from everywhere, to consecrate the churches he had built there. He also sent along some of the more loyal officials, distinguished for their piety and faith, ordering that everything should be generously supplied through them to all: not only to the high priests and priests and those accompanying them, but also to all the needy who were flocking together from everywhere, since an unspeakable multitude was streaming there from practically the whole of the East for the dedication of the new Jerusalem. The divine altar too was adorned with imperial hangings and with treasures of gold set with precious stones.

The impious Arius arrived at Aelia on the day of the dedication with great eagerness, especially since he had heard that Athanasius would be absent from that feast, and he was gladly received by those of his own mind, that is, by the party of Eusebius of Nicomedia and Patrophilus of Scythopolis. But those who upheld the orthodox faith, on seeing Arius, turned away from him as from an abomination, drove him out of the church and ordered him to be expelled from the synod, decreeing that he should be heard at the synod in Alexandria, where he had also been condemned, just as, they say, our Christ-loving emperor Constantine had commanded. So, with the destroyer out of the way and the feast proving most peaceful and most splendid, the all-praised and most faithful emperor, on learning of the splendour and magnificence of the festival, was filled with the greatest delight and sang the highest praises to the Ruler of all good things, because he had granted him this request too. When the feast of the dedication had been so gloriously completed, most of the bishops went back to their own homelands, especially those who had not sat at the synod held in Tyre. But those of the faction of Eusebius of Nicomedia, all who together with him had embraced the pestilence of Arius, went back to Tyre with Eusebius himself and the other bishops, to wait there for their like-minded colleagues from the Mareotis.

Meanwhile the great Athanasius reached the imperial court, approached the most pious and God-beloved emperor Constantine, and told him the whole drama that had been dared against him. The most compassionate and kindly emperor Constantine was deeply grieved at heart by what had been dared against Athanasius and moved by the unjust judgement passed against him.
