And since Athanasius begged him, with tears above all, that both the accusers and the judges be summoned and that the trial be held anew before the pious emperor himself, the emperor sent a letter to those who had returned from Aelia to Tyre, informing them that Athanasius was with him and that they were to come to Constantinople as quickly as possible. What he wrote is as follows:

"Constantine the Victor, Greatest, Augustus, to the bishops who have reassembled at Tyre. I do not know what decisions your synod has reached amid such uproar and storm; but it seems that the truth has somehow been distorted by a disorderly confusion, evidently because, through your wrangling with your neighbours, which you wish to see undefeated, you do not perceive what is pleasing to God. But let it be the work of divine providence to scatter the evils of your contentiousness, or rather your malicious fighting, now that they have been plainly exposed, and to show us clearly whether, in coming together there, you took any thought for the truth, and whether you reached your decisions without any favour or hostility. I therefore wish all of you to come quickly to my Piety, so that you may present in person before me an exact account of what you have done. Why I have thought it right to write this to you and to summon you to me by letter, you will learn from what follows. Athanasius, the bishop of the church of Alexandria, the student of the divine law, is with me. As I was entering our eponymous and most blessed Constantinople, returning from a procession, he approached me in the middle of the highway with some others whom he had with him, mourning and lamenting, and he made his approach so suddenly that it gave me cause for astonishment. For God, the overseer of all, is my witness that at first sight I could not even recognize who he was, until some of my attendants, when we asked, told us who he was and the injustice he had suffered at your hands. We saw the man so humbled and downcast that we fell into unspeakable pity for him, realizing that he was that Athanasius whose holy appearance is enough to draw even the pagans to reverence for the God of all. Long ago certain wicked men, strangers to peace and concord, entangled him in no ordinary slanders, so that I myself was swept along by their elaborate deceit and was on the point of sinning against the man, had I not, moved by divine judgement, ordered him at that time to come quickly from Alexandria to the court of our Clemency. And so, when he had been examined by my Piety concerning the falsehoods dramatized against him, the man, standing before us, refuted the lies of the charges himself; and having been declared innocent of all of them, he was sent back by us to his homeland with the very greatest honour, restored in peace to the orthodox people under his guidance. But now he cries out that a second set of outrages, worse than the first, has been dared against him, and with greater boldness he asks nothing else of us but that you come to us, as he has asked to be granted, so that in your presence he may be able to lament what he has necessarily suffered. Since this seemed to us reasonable and fitting to the times, I ordered this letter to be written to you, so that all of you who made up the synod held in Tyre may hasten without delay to come to our court and show by your very deeds the purity and integrity of your judgement, namely by setting before me (for not even you would deny that I am truly a genuine servant of God) what you have decided [?]. For through my service to God everything everywhere is at peace, and most of the barbarian nations themselves now sincerely revere the name of God, nations which until now were ignorant of the truth. And it is clear that whoever is ignorant of the truth does not know God either. Nevertheless, as I have said, even the barbarians themselves have now, through me, the genuine servant of God, come to know God and have learned to revere him, since they have perceived from the facts themselves that he shields me and provides for me everywhere. This above all is how they know God, whom they revere out of fear of us; while we, who appear to champion (for I would not say to guard) the holy mysteries of his kindness, do nothing but what tends toward discord and hatred and, in a word, what leads to the ruin of the human race. But hasten to us quickly, as I have said, in the conviction that I will try with all my strength to ensure that in the law of God those things are kept especially unfailing to which neither blame nor any false belief can attach itself, once the enemies of the law of God have been scattered, utterly crushed and completely destroyed: those who, under the pretext of the holy name, put forward various and diverse blasphemies to deceive the simpler folk, longing as far as they can [to destroy] the purity of the catholic Church, which our Saviour keeps spotless, holy and blameless, having purchased it with his saving and precious blood, as his divine and unbreakable laws declare."

This letter threw those at the synod into anxiety, especially the party of Eusebius of Nicomedia. Those whom they had sent to the Mareotis, however, having written down falsehoods as truth and compiled a one-sided record of proceedings against the great Athanasius, reached the synod of the admirable bishops at Tyre before this imperial letter did. But not all of them accepted that forged record against Athanasius, full of those abominable slanders. Consequently most of them, having learned from the reading what the imperial letter contained, took fright and went back to their own sees. But the party of Eusebius of Nicomedia and Theognis and those with them lingered at Tyre for the time being, deliberately dragging out the time. They wrote to the pious emperor that they were being detained there against their will although they were eager to set out to him, and [they sent] the record of the forged proceedings [?]; but the most faithful emperor rejected it as an abomination and would not even consider accepting it, ordering the wicked men to come to him once and for all. Meanwhile, as they delayed (I mean the party of Eusebius), he sent Athanasius back to Alexandria with the very greatest honour, writing once again to the church of the Alexandrians that their bishop Athanasius had been falsely slandered and that his purity had shone out brightly in every respect. While Athanasius was in Alexandria, the matter of Arius came up, in accordance with the imperial orders and the decrees of the orthodox bishops who had assembled for the dedication in Jerusalem, to be dealt with by a synod. There was a great gathering of the multitude, and expectation hung on an outcome still in the balance, especially as everyone saw that what so many bishops of such standing had unanimously resolved and decided was being disturbed again. So when the divine Athanasius saw Alexandria and all Egypt in turmoil, he did not keep silent, but made the matter known by letter to the pious ears of the altogether excellent and God-beloved emperor.

When the emperor learned that Arius had once again been perverted, he ordered him to be summoned and brought to Constantinople to give an account of what he had dared to stir up again, and he wrote to him and to those with him a letter full of his indignation against them. But these men (Eusebius and Eutocius) were eager to bring Arius back into the Church. Divine justice, however, did not allow the enemy to dance in triumph over her temple and the bridal chamber within it, but sentenced him to end his life in a latrine, on the very day on which he and his partisans had determined to profane God's church and its holy things by his entrance. And his end was public, for the latrines were near the forum. He writes that Constantine the Great rejoiced at this, since the impartial Judge had settled every dispute by his verdict, and that he wrote letters to many people publicly denouncing the just death of Arius. That is what he says, agreeing in this with Athanasius the Great, Theodoret and many others; but some have seen fit to write that Arius was removed from among the living in this shameful way not in the time of Constantine the Great, but in the reign of his son Constantius.

The work ends with the death of Constantine the Great, at which he received the divine bath of forgiveness, washing away the stains of his life, which, being human, he would naturally have incurred. He says that Constantine received baptism with an orthodox minister initiating and performing the rite, and not, as some have supposed, at the hands of one of the heretics. The postponement of his baptism had been drawn out because he greatly desired to be baptized in the waters of the Jordan.
